Thi3 is the scene—a red ploughed field To the feet of spectator inclining: He can see in the furrows, here and there The mark of the plougiashltre shining. liter above, with his arms a-swing In the blue sky arching o'er him, One who walks straight down the field, Weaving his way before him. No other person is on the stage, He is the sole attraction; He comes and goeii, and comes and goes— That-is the whole of the actioit.•

' ACT lI.—THE SUN. Seene for the second act's just the same, But enters never a person: There's either a hitch, or behind the scenes The actors are busy rehearsin'. —They're all in the village below Drinking and debating! Provincial actors are so slow! And meanwhile the piece is waiting. No! there's an actor up in the air, He belongs to the GLOBE moreover; His part is easy, but acted well— It's only crossing over. He crosses, and Crosses, and crosses again; But there never enters a chap in.— What's this? The stage—it's turning:green ! something's going to happen!. ACT REAPERS. , The scene is a golden harvest field, And indeed there's's splenilidyield here; The village is left to the old folk to-day, The rest are all in the field here. The scythe and the sickle—how brightly they glance There are thirty people, and over,— Getters, and lifters, and bandsters, and bairns, The farmer on horseback, and Rover. There's movement and bustle, the swish of the scythe, Joking, and singing, and laughter And flirting and wooing the maidens among, And possible weddings thereafter! , Logie Robertson,in " Good Words" for May.

The key-note--" Wife, let me in!" Passing round the hat (says an, American humourist) is an old and excellent method of getting at the cents of the meeting. An advocate for cremation gar* as one,great point in its favour, that it saves many a dead person from being buried alive. "These apples are not fit for a hog to eat," said a kid- gloved dandy to an apple woman. "You just try one and see," she retorted. "What is the uie of a wooden coffin?" said an Irishman to his friend. "Sure it will decay very soon. Bedad, 1.11 have an iron one, and it will last me all my life!" - One poor bean told another that his new coat was too short for him. "True," answered he of the short skirts; "I assure you, however, it wilt be long enough before I get another." A doctor gave the following prescription for a sick lady a few days since :—"A 'new bonnet, a cashmere shawl, and a_pair of fashionable boots!" The lady recovered imme-

An Hibernian gentleman, when told by his nephew that he had lust entered college with a view to the Church, said, "I hope that I may live to hear you preach my funeral sermon." "Oujda" once asked Mr. Charles Reade what would be a good name to give her_new pet dog. The illustrious author at once answered, "Tonic," for it is sure to be a mixture of bark, steal, and whine." Mrs. Smith, triumphantly, "The hand that rocks the cradle is the hand that rules the world." Mr. Smith, cynically, "Yes, indeed, my dear; and that's why the world is se _

deuced badly governed." Al! pleasure must be bought at the price of pain; the difference between false pleasure and true is just this: for the true, the price is paid before you enjoy it; for the false, after you enjoy it.—Crohn Foster. "Is he honest?" Inquired a banker of a friend, who re- _ . _

commended a man for janitor. " Honest ?" he echoed. I don't know what you call it; but he returned a borrowed umbrella to me yesterday." The man was engaged as cashier. It takes twenty blows_ of a hammer in the hands of a woman to drive a tenpenny nail three inches. She misses the nail twice where she hits it once. How many blows does she strike in all, and how far can her voice be heard when she strikes her thumb? "William, my son," says an economical mother to her boy, "for mercy's sake don't keep on tramping up and down the floor in that manner. You'll wear out your new boots. (He sits down.) There you go—sitting down! Now you'll wear out your new trousers. I declare, I never gee such a boy !" A diner-out, who has had more than his share of the wine, is carefully feeling his way home at night, when he un- fortunately stumbles against the circular railing which surrounds a statue: After having gone round it about seven times the hopelessness of his situation flashes upon him , with vividness, and he sinks down upon the pavement out- side with a desnairing shriek, "The scoundrels, they've el, Shut me in here!" •ro. Prince Krapotkine, while staying in Geneva, observed zit, that wherever he went he was followed by a spy. His mind - was soon made up as to his course of action, and upon the first opportunity that presented itself he walked up to this man and dealt him a whack on the aide of the head that al- most felled him. "Here, my friend," the Nihilist Prince went on, putting a louis into his hand, "if you make any outcry this is the maximum amount that I shall be fined. You may as well have the money as the public treasufy. Take it. and whenever you want a loui3 come to me!" BERLIOZ' REGIMENT or CoLowni.s.—A wealthy country gentleman went to Berlioz, accompanied by his son, a young man of two-and twenty, who, by his own confession, could not read a note of music. "I am come to beg you, mon- sieur," he said, "to have the Foodness to give lessons in high composition (haute compontion) to this young man, who, I expect, will do you credit. His first idea was to be a colonel; but, in spite of the attractions of military glory, he decidedly prefers artistic fame. He thinks it better to be a great composer." "0, monsieur," Berlioz exclaimed, "you are making a sad mistake. If you only knew the mortificatiens nnd disappointments inseparable from that career! Great composers tear each other to pieces. And, besides, there are so many of them. In my opinion, your eon had much better stick to his first idea, and enter the regiment you just now named." "What regiment ?" "Par- bleu! the regiment of Colonels." " Monsieur, your plea- santry is quite uncalled for. I will not trouble you any longer. Happily, you are not the only music-master, and , consequently, even without your help, my son can still be a great composer. We have the honour to salute you."—Lent- don Society. FONDNESS OF THE GLADSTONE FAMILY FOR RFASONING.— Mr. John Gladstone liked that his children should exercise their judgment by stating the why and wherefore of every opinion they offered, and a college friend of William, who went en a visit to Fasque, in Kincardineshire, during the summer of 1829, furnishes amusing particulars of the family eustoms in that house, "where the children and their parents argued upon everything." "They would debate as to whether the trout should be broiled or boiled, whether a window should be opened, and whether it was likely to be fine or wet next day. It was all perfectly good-humoured, but curious to a stranger because of the evident care which all the disputants took to advance no proposition, even as to the prospect of rain, rashly. One day Thomas Gladstone knocked down a wasp with his handkerchief, and was about to crush it on the table, when the father started the question as to whether he had the right to kill the insect; and this point was discussed with as much seriousness as if a human life had been at stake. When at last it was adjudged that the wasp deserved death because he was a trespasser in the drawing-room, a common enemy and a danger there it was fouod that the insect had crawled from under the handker- chief, and was flying away with a sniggering sort of buzz, as if to mock them all."—Temple Bar. Borrow MEDIUMS.—One gentleman told me how he, lace _ . ourselves, a total stranger in Boston, had, from the merest curiosity, sought an interview with a medium, selected quite at random. She at once proceeded, unasked, and greatly to his distress, minutely to describe his dead father and brother, and other kinsfolk who had passed over to "the majority." Anxious to tern her attention from topics Which he felt to be at once too sacred and too painful to be touched upon under such circumstances, he asked if she could give him any particulars concerning an absent friend. He gave her no clue whatever to the person of whom he was thinking; and, much to his astonishment, she almost immediately proceeded to describe him, and the room in which he was sitting • also two ladies who were present— one elderly and gray-haired, who sat in a corner of a sofa, the other young and handsome, a Spanish-looking girl, with glossy raven-black hair. The gentleman was sitting at the piano. When asked whose music he was playing, the medium replied, "His own." She was asked his name, and replied that she could not tell till she heard it mentioned. Soon afterwards she mentioned a very uncommon name by which he was very rarely addressed, and said it was the name by which the gray-haired lady called him. She then added his surname. A few days later our traveller returned to the town where his friend lived, and made a point of going to see him as soon as possible. He inquired where he had been the previous 'week. His friend replied that he had been absent, but had been obliged to return unex- pectedly on a certain day (the very day in question). "Who had he found on his return?" " Only his motner. "No one else?" "Oh, yes; late in the afternoon Miss chanced to arrive." (Then the accuracy of the medium was undoubted. Her description of therhandsome Spanish- looking girl, with glossy raven-black hair, exactly answered to the lady in question.) "And what were they all doing at aunset "Nothing special. He was playing the piano, and they were listening." "Whose music was he playing?" "Oh, he was improvising." "Might he see the room in which they were sitting?" "Why, certainly." So he led the way to a room exactly answering to that described by 'the medium, and the gray-haired mother pointed out the corner of the sofa which was her accustomed seat in the _ _ _ _
twilight , and the chair occupipd by the dark-haired girl; and the picture wal recognised as being altogether accurate. Bloclocood's Maya:ine" for !Kay.

div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Nature gives the following extract from Mr. Raphael Meldola's paper on "Darwin and Modern Evolution— "Mr. Wallace has narrated to me that one of his coTrres- pondents, a well-known entomologist, wrote to say that it, was a general remark in natural history circles, with respect to the paper, that it was much to be regretted that the author had .not, more confined himself to statements of facts." The paper thus referred to was the epoch-making communication to the Linnman Society of the theory of natural selection! Some twenty years ago therevas a fire at Sherburn Hos- pital, near Durham, and the brass from the grave of Thomas Lever, which then disappeared; has only recently been re- covered. It was lately "presented," as we learn from the Athenceunt, to St. John's College, Cambridge, and by the authorities of that place very properly restored to -its origi- nal place. Lever was a Lancashire man by birth, and his sermons, which have been reprinted by Mr. Archer, are in- teresting and vigorous specimens of the pulpit oratory of

*id liefornaatio.n. M. Pasteur has replied to the Turin critics of his anthrax vaccination method. He argues that instead of taking the virus for cultivation from an animal just deed of splenic fever, the Italian experimentalists did not take the virus until 24 hours after death. , Hence the ." cultivations" in- cluded septic germs, and the inoculated animals, whose deaths-are attributed by the Italian professors t 6 the White of Pasteur's method, really died of septiecemia. As already announced, Pasteur has offered to go to Turin and perform the experiments himself. The confidence of Pasteur and his followers is significant., In a recent communication to the French Academy of Sciences, Captain Treve suggested a means of diminishing the risks-of steam boiler explosions. The suggestion rests upon the fact that water deprived of air passes into a state of vapour less easily than under normal circumstances. Hence water which has been boiled over-night over low fires sufficiently to expel the air contained may become over-heated when the fires are built up ,in the morning without steam being formed. When in such a condition any cause should happen to form a surface of evaporation, steam will be rapidly produced at high tension in sufficient quan- tity to burst the boiler. Captain Trey° proposes to intro- duce a T-shaped tube into the boiler, through which air could be injected into exhausted water. GREENLAND EXPLORATION.—Professor Nordenskjold in- tends to explore the interior of Greenland during the summer. The Swedish Government will place the steamer Sofia at his disposal, and Oscar Dickson, of Gothenburg, will supply the funds. Professor Nonlenskjold believes the interior of the country to be partly free from ice during summer, Whereas it has hitherto generally been supposed to be a huge plain of ice. He, base his opinion on the fact that winds which croAthe island exhibit greater warmth and dryness after they have passed the inland tracts. The Sofia is to leave Gothenburg on May 20th, and to pick up the celebrated traveller on the Scotch coast. Then it will make for Anleitsivik Fjord, on the 'West Coast of Green- land. Nordenskjold will be accompanied by three or four naturalists, and by Wilhelm Schoenlanck a Berlin mer- _ chant. _

NEws FROM AIITSSINIA.—An interesting account has been published by the African traveller, Gerhard Rolalfs,'of his mission to Abyssinia, undertaken at the command of the German Emperor, as whose Envoy to the Negus Negesti Johannes, the now reigning Emperor of Abyssinia, he acted. Gerhard Rolairs, starting from Missowa, on the 'coast of the Red Sea, and touching the Egyptian frontier, had to en- counter many hardships on his journey, notwithstanding his knowledge of the country and people acquired in accona- panYing the British Expedition to Abyssinia. His way led over high mountains in comparison :with which the Swiss Alps appear insignificant hills, and through towns and vil- lages still suffering from the last war. Enormous ruins of old castles, monasteries, and churches are described by him, as well as. the huts of the people on the road:Having reached the capital,`Rohlfs presented on a cushion of blue velvet the Emperor William's letter, written on parchment with much caligmphic art. The Negus accepted it with a joy re- sembling that of a child receiving a new toy, and then be- gan at once to ask a series of questions. Confused ideas were entertained by the Negus regarding the extent of power of the several European countries.. Greece he con- sidered as the first power of the world, because according 'to his opinion, it had compelled Russia to make peace with Turkey after the last war. Great Britain and France ap- peared to the Negus as States of minor importaiice. The German Envoy was silent, as the Negus's question was in- terpreted to ihim, whether Germany and Russia together were as powerful as Greece. Rohlfs gives the people a good moral character, and states that they have generally a desire for improvement. He further says that a very perceptible amelioration of the condition of the people has taken place since the overthrow of Theodore by the British troops. . .

CHEAP Gas LIGHT.—Very few know that the light given by an ordinary gas burner can be greatly increased by simply turning the burner over sideways until it slopes slightly downwards. The flames is thrown out as a hori- zontal sheet formed into a saucer-shape by the natural curling up of the edges. -Mr. Fletcher' of Warrington, who is evidently imbued with the idea that he will not only save trouble by utilising gas as a fuel, but also is never con- tent without a very large sixpennyworth of work for six- pence, has been testing the difference in duty obtained by an average upright and a horizontal saucer-shaped flame, and finds it averages by photometer about 10 per cent. in favour of the latter, but owing to the fact that with his position of flame the light is thrown downwards and is per- fectly free from shadow, the actual results in his own woiks and offices have proved that a burner consuming five cubic feet per hour with a hsrizontal flame giles a better light and is better for work than an upright flame consuming six cable feet per hour. It is, in fact, somewhat of an ap- proach to the principle of Siemens' regenerative burner with the advantage of costing nothing. This is not new to ex- perts, but it is a bit of useful information to the public, who may by this means eitheOncrease their light or reduce their gas bills without any expense. It is something to make a little profit or effect a little economy now-a-days without having first to put one's hand in one's pocket. Our better halves will probably still adhere to the wasteful glass globe and upright flame, which make'our living rooms so unpleasantly close; but there are millions of burners in offices and works which can be simply turned over to the advantage and profit of the users. The improvement is I easy to demonstrate without any cost whatever, and no I doubt thousands will profit by the hint. No advantage is I gained over a large and perfect upright flame regulated to very low pressures the real action of the change of position being that the excessive pressure invariably given in the mains is neutralised by turning the flame downwards, and the rush of air causing the gas to be over-burnt is pre- vented.—Mechanical World. EYESIGHT OF SCHOOL CHILDREN.--A lecture OR the effect of reading and writing on the eyesight of young children was recently given at Berne by Professor Pfliiger. The lecturer first called attention to the portentous fact that more than one-half of 45,000 children lately examined I in Germany were found to be suffering from defective I vision. In some schools the proportion of the short-sighted ; was as high as 70 to 80 per cent, whilst in the Heidelberg Gymnasium every lad in the school had bad eyesight. This lamentable state of things arose from insufficiently lighted schoolrooms, bad print, and bad paper, the method of writing in voiue, and ill-contrived desks and forms. The burdening of children with too many lessons, and the con- sequent restriction of their hours of play, is a still incre potent cause of defective vision. In order to solve the vexed question of the influence of German caligraphv on the eyes of those who adopt it, the Government of Wiirtem- burg, some time ago, appointed a Commission, consisting of three scho3lmasters and three physicians, to investigate the matter, and make a report. In the opinion of these gentle- men, the mere writing is least among the causes which un- favourably affect children's eyesight. They found that, while comparatively few children write with their backs bent towards the left, fully 80 per cent, give their back, when writing, a right inclination. The latter position tends to produce a permanent elevation of the right shoulder, and ultimately caused curvature of the spine. In the schools they visited, the Commissioners actually found 20 per cent, of the boys, and from 30 to 40 per cent. of the girls, suffering from more or less pronounced curva- ture due to this cause. The difference between the two sexes is probably due to the fact that lads, besides being more energetic in play, are more rationally clad than girl scholars. As to position in writing, the distance between the desk and the eyes ought to be about 25 centimetres, yet it was rarely, indeed, that the Commissioners met with any children who could keep their eyes at this, the normal distance, from the paper. Many of them found it neces- sary to bring their faces within seven centrimetres (211 inches) of their copy-books. The general conclusion of the Commissioners, as of Professor Pfliiger, is that of all the evils enumerated, the worst, and those most in need of re- form, are the seats and desks at present in use. The Pro- fessor further remarked that only 10 per cent, of the chil- dren examined were naturally shortsighted, and that, as among wild races defective vision is almost entirely un- known, the trouble in question is peculiar to modern civi- lization and the existing system of teaching. Professor Pfliiger expressed the fear that he was like one crying in the wilderness, the prevailing tendency being to lay on thel children of this generation still heavier burdens, and to force their minds to the lasting injury of their bodies.— British Medical Journal.

DERANGEMENTS OF VISION.—In the February of 1837, a labourer had a severe fall upon the ice and was removed in an insensible condition to his home. Returning to consciousness, he complained of a slight pain in the right super-orbital region, where the blow caused a tumour to arise equal in size to a closed fist. Both the pain and swelling disappeared in two days, and on the fourth day he returned to his work. But he soon found himself unable to cticulate distances, tumbling over things which seemed to be some distance from him, and omitting to descend steps down which he fell because he thought he had not reached them. An object within a foot of him appeared to be six feet or more away, and a man forty paces off had the ap- pearance of being distant about a quarter of a German mile. Colour and form he perceived accurately enough in objects ' which he believed he was near, but those which he was ac- tually near, but which he conceived to be distant, had their forms less distinct and their colours faint. By closing the left eye objects were made to appear, as they actually were, near or distant; but they retreated immediately when lie opened it, and after looking at them some time" their out- lines became doubled, worm-like spectra began to appear ' with moving lines, and his ideas becrne strangely confused. grew thew g isad dnyi Closing ng he the left experiencedeye immediately a tingling uncomfortable effects. The only outward sign of deranged vision was a slight squint in the left eye when it was turned upwards.—The World of Wonders.

47:Mr. Robert Bayles, of Barton, has a Sow which has had three litters of pigs within twelve months, making a total of 49 pigs. The employment of cocoa meal in the rations of French cavalry horses has produced such satisfactory results that the practice Will be continued permanently. A. cow belonging to Mr. William Stanbury, of Torrington, Devon, has given birth to three bull calves, all of which are livisg and iell. The cow has somewhat suffered from the effects of the treble birth, but appearklikely to do well. CURIOUS LAMBING FREAK.—A few weeks ago a ewe on a farm at the higher part of Grange presented her owner with a fine lamb, which performance she repeated three weeks afterwards. ' Both lambs were fine healthy ones, aid are doing well. Fowls do not like to scratch in their own manure: Ad- vantage may be taken of this fact to keep them from 1 scratching up seeds sown in the garden, If the droppings I of the hen roost are scattered over freshly-planted beds, the fowls will scratch eliewhere. The rain and cultivation will soon carry the fertility given by the manure where roots can reach it. .

The Agricultural Society of the department of the'Tarn is proving itself a benificent aid to the agriculturists of that department, by obtaining the newest and most approved machinery at reduced prices from the manufacturers, and disposing of them to farmers for four-fifths of the cost, on condition that the machines ate actually used by the pur- chaser, or otherwise let out for two years. HARVEST- IN NEW ZNALAND,—A gentleman who is a native of Milbutn,,Westmorland, writes from New Zealand that, the harvest there has been a niost successful one. Wheat crops mostly forty bushels, many fifty and sixty per acre; prices fair, 4s. 2d. per 601bs. Already twice as much has gone into port in a fortnight than was shipped last sea- son. Last year £300,000 worth was swept awayky one wind in Canterbury. The Eastbourne magistrates having sentenced a shepherd to fourteen days' hard labour for beating a dog which Was

hunting his master's sheep, a meeting ol flock-masters was held at Lewes on Tuesday to protest against the decision. A rojolation condemning the sentence was passed, and the chairman of the meeting was requested to send it to the Home Secretary. The sum of £l2 was collected for pre- sentation to the shepherd. Gmtnwsticaa Sonocrts IN FRANCE.-Throughout France gardening is practically taught in primary and elementary schools. Each of these (28,000) schools has a garden attached, and is under the care of a master capable of im- • parting a knowledge of the first principles of horticulture. Even in schools to which no garden is attached, the theory of cultivation is taught, but it has been recently decided by the Minister of Public Instruction that the number of school gardens shall be largely increased, and that no one phall be appointed master of an elementary school unless he can prove himself capable of giving practical instruction , in the culture of the soil.—British industries. THE PREMIER TENANT-RIGHT.—At a recent meeting of the Wirral Farmers' Club, resolutions were passed in favour of giving agriculturists compensation for unexhausted im- provements, the abolition of the Law of Distress, the amendment of the Ground Game Bill, absolute freedom of ,cropping with compensation to landlord in case of damage, and notice to quit to be in no case less than 12 months. These resolutions were forwarded to Mr. Tollemache, M.P., for presentation to the Premier. Mr. Gladstone has acknowledged their receipt, and adds that he has not failed to take notice of the club's representations, and refers the members on the entire subject to the announcement in the Queen's Speech and in Parliament. MIXING SWEET AND SOUR MILL—It is of pecuniary importance to those engaged in the creamery business to know that the extensive practice of mixing sweet and sour cream, just before churning, not only results in the produc- tion of a poorer quality of butter, but in a diminished yield. Sweet and sour cream of the same quality yield the same per cent. of butter when churned separately. But it is not so when they are mixed. The acid in the sour cream does not have immediate effect in weakening the membranes en- closing the butter, as has been frequently supposed. And hence, by mixing, the per cent. of globules of sweet cream that would have otherwise been broken is greatly dimi- nished by a diminished time in churning. It may be sur- prising to know that the difference in yield of batter be- tween allowing mixed cream to stand twenty-four hours and churning immediately, is proximately five per cent. in favour of the former.

-"Lovz ME, Love MY Resmrs."—The Squire of Pea. more is fond of peafowl. Whether or not he is a devoted follower of the late Lord Beaconsfield I am unable to tell; but a report in the Western Times states that this Devon- shire landlord is in the habit of keeping these beautiful, but exceeding mischievous, birds in extraordinary numbers on his estate. He has, too, a liking for another mischievous animal, the rabbit. Now, strange though it may be, the Squire's tenant, Mr. Baker, who occupied the home fatal, was less esthetic than Mr. Kekewich, and he ventured to object to the peafowl, said only to be half-fed, getting their living on his crops. Still more strongly did he object to the rabbits, which were allowed to increase so greatly that, it is reported, Mr. Baker lost MOO by them in one field. Mr. Baker complained, and asked for compensation, and as he appears to have paid the very satisfactory rent of £5OO for 240 acres, it may be admitted that he had some right to expect to reap his own crops instead of feeding his land- lord's peafowl and rabbits on them. The result of his com- plaining was that he received a six months' notice to quit, and his sale was held the other day. As Mr. Baker was an excellent farmer, it can easily be believed that, as the farmers at the sale estimated, he leaves £5OO on the farm in the form of unexhausted manures and improvements, for which he does not get a penny. Great sympathy was ex- pressed for him, and his fellow parishioners are full of re- gret at losing him from among them after a residence of 50 years on the farm.—Mark Lane Express. A HEREFORD SHORTHORN CROSS.—The following letter from a North of England breeder of cattle has appeared in the columns of a contemporary; it was addressed to a breeder of Herefords, but the names are not given :-- " Having some three years ago bought some Hereford cattle from you, I think you might like to know that they have done remarkaioly well ,• though I find it takes a long time to make a name as a Hereford breeder. At the same time

that I bought the Herefords from you I purchased ten Yorkshire dairy cows—Shorthorns—from Mr.Gothorp, near Bedale, in Yorkshire, and after these cows had calved I was determined to try a cross of the two breeds, which I did by using a Hereford ball I bought from you on the shorthorn cows; the result was beyond my expectation. I reared the calves on skim milk, &c.; they had a little cake till they were six months old, when they took their luck ; at 18 months old I gave them 41b. each per day when grazing (this would be in September last) ; on the 12th of October I put them up to feed, giving them 81b. of cotton and lin- seed cake mixed, and 61b. of meal with pulp each per day. The week before Christmas I sold two of them, averaging £2l 10s. each, and also some shorthorn bullocks, which I

had bought from the same Mr. Gothorp ; these latter were three months older, and only realised £l9 158. per head, though similarlv fed. In the second week of January I sold some more of the cross-bred bullocks (they were then 23 months old), and they averaged £24 ss. 6d. per head, and the remaining shorthorn bullocks averaged £22 17s. per head, being, as the others, three months older. I cer- tainly am of opinion that the bullock obtained by this cross is better than the pure-bred shorthorn for the quick production of beef. I have also some heifers of this cross about to calve, and they carry plenty of flesh, and promise to make equally as good milkers as their dams. I have written this as I consider the result of the cross satisfactory, especially on poor, cold clay soil."

One of the most notable coantry seats is mentioned by Lady Dufferin in her ballad commencing "I'm sitting on the stile, Mary !" TARING A LIBERTY WITH FOOTR.—In the winter of 1774-5 Mr. McCulloch visited his country mansion of Ard- well (near Gatehouse in Kirkcudbright), which is still pos- sessed by his descendants, in order to be present at an elec- tion, together with a friend named Mouat. After a week or two they set out on their return to Edinburgh, Mr. McCul- loch bringing with him his infant son, familiarly known as "Wee Davie," and the trio, after quitting Dumfries, were compelled by a snowstorm to tarry at Moffat for the night. Early next morning they departed in a chaise with four horses from the King's Arms Inn, at the same time that two strangers did so in another vehicle and with difficulty amid the drifted snow they all reached the summit of Erick- stane Brae, a lofty hill at the head of Clydesdale, along the side of which, above a most perilous declivity, the public road passes. Further progress being impossible, a consul- tation was held, and they all resolved to return to Moffat ; but, as wheeling the carriage round proved a dangerous operation, "Wee Davie" was wrapped up and laid on the snow till that was accomplished, and after reaching the inn Ardwell discovered that his two companions were Samuel Foote, the celebrated player, and another favourite son of Thalia. On reaching the inn, Foote entered it in no good humour—as he walked with difficulty, having lost a leg— and ordered breakfast, while his luggage was taken off the chaise; and after this was done, he found a written paper affixed to the panel. In some anger he demanded, "What rascal has been placarding this ribaldry on my carriage?" Then pausing, however, he read the following lines : While Boreas his flaky storm did guide, Deep covering every hill o'er Tweed and Clvee, The North-wind god spied travellers seeking way„ Sternly he cried "Return your steps, I say; It not one foot, 'tis my behest, profane The sacred snows which lie on Erickstane " I should like to know who wrote that," exclaimed Foote, with a smiling face; "be he who he may he is no mean hand at an epigram." Ardwell came forward to apologise for his fun. "My dear sir," said Foote, "no apology is necessary; I am fine game for every one, and I take any one for game when it suits me." So an intimacy began which proved to be a lasting one, and the parties now joined at table, as they had to do for twenty days, till the storm abated, the snow cleared away, and they were enabled to end their journey at Edinburgh.—Front "' Cassell's Old and New Edinburgh" for May. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

A Melbourne despatch, dated March 28, says the Premier of Queensland had publicly anhounced that' his Govern- ment intended taking possession of such portions of New Guinea "as were not cLiined by the Dutch." Tbe Princess Dolgorouki, the morganatic widow of the late CzAr, has arrived in Paris. with her children, and is staying at the Hotel d'Albe, in the Champs Elysee, where she will remain for a few weeks.

The rebels against the Government of Ecuador having estiblished themselves in the neighbourhood of-the city of Guayaquil, the Government officers .in that city have thought proper to rob the safes of the( Bank of Ecuador. No explanation of the act of plunder is given, but the officials probably desired to "make ct purse for themselves before the rebels entered."

A considerable number of Maofies, including a "chief, have been sentenced to imprisonment by the Supreme Court of New Zealand for attacking a Government surveying ex- pedition. The prisoners were followers of the "King" Te Whiti. The affair appears to have been rather serious. It is satisfactory to see that thp more influential chiefs sup- ported the Government authbrities. -;

A telegram from Cairo infoims us that the claims allowed by the Indemnity Coultniseion ip till the sth inst, reached a totaF of about £BOO,OOO. The number oi krigiish ciaima allowed is 210, the' 3 inount a*arded being £16,400, which is £2,300 less than was claimed. There were 145 Italian claim 9, in satisfaction of which a sum of £9,300 has been awarded, this being £1,400 less than was claimed. In all 1,876 claims haye been settled.

• CHARGE AGAINST A BEIAHLE FINANCIER.--N. Philip- part, the well-known Belgian financier, was on Monday morning surrendered by the French authorities •to the Brussels police on a charge of forgery. M. Philippart has been etayinz in France for some time past, and his extradi- tion wasoriginally demanded On a charge of falsifying the honks of a.public company with which he had been con- nected. He denied the charge and successfully resisted the demand for his extradition. He was subsequently accused of forgery, whereupon be expressed his willingness to meet his acensera, and wrote to the Minister of Justice in Paris requesting that the fresh demand for his extradition shou!d be acceded to. This has been done, and the judicial pro- ceedings against M. Philippart will be commenced forth- with. They promise to develop into a cause cilebre.

Tit Eye AND RECOVERY OF JRWELLS.—A New York tele- I gram in the Standard says :—Franz Kramer, of 330, Rue St. Honore,. Paris, entrusted a quantity of jewellery, vAlued $lOO,OOO, to a young EnAishman, named James Henry Marriott, to dispose of. It is stated that Marriott tried to pawn some of the jewels in London; but being afraid of arrest he fled, leaviug some of them behind.. - He came to America, where he was arrested. His companion Marie Pereux, surrendered, and handed over a pair of earrings of thirty-one carats. On their lodgings being searched, the authorities found concea!ed in a seal muff a 36-carat soli'aire and in the man's trousers pocket 24'magnificient loose stones, besides a necklace with 56 brilliants, jewelled bracelets, watches and sprays. One of the gems was estimated to be worth $50,000. When collected together the jewels fairly covered the police serjeant's desk. Marriott was held by the authorities to be liable to the charge nf bringing stolen goods within the State, and on being handed over, was placed on board the steamer Britannic, which sailed on Saturday for England. _ _

THE FENIANS- IN AMERICA —Alarm has been created in Halifax by a report current there alleging that the Lieu- tenant Governor of Nova• Scotia had received a letter warn- ing him of the expected visit of two suspicious American vessels, and recommending him to take measures to protect life and property. It is stated that the Governor admits having received a warning letter, but refuses to divulge its contents or what' precautionary measures will be taken. Other rumours on the same subject assert that vessels manned by Fenians have left Boston for Halifax preyided with torpedoes and other explosives to be used for tile des- truction of the shipping in the harbour. It is added that the authorities have been warned to be particularly watch- ful on the 14th inst., the data fixed for the execution of the Phcenix Park murderers. The watch has been strengthened on board Her Majesty's corvette Tenedos, and sentries have been stationed at various points of the city. The story "awaits confirmation. "Roses and his followers have formed an "Irish Revolutionary Brotherhood" for the promotion of the cause of Irish independence by the means lately' dis- cloSed in Birmingham and London. A VISIT TO KARS.—A correspondent of the Daily News, who has very recently visited Kars, sends a description of that famous city under Russian rule. The Turks, as we know, did nothing for Kars; they did not even place it in a passable state of defence. The correspondent states that upon Kars itself the Russian Government has spent nearly a million sterling during the last five years on public build- ings and road making in and about the town. The local government has also founded a college and one or two schools, at which Armenian pupils are in the majority. The correspondent questioned the Armenian Archbishops, among others, as to the general condition of Kars before and after the war. The prelate replied at first that the Armenians had exchanged one kind of governmental severity for another. He meant the weight of Russian taxation. But he admitted after a while that the com- paratively heavier taxation was, under the circumstances, the unavoidable accompaniment of a stronger, more just, and more progressive administration. There is a steady immigration of the more industrious population in Turkish Armenia, and no one complains of corrupt law courts or ruinous delays in the administration of justice, the two fatal evils of legal administration in the Turkish- provinces. The correspondent says that the reports of the augmentation and concentration of the Russian troops on the frontier are quite without foundation.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. Lord Justice Deasy, of the Mak Court of Appeal, died on Sunday night. The deceased judge was Solicitor-General for Ireland in 1859, and Attorney-General in 1860. In the following year he was made Baron of the Exchequer, when he quitted Parliament, in which he had sat for Cork for six years. On Saturday night a man named Kinsella surrendered and self-coufessed that he murdered Lord Leitrim. He worked at Inchicare works, but he states that he murdered Lord Leitrim in the Co. Wicklow, whereas the murder took place in the Co. Donegal. He is at present a pauper in tbe South Dublin Union. The belief is that he is Nnother Westgate. Since Mr. Curran has commenced his second inquiry into the Stephenite party, the Council party, and the Viailance party, it is reported that no less than 200 men, some of good position, have left the city. He summoned within the last 10 days about nine persons to give evidence, bat in all cases the summonses were returned with the announcement that the parties had left the country. The Freeman's Journal prints under the head "A Mys- tery Unravelled" a statement which will scarcely be sur- prising to people who have watched the course of recent events. The dynamite plot, says the Freeman, was betrayed to the British Consul in New York, and the police at home were put in possession of the names of the conspirators and all the particulars of their mission before they landed in England. The Freeman thinks that a member of the go- verning council of the conspirators alone could have fur- nished information so great and so extensive. THE IMPRISONMENT 00 MESSRS. HEALY AND DAVITT.— On Taesilay Mr. Healy, M.P., and Mr. Davitt, the founder of the Land League, completed three mouths of the sen- tence of six months' imprisonment in Richmond Gaol, Dublin, for using seditious language and failing to find eecu- rides to be of good behaviour. Some surprise has been ex- pressed that no questions have been asked or attention in any way called to their case in Parliament ; but it is said to be their desire that no appeal, direct or indirect, should he made on their behalf. Their quarters in gaol are com- fortable, and they make no complaint. Evidence was taken in Dublin on Saturday upon the claim for £lO,OOO compensation made by Mr. Field, the juror who was grievously assaulted in that city last November. It was stated that Mr. Field was completely shattered in body and mind, and that as soon as his claim was settled he intended to give up his business, which was worth about £4OO a year. Counsel for the Corporation of Dublin argued that the "innocent ratepayers" were also entitled to " some compensation and mercy," and Viat the award. ought to be

, as moderate as the circumstances would allow. The evidence will be reported to the Lord Lieutenant, whose decision will be published in due course. THE ADDITIONAL REVELATION IT DITBLIN.—SyIVeSter Kingston, James Gibney, and Thomas Healy have been again charged on remand at the Dublin Police Court on the charge of conspiracy to murder Joseph Poole and others. The only witness examined was William Lamle, and he did not contribute many new facts to those previously supplied by Robert Farrell. In explaining the division of the Fenians into Stephenites and Councilites he said that the split took piece in consequence of Poole falling out with Curley, who was the centre of the Council party. James Burne was the centre of the Stephenites until about two and a half years ago, when he was succeeded by Poole. Altogether there were ten centres, and when it was decided to form a " Vi2i- lance," each centre nominated two men to that body. Sylvester Kingston was the chairman of the Vigilance, of whose proceedings, however, Lamle did not know much. Its first business seems to have been to consider Poole's charge against Kenny, and when Kenny was killed Poole reported the fact to Lamie, and told him that when stabbed Kenny cried out, "Oh, Joe, Joe." At the close of Lamie's cross•examinatiou the prisoners were again remanded.

A STRANGE SUICIDE. - On Tuesday, James Daniels, engine-tenter at Blundell's Queen's Pit, Pemberion, ne.ir Wigan, committed suicide by hanging. The deceased lowered the men and boys down to work in the morning at the colliery and then went home. Shortly afterwards he was found banging by his pocket handkerchief from a vas bracket near the kitchen fireplace. The deceased had formerly been addicted to drink, but for the last two years had been a total abstainer. He leaves a widow and seven children.

A PREDICAMENT. On Friday, at the St. Helens Police Court, Jos. Tideswell, keeper of the Town Hall, was charged with having allowed a chimney to be on fire. It was stated that defendant had before been fined for a similar offence in regard to the same chimney. Mr. Tideswell, however, in defence, said this particular chimney was so constructed that it could not be got at by the sweep, and, although he had brought the matter before the Parliamentary Commit- tee, they would not get it put right, and what was he to do ? —The Bench said they had no option but to fine him, and a fine of is and costs was imposed. It is &can in we. All furs wGolens should be well powdered before putting away.. Be. ware of imitations.—Advt,

div.head: COTTAGE GAROENING
div.p: COTTAGE GAROENING

BEETROOT.—Most people enjoy this vegetable when set before them, and it must be admitted that it is a valuable adjunct to the cold meat dinner, ar.d by pickling some may be conserved for use during the summer. It is more whole- some and nutritious than red catbage and other pickles. The beet prefers light soil as a rule, but we have seen splen- did crops produced on stiff soils. Much depends on its quality, and the varieties, though all are good in their way. We have seen vigorous growers, such as Cattell's Blood-red, on rich heavy soil, grow in a moist season more like mall mangold wurtzell, whilst on rich light soil it has possessed all the good qualities of a beetroot. Dell's Black-leaved variety, on the other hand, is a smaller variety. Trough- ton's Crimson is intermediate, and if the cottager will only consult the soil of the garden he can select what will suit it from either of these three. The soil must be loosened 18in. deep, and should have been n2anured for a previous crop; 12in. to 15in. is usually the distance allowed between the rows, and if the seeds are dropped an inch apart it will allow for selection at the time of thinning. In the vicinity of towns the sparrows are great enemies to these. Where such has been proved the case, we would advise that the , roots be protected. LErrucE.—A sowing of these may be made now; bearing in rainj that small and frequent sowings are preferable to A glut at one time and none another, Amongst thi cos, we have found nOne better foi kill:1111er Chan the LOndon Giant 'White, and the Alexandra. Amongst the cabbage varieties, •Drumhead or Malta and Neapolitan may be selected. Scarcely too much manure can be given to these. The rain , has made it a perilous time for these and similar subjects. During the dry weather slugs had not been able tb travel even at a- snail's pace. A dry surface proves to be un- favourable to their movements, and seldom has their, num- ber been so few at this time of the year; but the' cottager must look 'out now, or they will assuredly steal a march on him.
POTATOES.— We see the earliest planted just coming through the ground, and, as we are not safe from frost, we shall draw soil sufficient to cover them over.

CELERY will now require pricking out, and if the plants have to be purchased, we would select to have them now and nurse them, in preference to getting them at planting-out time, more especially if they have to be. procured from a distance. At that time celery suffers severely if exposed to drought, which it must necessarily do in transit. Another disadvantage in having plants of -large size from a distance is that the travelling, packing, and unpacking cause most of the soil that would otherwise adhere to the roots to be removed from them. The consequence will be that they will hang_ down their heads for days, which is a serious drawback.

Tsr FRowr GARDEN.—Now that all the occupants of this have developed themselves, there is apparently a great want of taste in arrangeknent. We would therefore urge that the subject should engross a larger share of the cot- tager's attention. In the first place note should be made of the colour of all bulbous plants, with the view. of disposing of them in a Uniform manner at the proper time, and not have two or three of a variety crowded in one spot, and another not very dissimilar in proximity to them-. Yellow and white should always be separated by a colour that will create a contrast. The height of plants should also be taken into consideration. Short ones should always occupy front ranks. A little study and forethought in this direction would alter the somewhat chaotic condition of many a front garden. We notice the following plants in, flower at pre- sent, some gardens having scarcely more than two or three varieties instead of as many dozens :—Odd plants of wall- flowers, polyanthus, auriculas, violas, primroses, few hyacinths and tulips, double daisies, Arabia Albida or the Sicilian rock cress, anemone. Even these, if planted with a little taste, would make many a garden look gay. Those who prefer grass plots to flowers in front of their houses should see to the cutting of the grass. When left long, as we have recently seen some, there is much iniury done; the weaker kind of grass is destroyed by the stronger being allowed to smother it. When the grass is cut the surface will have for some days a bleached appearance, which in dry, sunny weather is changed from yellowish white to brown, a state of things by no means desirable. Why, then, is it left until higher than one's shoes? THE WlNnow.—ln our remarks on potting in a previous issue, we got to the point at which the plant was ready to be transferred into its new pot, which should be 2in. larger than the one it is in, so as to allow a supply of soil to be placed all round it. To turn the plant out, spread out the fingers of the right hand over the surface of the soil in pot, allowing the stem Of the plant to pass between the second and third fingers; take hold of the pot with the left hand, still keeping the right as stated, and with a combined action invert the plant, tap the edge of the pot gently on a solid base, such as a firm table or window-sill, and it Will slip out of its pot, soil and all, and will be a model of the interior of the pot. ,If the soil is not well permeated by roots, place the pot on again, for it has still something to feed upon; on the other hand, if the roots are well matted, remove any crocks or other material that may have been placed as drainage, turn the plant into its natural position, and having satisfied yourself by measurement that the base of the, plant and the depth in the pot correspond, allowing at least one inch for room to water, drop the plant gently in,

. . guiding it with both hands, with the fingers spread all round so as to clip the whole. Fix the plant perpendicular, and in the centre of the pot, fill the surrounding space with soil, pressing it slightly with a blunt, pointed stick, or a flat one an inch wide and half an inch thick; fill up to an inch of the rim of the pot.

'Twas ever so—to owe is human, to pay divine. Electricity in Franklin's time was a wonder, but ive now make light of it. Crime, small and great, can only be truly stayed by edu- cation; not the education of the intellect only, which is on I some men wasted, and for others mischievous, but education I for the heart, which is alike good and necessary for all. To-day is not yesterday. We ourselves change. How can our works and thoughts, if they are always to he the fittest, continue always the same? Change, indeed, is painful, yet very needful; and if memory have its force and worth, so also has hope.—Carlyle. A racy story is told of an old lady who refused to be comforted by her pastor's assurance that when he left the Lord would send a better pastor as his successor. "Na, na " she said, "1 hae seen fourteen changes in the ministers since I attended the kirk, and every ane has been waur than anither."

A Spanish magistrate, shocked and exasperated by repeated proof of the adulteration of food in his district, has issued a proclamation aflame with righteous wrath, declaring that "all articles in the shape of wines, groceries, and provisions which, upon examination and analysis, are proved to be in- jurious to health, will be confiscated forthwith and distri- buted to the different charitable institutions."

A boy proposed to his father that he should go fishing, but 'his father had other business for him that day. "Father," said the young man, "do you know what Solo- mon said about young boys going fishing ?" "Solomon didn't say anything about it," said the parent. "Yes he did. He said if you spare the rod you spoil the child." "I won't Tare it," said the old gentleman promptly. And he didnt'. But the son thinks he got hold of the wrong rod. SLAVES IN THE CENTRAL ASIAN DE,SERT.—Partieularly heartrending was it to see the old and decrepit under the burden of heavy fetters. Whilst dragging their feet along the muddy or sandy streets they used to throw a glance, full of pain and sorrow, towards the sky, as if imploring the Supreme Being and merciful Lord for assistance. When- ever I met with such pitiable glances I felt as if a dart had pierced me; yet to show the slightest sign of compassion would have been looked upon as sympathising with those heretics, and would have endangered my own safety. Only when at some distance from the tents, and when not ex- posed to the suspecting look of the Turcomans, did I ven- ture to address a few soothing words to the unhappy slaves. When I thus made inquiries about their fate and their rela- tives in Persia, the look of amazement cast by these un- fortunates, who could not conceive that a man dressed as a Hadji (pilgrim) and as a Sunnite should pity them, very frequently quite disconcerted me. "Art thou a lamb in the skin of a wolf ?" said an elderly Persian from Firuzknh one day to me. "I see thou speakest my mother tongue as if thou hadst visited the college of Meshed or of Nishapur. Tell me, pray, will these children of hell (i.e., Turcomans) be permitted any longer to ruin the face of the earth, and will not Allah soon send the avenger of their horrid vices ?" —Professor Vambery, in "Good Wards." A SPRING DAY.—There is sunshine to-day after rain, and every lark is singing. Across the vale a broad cloud- shadow descends the hillside, is lost in the hollow, and pre- sently, without warning, slips over the edge, coming swiftly along the green tips. The sunshine follows—the warmer for its momentary absence. Far, far down in a grassy coomb stands a solitary corn-rick, conical-roofed, casting a lonely shadow—marked because so solitary, and beyond it on the rising slope is a•brown copse. The leafless branches take a brown tint in the sunlight; on the summit above there is furze; then more hill lines drawn against the sky. In the tops of the dark pines at the corner of the copse, could the glance sustain itself to see them, there are finches warming themselves in the sunbeams. The thick needles shelter them from the current of air, and the sky is bluer above the pines. Their hearts are full already of the happy days to come, and when the moss yonder by the beech, and the lichen on the fir-trunk, and the loose fibres caught in the fork of an unbending bough, shall furnish forth a suffi- cient mansion for their young. Another broad cloud. shadow, and another warm embrace of sunlight. All the serried ranks of the green corn bow at the word of command as the wind rushes over them.—Good Trords. NEWTON FOOTBALL CLUB ANNUAL DINNER.—PRESENTA- TION TO THE SECRETARY.—The annual dinner in connection with this club was held at the house of Mr. William Gorse, the Oak Tree Inn, Newton, on Saturday evening last. The repast provided was a splendid one. At the subsequent pro- ceedings Mr. George Lane (captain), occupied the chair. The secretary (Mr. Thomas Fairclough), read the annual re- port. which showed that during the season just concluded eighteen matches had been played. Of these seven had been won, eight lost, and three drawn. The Newton team had scored 7 goals, 12 tries, and 44 minor points ; while emir opponents bad secured 3 goals, 15 tries, and 42 minor points. The club was at present in a very satisfactory condition, and a balance of £4 remained in the hands of the treasurer. The toaats of the president, vice-presidents, captain, and ocher officers of the club were duly honaured ; the proceed- ings being interspersed with songs by Mr. S.Swan, of Earles- town ; Mr. J. Fairclough, Mr. H. Liptrot, and Mr. T. Brad- dick. In the course of the evening, the secretary (Mr. T. Fairclough) was presented with a handsome writing desk. 1 he captain (Mr. Lane), made the presentation on behalf of the club, and commended Mr. Fairclough for his efficient ser- vices during the past two years.—Mr. Fairclough acknow- ledged the gift in appropriate terms.

div.head: PRINTER'S DEVIL-111.
div.p: THE PRINTER'S DEVIL-111.

[By ANGLO-SCOTUS.] A printer's widow in Germany—and who no doubt con- templated a second marriage—while a new edition of the Bible was being printed in her establishment one night took an opportunity of going into the office to alter that sentence of subjection to her husband pronounced upon Eye in Genesis, chapter iii., verse 16. She took out the two first letters of the word " herr," and substituted a a in their place, thus altering the sentence from "And he shall be thy lord" (herr), to "And he shall be thy fool" (narr). Poor widow! It is said she paid forfeit with her life for thus attempting to assume the role of the Printer's Devil. Copies of this edition have been bought up at enormous prices by bibliophiles. That widow was not so clever as the wife of whom the following story is related :—A wealthy man once premised to give a poor gentleman and his wife a large sum of money if at a given time they could tell him the devil's age. When this time came, the gentleman, at his wife's suggestion, plunged first into a barrel of honey, and then into a barrel of feathers, and began to walk on all fours. Presently up came hie satanic majesty, and said, "I and a• years have I lived (neining the exact number), yet never saw I animal like this." LSo the ingenuity of the wife enabled the hus- band io ansiVei the apparently puzzling goestion. The present writer can well retneillber the puzzled expres- sion that came over the face of the then manager of one of the Messrs. Virtue's issuing establishments on his being shown one of the most curious blunders that possibly ever occurred in the press; and which gradually gave way to pleasant laughter, as he realised the comicality of a sentence which should have read somewhat as follows: 'Unlike most youths of his class, at the age of fourteen he had to shift for himself ;" but which, by the accidental omission of a letter read quite differently to the sense intended by the noble lord who wrote the popular novel in the second edi- tion of which the mutilated sentence is to be found. The omission of a consonant also quite recently made an adver- tiser descant in the columns of the Guardian on "the value of painted widows as memorials of departed worth." The poor widows again; as if they were the only class that went in for paint or cosmetics; yes, or corsets either. The existence of Mashers to wit. I may also mention in this connection the bombards, or padded breeches, worn by male " exquisites in Queen Elizabeth's time. A swell in full fig in those days, looked about as abnormally shaped as a modern female opera bouffe artist or ballet girl. No, dear readers, the ladies in private life are not the only sex that go in for affectation or monstrosity in the way of dress. I have seen some "neat" things in clogs and caps worn by men before now. And a young man I saw in Warrington the other day would have taken the "quiver cake" for the cut of his trousers and the style of his dress generally. Many readers will possibly &collect how the substitution of one consonant for another in an article in the Daily Telegraph made it appear as if a well-known politician was an 'authority on the millinery, See., worn by female exponents of opera bouffe, instead of his being an advocate of the rights of women. The substitution of a for an r did the trick, and "tights" appeared instead of "rights." It is a curious fact that this article was reprinted (the day after it originally appeared) in a country newspaper without the blunder being discovered. The verdict of the coroner's jury in the Hornsey railway aecident case, as it appeared in the Daily News, is really too good to be lost to posterity. It was, "That the deceased was run over and killed by a train on the Great Northern Railway, but how his death was occasioned there was not sufficient evidence to show." And it must have been a com- positor who had given up dram-drinking for drug-consum- ing who put it on record that the service at a certain mar- riage in high life would be a "chloral" one. There was more of the eomnolent than the savage Omit him, Or possibly he meant to convey the lesson that people who enter into matrimony cannot have their eyes fully open. I leave the problem of the state of mind of this Caxtonian to be solved by the serious disciples of " Stuttering Dick." Extremes in all things are very dangerou9. The editor of Truth not very long ago published the following as a take-down for the editor of the World :—" The post. office has been benefited to the extent of 3,331 penny stamps and 7,803 halfpenny postal cards by your having last week informed your readers that Lord Stradbroke's party killed in three days 2,150 grouse, of which 1,300 were pheasants." As a rider, "Henry " playfully asks " Ed- mund "the following question e—" Do you do this sort of thing on purpose, as a delicate mode of paying conscience money ?" Readers of The Examiner will thus see that the " devil " does not at all times confine his pranks to the printing office, but occasionally takes his fling in the edi- torial sanctum,. In a criticism on " Ajax " one of the "young lions of Peterborough Court," not long ago, de- livered himself of the following :—" We are on stone seats, under the open sky, on the southern slope of the Acropolis, in the beautiful theatre of Dienysius; just on the left hand rise the pillars and the porticos of the Odeum, while in front, at our feet, is seen the splendid temple of Olympian Zeus. and the winding thread of the Ilissus, while beyond is Hymettus and the purple sea. . . We are sitting amid , a crowd, who in the intervals of the drama chatter about the late news from Seines, where Pericles is fighting." And this is how " the naughty boy who broke the butter- dish" came down upon him :—" As the theatre of Bacchus, in which the writer of this gush supposes himself to be seated, was under the southern sieve of the Acropolis Hill, I greatly doubt whether either the Ilissus or the purple sea could be seen from it. One thing, however, is absolutely certain ; that the Temple of Olympian Zeus could never have been seen by a crowd chattering about the late news from Samos, where Pericles is fighting,' for the excellent reason that the temple was built by the Emperor Adrian, about 500 years after Pericles died." Shakespeare makes one of his characters say, " Give me an ounce of civet, good !apothecary, to sweeten my imagination." The D.T. man mast have consumed at least a pound of the odoriferous se- cretion of the Viverra civetta.

A PUBLIC SCANDAL AT STALYBRIDGE.—At the Staly- bridge Police Court, on Monday, about a dozen men were fined for being drunk in the streets on Sunday. In every ,case the defendants had been seen to leave the ‘lStalybridge Workingmen's Social Club "—a place which was opened [About a month ago and one of the rules of which is that it LI than be opened on Sundays during the time that the public- .houses are closed. Every week since it was opened several I men have been brought up for leaving it drunk, the majority of them in the forenoon, and some as-early at eight Alocla on Sunday mornings.—The magistrates, comment- ing on the facts, said it was a perfect disgrace to the town that•the streets should be kept in an uproat on Sundays by men, apparently respectable, frequenting such a place.— The Chief-constable said the charges of drunkenness on Sundays during the past month had been more numerous than for -several years past. The prisoner was committed THE CUSTOMS AND IRELAND REVENUE BILL—On clause to the assizes. 13 of this bill, Mr. CHILDERS stated that the collection of the income under Schedules I) and E in Scotland and Ire- land was made by the officers of the Inland Revenue, but in England by the local officers. This clause proposed to em- power the collection of the Schedule D and E tax by col- lectors under the Inland Revenue Board, but the Change would be gradual, as it would be made only on the occur- rence of vacancies on the local staff, and only if the Treasury were satisfied that the change would conduce to economy. He argued, however, that if the Scdule D and E collection was made by the Inland Revenue there would be a large saving to the country.—After some discussion a division was taken, when the Government was defeated by a majority of seven. TENANTS' COMPENSATION BILL.—The orders of the day having been gone through, Mr. DODSON asked leave to ha- troduce a bill to amend the law relating to agricultural holdings in England. Any tenant making any of the im- provements enumerated under the bill would be entitled on quitting his holding to obtain compensation from the land- lord, and the measure of the compensation would be the value of the improvements to the incoming tenant. The machinery for ascertaining the value was that of the Agri- cultural Holdings Act, and the improvements to which the bill applied were enumerated in the schedule. Where any particular agreement in writing secured to the tenant for any temporary improvement, reasonable compensa- tion, then the compensation should be deemed to be substi- tuted for compensation under this Act. For drainage works notice should be given to the landlord, and if be did not make them the tenant could do so and claim compensation. The Act was to apply to existing contracts. The landlord would be entitled to make a charge on the estate equal to the compensation given. The bill substituted twelve months' for six months' notice, and it was compulsory to the extent that a tenant would be always entitled to receive compensatien under the act unless he agreed to take a substitute compensation or an eqUi- valent in some other form. Distress was to be limited to one year's rent.—Mr. BARCLAY wanted to know what provision was to be made for Scotland.—The LORD ADVOCATE said the principles of the bill would be extended to Scotlond. He asked leave to introduce a bill for that purpose.—Leave was granted for both bills. Mr. J. HOWARD, who expressed great dissatisfaction with the Agri- cultural Tenants' Compensation Bill, gave notice that he would move its rejection.—Mr. BARCLAY gave a similar notice with reference to the Scotch Agricultural Holdings BBL—The House adjourned at 1-40.

Fitzmautice, stated that the Portuguese Government had promised to send instructions to Angola that the regulations issued there as to putting the visa on bills of health should not apply to British steamers. THE NEW DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE.—The PREMIER explained, in reply to a question, that the new department of agriculture would deal with cattle diseases, with agricul- tural statistics, and all special matters in connection with agricultural investigation that might arise, but be could not say if agricultural education would be dealt with by the new department. THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES Acrs.—Replying to a ques- tion from Mr. Puleston, the Marquis of HARTINGTON said the Government did not propose to annul the provisions of the Contagious Diseases Acts, but to preserve such a mode of revision as they could reasonably expect the House of Commons to agree to.—At a later stage Mr. PULESTON moved the adjournment of the House in order to discuss the action of the Government in this matter. He argued that the towns subjected to the Acts were almost unanimous in their favour.—Lord Hamm:rem justified the conduct of the Government.—Lord H. CHURCHILL said that the ab- stract resolution upon which the Government had acted was carried by a snatch vote. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE thought there had been great pre- cipitancy in the action of the Government. A very im- portant principle was involved in the proposal to act on a single resolution as the Government were now doing.—Mr. GLansroxu said that by the structure of the Acts the Legislature had left it to the House of Commons to deter- mine from year to year whether the funds should be pro- vided for the administration of the Acts • yet the echitentien of the Opposition now was that the Government, in the face of the large majority against compulsory examination, should spend the money of the people for a purpose condemned by the resolution which was passed.—Mr. W. H. SMITH said the Government should have asked for a vote for the continuation of the Acts until they passed a bill to alter them.—The motion was eventually with- drawn. THE NAVY ESTIMATES.—The House went into Commit- tee of Supply on the Navy Estimates.—Lord H. LENNOX drew attention to the condition of the English navy as compared with the navies of other countries, and drew the conclusion that our maritime supremacy could not be said to be assured.—Sir T. BRASSEY said the Admiralty had endeavoured to make an effective application of the money at their disposal rather than propose unnecessary increases in the Estimates. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

THE INCOAIE-TAX.—Last night's Lon(lon Gazette contains an Inland Revenue order convening a meeting of the Land Tax Commissioners for the County of Chester to be held at the Sessions-house, Daresbury, on Saturday next, at eleven o'clock, for the purpose of choosing fit and proper persons to be commissioners to supply vacancies amongst the com- missioners for the general purpose of the income-tax for the division of Bucklow, West Cheshire. FRODSHAIII. CHANGE-RINGING AT THE PARISH CHURCIL—OR Satur- day three ringers from Daresbury Church. assisted by three ringers from St. Paul's Church, Warrington, visited Froth sham Parish Church and rang on the towEr bells a peal of plain bob minor. The ringers stood as follows :—J. Webb (Warrington), Ist; P. Johnson (Daresbury), 2nd; Critoll- ley (Warrington), 3rd ; P. Hamblen (Daresbury), 4th; G. Bebbington, jun. (Warrington), sth ; T. Houghton, jun. (Daresbury), tenor; conducted by J. Webb; time, 30 minutes; weight of tenor, 18 cwt. After tea they rang another peal of plain bob minor in very good style in 28 minutes. HALE. At the Woolton Petty Sessions, on Friday, Ellis Hughes, Hale, was fined 2s. 61 and costs for keeping a dog without a license on the 18:h April last. ROSE IN nu. VALLEY DIVIDEND SOCIETY.—On Sunday morning the members of tills sosfrety attenthd the Pari.,?ir Church, Lymm, to pay a tribute of respect to their deceased brother, Thomas Cheetham. The rector, the Rev. W. Guest, was the preacher, and his remarks on 'Sympathy" were listened to with great attention. After the service the mem- bers re-formed in procession, and conducted the widow and fatherless to their residence. SUNDAY SCHOOL CHORAL SontETY.—The first choral fes- tival took place in the Congregational school-room, on Tuesday evening, when there was a large attendance. The instrumentalists were: Violin, Mr. W. Kirkpatrick; violon- cello, Mr. W. Skil ling ; flute, Mr. T. Gregson ; and pianoforte and organ, Mr. E. Browo, jun. The programme consisted of two anthems, choral pieces, glees, part-smigs, Sic., in which the following took part :—Mrs. Chor ley, Miss Ellen Moston, Miss Hazeldine, Miss Emma Moston, Miss Ellen Holt, Miss Thomason, Miss Jane Ellison, and Miss Bertha Leigh. The chorus singers represented the schools of the Congrega- tional, Wesleyan, Primitive Methodist, and Independent (Cherry-lane) congregations. Mr. George Jones efficiently acted as conductor.

OPENING MVSELIMS ON SUNDAY.—Lord DIINRAVEN sub- mitted his motion in favour of opening the national museums and galleries on Sundays.—Lord PIOWERSCOURT, in second- I hid the motion, suggested that the Fisheries Exhibition should also be opened on Sundays.—Lord SIIAFTESBERY moved an amendment in favour of opening the British Museum and National Gallery on three evenings per week, and opposed the Sunday opening.—Lord CAIRNS refused to accept Kew and Hampton Court as illustrative of the results that would follow the adoption of the motion.— Lord GRANVILLE was in favour of Sunday opening, and did not think Lord Shaftesbury's proposal would meet the re- quirements of artisans. On a division, 67 voted for the motion and 91 against it; and subsequently an amendment •of Lord Shaftesbury's motion recommending the week-night opening of the British Museum and the National Gallery, as far as le consistent with their safety and welfare, was I adopted.

div.head: DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.
THE PRISONERS AT BOW-STREET.

The seven prisoners charged with treason-felony in con- nection with the seizure of nitro•glycerine Thomas Gallagher, alias Fletcher; Bernard Gallagher, Dalton, alias O'Connell, Whitehead, Wilson, Curtin, and Augsburg, were I again brought before Sir James Ingham, at Pow-street Police Court, on Thursday morning. Evidence was given to the effect that" Dr." Gallagher had sent money from London to Bernard Gallagher and Curtin in Glasgow, and that the 'first - named prisoner and Wilson had been seen together in London on the day when Wilson brought a heavy box (suspected to contain explosives) from Whitehead's house at Birmingham, to an hotel in the Strand. Colonel Majendie, the Govern- ment Inspector of Explosives, stated that on April 5 he examined some liquid contained in two large fishing stock- ings at Woolwieh Arsenal, and found it was nitro-glycerine. There was about 80Ib. of the explosive. The bag found in Dalton's box contained 1961 b. He went to Whitehead's house in Ledsam-street. Birmingham, and found that the manufacture of nitro-glycerine had been carried on there. There was about 1701 b. of explosives on the premises, completely manufactured, besides carboys containing several hundred pounds of nitric and sulphuric acid and two tins, each containing 601 b. of glycerine. The prisoners were again remanded.

div.head: PIKENIX PARK MURDERS.
div.p: THE PIKENIX PARK MURDERS.
THIRD TRIAL OF TIM KELLY.

Timothy Kelly was on Monday for the third time ar- raigned at the Dublin Commission for the murder of Mr. Burke, on the 6th of May, 1882, before Mr. Justice O'Brien and a special jury. He was again defended by Mr. Sullivan and Mr. Wlnerney, and the Attorney-General, Mr. Murphy, and Mr. Peter O'Brien prosecuted for the Crown. After the jury had been sworn, the Attorney-General opened the case for the Crown, dwelling upon the prisoner's connection with the Invincible Society. One of those to be examined was Joseph Hanlon, who was a witness of the murders, and saw the blows struck, and be would tell the jury that the account given by Carey, Kavanagh, and Smith was accurate. Robert Farrell was the first witness. He deposed to the prisoner's presence at the meetings on the quays and in Brunswick-street. Peter Carey described the continued at- tempts on the life of Mr. Forster, at which the prisoner was present. James Carey gave his account of the formation of the conspiracy ; and Joseph Hanlon, the latest informer, ex- plained that he had agreed to give evidence to save his own life," having been previously sold by the others." He clearly identified Kelly as one of the four men who actually perpetrated the assassinations. Before the Chief and Under Secretaries reached the spot where they died there had been a large gathering of the " Invincibles" in that vicinity, but I ringleader Brady ordered Hanlon and several others to go away, adding that "four would be enough." The four left behind to complete the work were Brady himself, Kelly, Caffrey' and Delany, and they were the four who drove off on Kavanagh's car. Witness, Fagan, and Curley were driven from the park by 'Skin the Goat. At the conclusion of Haulon's evidence the 'nowt adjourned. The trial was resumed on Tuesday. The Crown case. was I proceeded with. Thomae Huxley, gardener, identified the prisoner as one of the group of men he saw near the Chapelizod Road on the evening of the 6th of May as he passed through the Park. The other witnesses were Noud, the carman, Mr. Brown, the prisoner's employer, Jacob, the youth, who saw the scuffle, Dr. Myles, who made the post- mortem examination, and Meage, the bicyclist. Mr. Wlnerney addressed the jury for the defence, intimating that an alibi would be proved-. A number of persons, in- cluding the prisoner's brother, were then produced to prove that the prisoner was at a house in Aungier-street, at half- past seven, and at a public-house at a quarter to eight, and afterwards attended a delegate meeting. Michael Glynn, who was previously a Crown witness, was now produced for the prisoner, and expressed his disbelief that the prisoner was one of the men that the witness saw in the Park on the 6th of May. The trial concluded on Wednesday. Evidence for the defence was proceeded with. Three witnesses were ex- amined, two of whom swore to the prisoner's presence at the meeting of the Political Prisoners' Aid Society on the night of the 6th of May soon after eight o'clock. Mr. D. B. Sullivan then closed the case for the defence in an able speech of two hours and a half's duration. Mr". James Murphy, Q.O , replied for the Crown' and Mr. Justice O'Brien, in summing up, spoke for upwards of an hour and a half. At twenty minutes past six o'clock the jury re- tired. They returned into court in twenty-five minutes with a verdict of "Guilty." In reply to the usual question, the prisoner said he was not guilty of the charge of murdering Mr. Burke. He had to thank his counsel heartily, and might they long live to defend the innocent. His Lordship, in passing sentence of death, said he would not dwell upon the youth and unhappy fate of the prisoner. He sentenced him to be hanged at Kilmainham on the 9th of June.
