div.head: TRIAL OF JOSEPH MULLETT.
div.p: THE TRIAL OF JOSEPH MULLETT.

On Thursday Joseph Mullett was placed on trial for the attempt to murder Mr. Field. The prisoner refused to plead, and the trial proceeded as though he had answered 'Snot guilty." The Attorney-General said it was not alleged that it was the prisoner's hand that attacked Mr. Field; in fact, the prisoner was at the time in another part of Dublin, superintending the movements for an attack on another ob- noxious juror. But he was privy to the assault on Mr. Field, and, therefore, guilty of the attempt to murder. The Crown might have indicted him for the Plicenix Park murders, for it could be proved that he was present at a meeting of "Invincibles " held on the sth May, 1882, for the purpose of assassinating Mr. Burke.—The prisoner was a Fenian leader, and from diaries and papers found in his possession it was apparent that he was a fanatic, and looked upon political crime as justifiable. The Attorney-General read a number of remarkable extracts from the diaries. The prisoner called no witnesses, contenting himself with pro- testing against the trial and against the prejudice created by the English press against the persons accused of these crimes.—The jury found him guilty; and Mr. Justice O'Brien passed sentence of penal servitude for life.

div.head: NORTH WICH.
div.p: NORTH WICH.

A most melancholy affair is reported from Northwich. It appears that the gas manager of that town, Mr. John Askew, who up to ten p.m. on Thursday was assisting in an amateur dramatic perform nee in the Drill Hall, and at which he was playing the violoncello, mysteriously disap- peared. Almost before he could be missed the cause of his disappearance was explained, It seems that a young man who also had been attending the performance was passing a point near the river Weaver—perhaps a quarter of a mile away from the Drill Hall—and heard a splash in the water, and at once, suspecting some unusual occurrence, raised an alarm. Assistance was procured, but it was one o'clock on Thursday morning before Askew was recovered from the river, when, of course, he was found to be quite dead. The occurrence is the more extraordinary, since a young woman, a domestic in the deceased's employ, and who also had been attending the concert at the Drill Hall, was found floating in the Weaver at the same place and at the same time. She was lifeless when.taken out of the water. Mr. Askew, who had held his appointment as gas manager about two years, was about 40 years of age. He was married, and has left a wife and three children, for whom great sympathy is manifested. OVER.

MAT FESTIVITIES AT OVER. The annual May festivi- ties were held in a field adjoining Over Hall, on Saturday last. The weather was gloomy and very cold, but the rain kept off, and all present enjoyed themselves. The children began to assemble in the dockyard shortly after twelve o'clock, and by the time the procession started the streets were crowded with onlookers. The procession was headed by the Rifle band, and followed by the Whitegate, High- street, and Meadow-bank Board schools, and Sr. John's schools. Then came the Over brass band, Mrs. Wood's school, Weaver Navigation school, Darnhall school, Whar- ton National and Wharton Church schools, Dierden-street school, the sword bearers' Oulton school, Church Minshull school, the Weaver brass band. Succeeding them was the royal jester, who created some amusement, and was followed by 30 girls dressed as May-pole dancers and 30 boys as .morris dancers. The sceptre and crown bearers preceded her Majesty the May Queen (a pretty little girl, the daugh- ter of Mrs. Newman, of Whitegate), seated on a highly- decorated throne. The Queen was beautifully dressed, hav- ing a profusion of real flowers, and she was surrounded by her maids of honour, and followed by little girls represent- ing England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, and the four seasons, various nursery rhymes, &c. The Winsford Fire Brigade was in full force with their engine manned by the ICrewo brigade, the coal trade was represented by two enor- mous cobbles in carts, and there was an excellent show of turn-outs, each vehicle and horse being decorated, and the ' vehicles tilled with children. On arriving at the field the various May ceremonies were gone through with great pre- cision, thanks to the great pains taken by Mrs. and the Misses Turner, of Over Hall, who also bore all the expense of the dresses, &c., with the exception of the Queen's. The whole of the children belonging the schools were regaled with buns and coffee, &c. Captain Cctton proposed a vote of thanks to Captain Turner and family for the trouble and expense they had been at, and said he felt sure a Warne vote of thanks would compensate for the cold weather. The pro- position was seconded by Mr. Beckett, of Hartford, and was carried enthusiastically. The fire brigade contest excited much interest. The first prize for turn-outs was awarded to J. Knowles, Darnhall Hall, waggoner J. Davies; 2nd, J. Knowles, Stoker-lane Farm, waggoner, H. Pritchard. Single horse: Ist, H. Sheppard, London and North-Western Rail- way Company, waggoner J. Davies; 2nd, Winsford Co- operative Stores, waggoner, J. Houlbrooke; 3rd, A. Davies; 4th, J. Barker, ST. Mr. Beckett and Mr. J. A. Turner were the judges. A football match between Crewe and Winsford followed. In a pecuniary sense the day was a great success, there being a very large company, the receipts at the gates being upwards of £5O. The tents were supplied by Mr. Beeton, ci Winsford. WINSFORD.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.

THE LO-ND—O-N-i-ND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.—Mr. A. J. BALFOUR moved the recommittal of the London and North-Western (Additional Powers) Bill, in order that its provisions may be modified in such a manner that the powers of purchase of the St. Pancras burial ground be confined to such portion as may be necessary for the enlargement of Easton Station and the formation of a new street, and that such powers be conditional on a portion of the purchase money being applied to laying out the remainder of the burial ground as a garden.—After considerable discussion, the third reading of the bill was carried by 173 to 157. THE SOUTHPORT FORESHORE--The Southport foreshore question was introduced by Mr. Jesse Collings, who asked Mr. Dodson if the conference he had just attended had altered his views with repect to the sale of the foreshore. The Chancellor of the Duchy replied that he bad not had time to consider the arguments, but it must be uederstood that there must be no question of receding from a binding contract. He was willing, however, to act as meditaor between the Corporation of Southport and the riparian pro- prieters, awl he was not without hope that reasonable coun- sels might prevail and an amicable arrangement be arrived at. Mr. Collings returned to the subject later in the evening, and moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a matter of "urgent public importance." As more than 100 members rose, the bon. member was allowed under the new rules to proceed, and he expressed his disappointment with the answer he had received. He declared that in his 20 years' experience of municipal affairs he had never known treatment so cruel and lamentable to be inflicted on any borough as bad fallen upon Southport. A long discussion followed, and it was closed by Mr. GLADSTONE, who thought the riparian owners desired to act equitably, and advised the acceptance of Mr. Dodson'a offer to act as mediator. The motion for adjournment was then withdrawn. MR. BRADLAUGH.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL gave notice of a motion to the effect that a member whom the House had declined to let swear or affirm should not on re-election be allowed to take the oath till 21 days after the meeting of a new Parliament. INDIAN FINANCES.—Mr. STANHOPE then brought forward his motion relative to the finances of India.—Mr. Cztoss made his first important speech as Under-Secretary for India, in reply to Mr. Stanhope. Upon the necessity of curtailing expenditure in some directions Mr. Cross endorsed all the claims of the economists, but he declared the real me,tne of relieving India to be the fostering of her inter- national resources by means of wise and increased expendi- ture upon remunerative works, and larger employment of natives in the administration. To meet the immense superannuation charges which result from the general employment of Englishmen in public duties sixty millions of rupees are annually required for pensions payable in England, and upon the. reduction of this unproductive out- lay Mr. Cross firmly insisted. At the same time he showed the country to be advancing in wealth.—The debate was continued by several hon. members.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—Mr. STAVELEY HILL moved the second reading of his Agricultural Holdings Bill in the House of Commons yesterday. It was suggested by Mr. HENEAGE that as the Government Bill would be intro- duced to-night (Thursday) it would be better that the debate should be at once adjourned, so that they might have an opportunity of seeing what the provisions of the Govern- ment Bill were.—Mr. J. HOWARD was also of opinion that they should await the appearance of Aaron's rod, which would swallow up all the other rods of the kind.—Mr. STAYELEY Hirxaccepted the suggestion, and the debate was adjourned. THE THEATRES REGULATION BILL.—The second reading of the Theatres Regulation Bill was moved by Mr. DIXON- HARTLAND who mentioned that since he brought forward the motion last year, 28 theatres in Europe had been destroyed by fire. The rejection of the bill was moved by Sir. J. M,GAREIpHOGG, who held that in view of the Metropolitan Government Bill it would be premature to confer juris- diction with regard to theatrical regulations upon any body other than that which it was proposed to establish. The bill was opposed by Sir C. DILKE as a singularly despotic and arbitrary measure, and upon a division t was thrown out by 141 to 22. THE FACTORY AND WORKSHOPS AMENDMENT BILL.— Mr. BROADMIRST moved the second reading of a Factory and Workshops Act Amendment Bill, the object of which was to put a stop to young girls in the Black Country being taught the trade of a blacksmith, it being the custom in that district to allow girls under 14 years of age to work in the nail shops ánl at the forges.—The rejection of the bill was moved by Mr. BIONCKTON, who contended that it was a piece of class legislation conceived in the interests of the few against those of the many, and that if adopted it would ruin the Black Country trade.—Sir C. DILIIE thought it was undesirable to pass a special Act, as there were only 9 shops out of Bg6 to which the bill would apply, and in each of those shops only one person was employed.—The bill was defeated by 124 to 44. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TunnsDAY.

TEE IRISH LAND ACT.—Earl CAIRNS initiated a debite on the administration of the Irish Land Act, and especially on the mode in which certain Sub-Commissioners are dis- charging thelr duties.—Lord CARLINGFORD defended the action of the Land Commissioners.—The Marquis of Salis- bury, Lori Fitzgerald, the Marquis of Waterford, the Lord Ckancellor, and the Duke of Abercorn joined in the discus- sion, which had no practical result.—ln the course of a short conversation on the recent action of the House of Commons in reference to the Contagious Diseases Act, the Duke of CAMBRIDGE remarked that the places where the Act had been in operation would be the last to want it rescinded, and he thought it extraordinary that the matter should not have been more fully considered before any action was taken upon it.—The Municipal Corporations (Unreformed) Bill was brought up from the House of Commons and read a first time, and their Lordships adjourned until the 24th of May.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.--ThußsoAy.

A ScErrs.--11The early proceedings included reference to State-aided emigration, the Contagious Diseases Act, the commercial treaty with Italy, the Ballot Act, and other matters of little public interest; but considerable excite- ment arose on a question by Mr. Harrington as to the searching of a house in County Mayo and the removal of certain articles, including a photograph, therefrom.— Mr. TREMLYAN said he thought honourable members could not be aware of the meaning which underlay some of the questions Irish members put. Knowing what he knew, he was positively appalL2d at finding the House of Commons used for inch a purpose. Mr. HARRINGTON retorted that the facts he called attention to were a scandal to civilisation, and, being called to order, relluntid to tbe ebarge with a notice of

div.p: Ablb __ '7 -,

wood, and Mary Moran, his housekeeper. The condemned man weiit to bed at his usual hour on the previous night, and slept very soundly. He rose and dressed at five o'clock and at half-past five was visited by Father Pacificus, the Roman Catholic chaplain, who has been attending him sines his condemnation. At a few minutes to eight Marwood and the officials appeared at the condemned cell, and Carey was pinioned and led to the scaffold. He did not betray any tree pidatien, but walked firmly, submitting his hands to be pinioned and his head to be covered by the hangman with the greatest coolness. The bolt was immediately drawn, and the drop being eight feet death appeared to be itnsantaneons. Reporters were not admitted to witness the execution, but immediately afterwards Father Paciticus informed the representatives of the press that Carey was resigned. He acknowledged the justice of the law and that he deserved death, and died really penitent. Masses were offered up for Carey at the Franciscan Church at Chester. An inquest was afterwards held in the Grand Jury-room at Chester Castle before Dr. Churton. The de- censed lay in the mortuary-room, which is under the same roof as the scaffold itself. He was dressed as he appeared on his trial. Mr. Edward Lloyd, chief officer in charge of the civil prison: was the only witness oiled. He deposed that the I,w had been carried out on Carey, and the jury returned a verdict to that effect.

ALLEGED INCRNDURY FIRES IN CHESHIRE.—A fire was discovered on Sunday morning in the stackyard of Mr. Itberill, Upton Old Hall, Chester. Ten large stacks, the entire produce of the farm, lay contiguous to the hall, and four of these were discovered in flatn,e,. Two manna engines from Chester were qn:el='y Lhe spot, but before their arrival two other staels u become ignited, and were all consumed. About 100 tons of bay and 1;0 tons of straw were destroyed. The stacks consumal were two hay, one Clover, one beans, and two straw. The fire is evidently the work of an incendiary. At midnight on Saturday the out- buildings on the farm occupied by Mrs. Moore, at Gayton, near Neston, Cheshire, were destroyed by fire, and her son, John James Moore, is in custody charged with incendiatism. It appears that for some time hick the young man has been drinking heavily, and his conduct has been so bad that his mother was obliged to leave the farm, which was carried on by another son, who on Friday last put the stock into the hands of a Chester auctioneer to sell. On Saturday the auctioneer sent two men to take charge of the place. This aggravated the prisoner, who, at eleven o'clock at night, re- quested them to leave. Toe men refused to quit the pre- mises, and the prisoner then threatened to set fire to the buildings. He immediately afterwards went into thoshippon, where he remained two or three minutes, and on re-entering the house he exclaimed, "I've done it, and no one can stop it." In a short time flames issued from the shippon. and the fire spread with great rapidity. Every effort was made by the police and others to extinguish the conflagration, but as there was no fire-engine on tho ground to assist in stop- ping its progress, the outbuildings ware destroyed. The damage, which is estimated at £2OO, is covered by insur- ance.

Samuel Davies. baker, Wellington-street, W4B summoned for illtrtating a dog belonging to Mr. ( harles Hadiam, by throw- ing at it a brick—Defendant pleaded "guilty, but not with the intention of hurting the dog." (Laughter.) —lt appeared that the dog went home yelling through a cut over the eye, and on enquiry being made it was ascertained that the injury had been caused by the defendant. Defendant said he only threw the brick with the object of driving the dog from his master's premises. The Assistant Clerk (Mr. Browne) read a letter from Mr. B. Tnri PARCELS Poer.—The Postmaster-General intimates that on August let the department will be prepared to accept at any post-office in the United Kingdom parcels intended for transmission by the Inland Parcels Post, those not ex- ceeding llb in weight having to be prepaid 3d in ordinary postage stamps; exceeding llb and not exceeding 31b, ad ; exceeding 31b and not exceeding 51b, Pd; and exceeding 51b and not exceeding 71b, is. The dimensions allowed for an inland postal parcel will be: Maximum length, 3ft. Gin. ; maximum length and girth combined, Gft. Examples : A parcel measuring 3fl. 6in. in its longest dimension may measure as much as 2ft. Gin, in girth (i.e., around its thickest part); or a shorter parcel may be thicker (e.g., if measuring no more than 3(t. in length it may measure as much as 3ft. in girth—i.e., around its thick3st part). The regulations unner which certain articles are prohibited from transmission by the letter post will, with a few exceptions, apply equally to the parcels post. For instance, gunpowder, lucifer matches, anythin.; liable to sudden c)mbustion, bladders containing liquid, and live animals will be exclu- ded from the parcels past; but glass bottles, fish, game, meat, and all other articles not above mentioned, now ex- cluded from the letter post, will be admitted to go by parcels post conditionally upon their being packed and guarded in so secure a manner as to afford complete protection to the contents of the mails and to the officers of the post- office.

Wl:sr LANCASHIRE Blevcr.E Cum SPORTS.—The ninth amateur athletic festival (spring meeting) under the auspices of the West Lancashire Bicycle Club, was held on Kensington Fields on Saturday afternoon. The weather, unfortunately, was not very favourable for the occasion. There was an excellent piogramme of events, and the valu- able prises, chiefly consisting of articles of virtu, .brought together within the competing ring well-known Incycnsts from the principal centres of population throughout the country, and some of the most expert runners in Lanca- shire and Cheshire. The 120 yards' open handicap was run in eleven heats, there being 54 competitors. The following were the winners of the respective heats :—J. Kenyon, Man- chester, 7i yards' start; W. Hall, Live: pool, 10,1,1 yards ; J. J. Hartley, St. Helens, 81 yards; R. Ratcliffe, Warring- ton, 11 yards; A. W. Moore, Tuebrook, 10i wards ; E. Powell, Liverpool, 12 yards; D. A. Harding, Widnes, 10i yards; C. E. Ridehalgh, Liverpool, 10; G. Leathbarrow, Bolton, 10 yards; G. W. Rowley, Netherton, 71 yards ; T. Ellis, Cheltenham C.F.C., 11 yards. In the second round, which was run in two heats, Hartley won in the first heat, Pcwell coming in second; and Ridehalgh in the second heat, Harding being second. Hartley won in the final by a yard. time 12 secs., Ridehalgh being second. Three heats, comprising 34 competitors, were made up for the 440 yards' handicap (open), the final in which was for the greater part of the course a most exciting race between C.E. Ridehalgh, Liverpool (32 yards), and J. J. Hartley (28 yards). A few yards from home, however, the latter fell off, and was there- upon passed by C. J. Ashton (33 yards), Liverpool Harriers. Ridehalgh won by three yards; time 49 secs. At the con- clusion of the events the prizes Nero distributed by Mr. Alderman Boyd. During the afternoon the excellent band of the Orphan Boys' Asylum played a selection of music.

The object of both the reso- a"ion and amendment, it will be noticed, is to give 1, i public, and more especially the work- Classes, more opportunities for visiting Sc institutions and benefiting more fre- rently by their educating and elevating in- acillences• The two peers, however, would ...opt entirely different methods to secure the Cd in view. For ourselves we look upon sat)rd DUNRAVEN'S propc sal as simply a neces- GrY extension of the action taken by the r:vernment some time ago in opening the tt!lseurns and galleries in the suburban dis- a lets of London, and in the city of Dublin, ond We fail to find in the arguments of the PPonents of Sunday opening any valid rund for their objections. It appears to us et the very fact of some national institu- w9ns being already opened on the Sunday cithnut any injury accruing is in itself a suffi- thient justification for the proposal to extend oPening of, at any rate, all national gal- e. Lord SHAFTESBURY'S argument that opening of museums would lead to the eelling of theatres and workshops may be vrtanaissed with the observation that it is un- Orthy of that philanthropist; and we think ihl4 Lordship totally misunderstands the work- dm.g Man if he supposes that interesting in- Oriclual will ever be induced under any lalptation whatever to work seven days for ✓days' pay. The great defect of Lord 4APTEsBuRy's amendment is that it is not tacticable to make it meet the end in view. rilwe quite understand the des:rability of the usenms being open three evenings, or even ifvteirY evening, of the week; at the same time fr'Lle Working classes are to derive any benefit 1311.1 them they will have to be open on the innday as well. But assuming that the work- ela.sses could visit these institutions be iween seven and ten of an evening, which we enY, there would still remain a very large 4Pulation in the metropolis who could not. a. any tradesmen, and consequently many as- elstants, are at work till a late hour every h venin Sunday is the only day which they a g , ve to themselves, and it is a hardship that I.lese should be prevented, in the language of 111°.rd GRANVILLE, " from elevating their In• ds by visiting places of intellectual amuse- On the only day on which they have :I.sure to do 'so.' NEW POOR RITES TOR NORTON AND STOCICHA.M.—The Runcorn magistrates on Monday sanctioned the laying of a poor rate for the township of Norton of 101 in the £, to realise £277 4s 81d. A poor rate of Is in the to realise £39 3s 31 was also sanctioned for Stockham. SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNE3.— Mr. Tharme, of Liverpool, preached the anniversary sermons in this place of worship, on Sunday, to good congregations. In the afternoon the school children rendered a service of song in a pleasing manner. Collections were made at each service in aid of the school funds. THEATRE ROYAL, RuNconN.—Frank Majilton's comedy company has occupied the boards of this place of amuse- ment during the past week. "Round the clock," a most amusing production, was represented on the first four even- ings, the various parts being well sustained. On Friday evening "What's the odds" was produced, and to-night "Round the clock" will again be put on the boards. The company is an excellent one, and each performer is fully master of his part. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORIL—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglect- ing to send their children regularly to school :—Thomas Turner. Edward McTague, Mary Hayes, Thomas Welsh, Mary Riley, John Brown, John Murtz, Martin Connor, John Fenian, and Mary Keating. The cases were proved by the attendance officers, Messrs. Joynson, Davies, and Rowe, and the usual fine of 5s was imposed in each instance. RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS.—COMPETITIVE The last of three competitions for the selection of ten shots to compete for the Lord-Lieutenant's Prizes at the next Cheshire meeting took place on Saturday last, on Runcorn Heath Range, when the following were the winners : Colour-Sergeant Mort, Sergeant Harvey, Sergeant Dutton, Sergeant Shone, Sergeant Clarke, Sergeant J. H. Joynson,Carporal Holt, Private G. R. Joyuson, Private Kertnack, Private J. Frith. The above named will hold three more competitions shortly for the purpose of selecting the two best shots to compete for the Queen's and St. George's prizes at Wimbledon. BRUTAL TREATMENT OF A HORSE AT WIDNES. WaL Beesley, carter, and Edward Percy, contractor, were sum- moned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, on a charge of cruelly illtreating a horse. P.S. 'Macgregor said when in Waterloo-road, on the 13:h ult., he Saw Beesley driving a horse and cart, which belonged to Percy. Down the off-side of the animal three Or four streams of blood and matter were running, and the re- moval of the horse-cloth exposed to view a large raw wound, about five inches in length.—The charge against Percy was withdrawn, and Beesley was fined lOs and costs. ST. BEDE'S, APpLE•roer.—On Sunday evening after Ros- ary, a procession was held in this church in honour of Oar Lady. A large number of children, dressed in spotless white and carrying choice flowers, preceded the altar-boys and the pastor, the Rev. Father Finegan. Four altar-boys carried on a bearer a large statue of Our Lady, which was decked with flowers. Two new single-poled banners were also carried—one having a figure of Our Lady with arms out-stretched as if inviting her children's love; the other repres:nting Our Lord standing amid golden lilies. Both banners had gold fringe and massive gold tassels. The Young Men's Society followed also in procession, after which Solemn Benediction was given. The pastor of the church preached an appropriate sermon for the occasion from the words of the Magnificat: "Behold, from hence- forth, all generations shall call me blessed."

WRANGLING WOINIHN AT RIINCORN.—Before Mr. H. Rey- nolds and Mr. S. B. Chadwick, at Runcorn Police Court, On Monday, Mary Ann Williams, of 12, Surrey-street, was charged with assaulting Ann Skerratt.—The complainant alleged that on the 28th ult., whilst she was having "some words" with her sister-in-law, the defendant came up, knocked her down, and broke in pieces the umbrella which she carried. Subsequently, when she was leaving the house, the defendant met her at the end of the entry, knocked her down again, and " jowled " her face several times on the ground. Dr. Robinson, who was near, washed her face, which was bleeding profusely. Defendant had threatenPd to take her life, and she wished for protection.—This state- ment having been confirmed by several witnesses, a cross- summons charging Skerratt with using abusive language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace to Williams was heard.—After the et idence had been given, the Bench sad the parties were as bad as one another, and bound them each over to keep the peace for six months in their own recog- nisances of £5, each to pay their own costs-13s 6d.

A WIDNES PUBLICAN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.-At Widne3 Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Whittaker, landlord of the Stanley Arms, was summoned to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness, and of supplying beer to a drunken person.—Mr. R. H. Bartlett, of Liverpool, ap- peared for the defence.—lt was alleged for the prosecution that on Saturday night, the 21st ult., P.S. Macgregor, who was accompanied by P.C. Moore, entered the defendint's house about eight o'clock. At that time there were stand- ing at the bar four men and a woman. One of the men, named Joseph Hooligan, who was " mad drunk," had a pint glass half full of beer in his hand. He drank twice from the vessel, and was using very foul language to his wife. Eventually lie was taken into custody, but so violent was his conduct that four constables were re- quired to convey him to th 3 police station. Mr. Bartlett spoke of the previous good character of the defendant whom he called. He denied having 'supplied Hooligan with liquor, stathw that on the other band he had twice refused to serve him. Henry Mallinson, the barman, John Doyle, and Richard White, gave evidence to the same effect. It was stated that the liquor Hooligan had in his hand when the police officers entered the house belonged to a man named Purcill, a statement which the latter confirmed. Under the circumstances the Bench, although believing the account given by the police, dismissed the case.

WHITSUNTIDE TRIPS FROM RUNCORN AND WIDNES.— The railway arrangements for Whitsuntide are similar to a great extent to those of former years. By the 8-18 from Runcorn, and the 8-35 from Widnes, this (Saturday) morn- ing, the London and North-Western Railway Company issue cheap tickets for a three days visit to that popular watering place Blackpool, the return journey being made either on Monday night or Tuesday morning. Special fares are announced for those who are desirous of being present at the opening of tbe International Fisheries Exhibition to- day, the tickets being available for a week. Mr. Bellamy has made arrangements for a special fast excursion train from Liverpool to Llandudno on Whit-Monday, to stop at Runcorn. It is timed to leave Runcorn at seven a.m., and for 4s. a pleasant day can be spent in one of the most beauti- ful spots in North Wales. Excursions are also to be run to South Wales. The Widnes Sunday School Union announce a trip to Buxton and Matlock on Whit. Monday by the Midland route, to leave Widnes Central Sta- tion at seven a.m., while the Farnworth Parish Church ex- cursion affards the denizens of smoky Widnes an opportunity of viewing the beauties of the lake district at Windermere. It departs from Widnes at six a.m. on Monday. From Widnes, too' a trip, organised by the Rainford Mutual Im- provement Society, departs for Llanberis at 6-20 a.m., calling at Runcorn. The Haste to the Rescue 1.0.G.T. Lodge have arranged for a train to leave Whines for South- port at seven am. on Tuesday, while on the same morning steamer will leave Runcorn for Liverpool and New Brighton, also returning by water in the evening.

TIM SOCIAL EVIL IN RUNCORN. - At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Mary Ferrier, a young woman of bad character, pleaded guilty to riotously behaving herself in Penketh-lane on the Bth May, and with having at the same time and place assaulted P.C. Morris whilst in the execu- tion of his duty.—Ellen Ferrier, the mother, was charged with assaulting P.C. Morris on the same occasion.—Mary Bar- nett was charged that she being a bad character was guilty of riotous behaviour in High-street, on the Bth inst. P.C. Morris said about half - past nine on Tuesday night he met the prisoner Mary Ferrier, who was followed by a large crowd, at the end of Church-street. He requested her to go home, but she went up Penketh-lane and continued her disturbance. He there- fore took her into custody, when the mother seized hold of him and attempted to rescue her daughter. He then also apprehended the mother, who struck him on the right eye, while the daughter struck him on the mouth.—Mr. P. Smith, druggist, stated there were about 150 persons on the spot, and a most frightful row was going on. Both the Ferriers were on the ground and striking the constable, so he went to his aid, and conveyed one of the prisoners to the police station. Penketh-lane was the resort of bad charac- ters.—Dr. MacDougall said about three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon people were rushing from alldirectiens into High- street, where Barnett and Mary Ferrier were screaming and fighting. They were separated about four times, but with- out avail. They fought like fiends. He might take the liberty of saying that he hoped the Bench would really take some steps to punish these people. High-street was be- ccming the promenade for bad characters, who were a posi- tive nuisance, and a menace to respectable women and children. The children saw their conduct, and heard their language, and might probably imbibe a good deal of their bad habits. The street on this occasion was in a perfect uproar for 20 minutes.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench was d.termined to put a stop to the disorderly and riotous be- haviour of such characters as the prisoners. Mary Ferrier was committed to gaol for two months' hard labour, a month on each charge. Ellen Ferrier was fined 20s and costs, or a month's hard labour, and Barnett was sentenced to the latter term without the option of a fine.

DRUNK IN COURT.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, bAore Mr. John Brundrit, Thomas Costello was charged with being drunk on the 6th May, in Waterloo- road, and also for appearing in court on the previous day in a drunken condition.—P.C. Nodeu proved the case.—On Monday, when he appeared in answer to the first summons, he was drunk, and the magistrates ordered him to be taken into custody—For the first offence the prisoner was fined 53. and 93.61. costs, and for the second 103. and 53. c )sts. _

RUNCORN Y.M.C. A. HISTORICAL CLASS.—Mr. J. Craig, the principal of Runcorn Collegiate School, delivered a lecture on "The Tudor period " to the members of this class on Thursday evening. Mr. J. Le Couteur presided. The Tudor period includes some of the most momentous movements of England's history, and Mr. Craig described them in a highly interesting manner. He also briefly sketched the characters of the monarchs who occupied the throne during that period. On the motion of Mr. Beckett, seconded by Mr. Yates, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer.

- RUNCORN FOOTALL CLUB.—For the ensuing season the following officers have been appointed :—Mr. J. R. Frith, president ; Mr. C. Pownall, secretary; Mr. James Whin- yates, treasurer; Mr. Hugh Hughes, captain of the first team; Mr. W. Wright, sub-captain; Mr. W. Dunbivand, captain of second team; sub-captain, Mr. H. Speakman ; umpires, Messrs. It. Hughes and A. Riley ; auditors, Messrs. W. Brimelow and W. Biley ; general committee, Messrs. H. Andrews, J. B. Clarke, J. Gatley, T. Booth T. Johnson, F. Joule, J Hoffland, H. Wright, J. Littler, J. Booth, J. Stubbs. and W. Hughes. Rtnacotor OPEN AIR CONCERTS —These concerts bid fair to become a most attractive outdoor amusement. On Thursday evening, when the second was given by the National School Band, the vicinity of the market presented a most animated appearance, large numbers of people assem- bling to hear the pleasant strains. Th 3 following programme was gone through with admirable skill and taste:—March of the Peers, "lolanthe," Sullivan; waltz, "Rose of Eng- land," H. Round; contest glee, "The Forest Queen," H. Round; polka, "Pretty Foot," L. C. Desortmes; selection, " A String of Pearls," Lavillediea ; schottishe, "Dora," R. Smith; "God Save the Queen." ST. MICHAEL'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, DITTON.—OD Sunday, the annual charity sermons were preached at this church. High Mass was celebrated in the morning, Father Boenen, of Portico, officiating, with Father Weissmann, as deacon, and Father Amstadt as sub-deacon. Special music was sung by the German College Choir, under the direction of M. Louis Bonvin, in the admirable manner for which they are widely known. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Father Murphy, S.J., of St. Francis Xavier's, Liverpool. At the afternoon service the rosary was sung by the children, and an eloquent sermon was preached by Father Clare, S.J., rector of St. Francis Xavier's College. The morning ser- vice was well attended, but in the afternoon the sacred edifice was crowded. The collections were devoted to the Sunday schools. ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn police Court, OR Thursday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. A. Thomas, a man named Joseph Lowe was charged on remand with hav- ing on the 28th ult., assaulted Joseph Ackerley.—The pro- secutor stated that he lived in Dobson's-court. He was standing in the doorway of his house on the day named when the prisoner came up and asked him if he had any tobacco to give him. That question being replied to in the negative, the prisoner asked for money to buy a "pint," and a refusal again greeting him he struck the prosecutor on the eve, knocking him to the ground.—Mary Jane Wareing corroborated. Prisoner acknowledged that he struck the prosecutor, but alleged that he received provocation.—There was a black list against the prisoner, who was finedrOs and costs, or, in default, a month's bard labour. ALARMING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Thomas Palin, a boy, 15 years of age, who is employed by Mr. Hall, greengrocer and fishmonger, was very seriously injured on Tuesday afternoon. Palin and his master were engaged loading a light cart at the London and North-Western Railway Sta- tion when the horse in the shafts took fright at a passing train and dashed along the street at headlong speed. Mr. Hall, who was in the cart, was thrown into the road, but his injuries were not of a serious nature, and giving chase to the runaway animal he succeeded in stopping it. Vann, who was near the wheel at the time, was knocked down and run over, his thigh being broken and his back badly hurt. He was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, and attended by Dr. Cooper. His injuries were most serious, but he is making favourable pro- gress towards recovery. RUNCORN BRIDGE SLOPE.—Ina few days the new

slope at the Runcorn end of the bridge may be expected to be ready for traffic. Entrance to the bridge will then be gained from Lord•street, where at the bottom of the slope the ticket office has been erected, and the ascent will be much more convenient and easy than when several awkward

flights of wooden steps had to be mounted. Seeing what a long and persistent agitation has been required to gain this improvement from the railway company, our public men cannot do better than at once clamour for improved lighting on the bridge, as under any circumstances they may expect to wait a few years before they obtain what they ask for. Now, only about three gaa lamps light the "weary traveller on his way," and the greater part of the structure in the nighttime is in darkness, a state of things not at all pleasant to those who have the misfortune to often walk across. ROPE ROBBERY AT WIDNES. - Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. John Brock, Thomas Allman was charged on remand with stealing 37Ibs. of rope, the value of £l, the property of Richard Abel. Jos. Robinson, captain of the flat Samuel, and residing in Leinster•street, Runcorn, said the prisoner up to the Bth inst. was " aboard " on the flat. On that day the flat was lying in the canal at Widnes, and he discharged the prisonerjn the evening. Next morn- ing, about 10 o'clock, on returning to the boat he found that three ropes had been cut, and a part of each taken away. He at once went to Bibby's marine stores, where he found the prisoner standing at the door and the ropes on the scales. He told Michael Cannon, the assistant, he had not to pay , any money on them.—Michael Cannon, 15, of the Old Marsh, deposed to receiving the ropes produced from the prisoner on Wednesday morning; and P.S. Robinson stated that he received the prisoner in custody from the Runcorn police.—The prisoner, who is a convicted thief, was com- mitted to the sessions for trial.

EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT OF A RUNCORN WIFE BEA/ER. —At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Arm- strong Waterman, Lyon-street, off Waterloo-road, was brought up in custody charged with assaulting his wife on the 4th inst. With great difficulty Mr. Johnson, the deputy magistrates' clerk, obtained the facts of the case from the complainant, who gave her evidence with great reluctance. She stated that she " crossed " her husband, and he struck her several times with his -fist. He had been previously fined and bound over. She did not wish the prisoner to be sent to prison, and informed the Bench that she would live with him again if he would be comfortable.—Dr. Robinson said he had examined the complainant's face. The bridge of the nose was broken. The injury must have been caused by a violent blow.—Mr. Reynolds (chairman) said the as- sault was a very brutal one. Only in September last the prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, and was bound over for six months for a similar offence. This term had only just ex- pired, and the prisoner would now be sent to gaol for three months with bard labour.

SAD DEATH AT FARNWOUTIL—Under somevrkat strange circumstances Miss Margaret Woodier, 26 years of age, died suddenly at Farnworth, on Sunday. Miss Woodier, who lived with her aunt, Mrs. Latham, Boundary Farm, Burrows Green, left home about ten o'clock for the purpose of attending the Farnworth Wesleyan Chapel. On leaving the chapel at the conclusion of the service she proceeded along Derby-road, but had not walked more than 200 yards when she was seen to suddenly fall backwards, and lie motionless on the ground. There were numbers of people in the neigh- bourhood, and two men named Thomas Burke and John Hewitt went to her assistance. They raised the poor woman from the ground, but with a moan she expired. Dr. Cooper, who was leaving the Parish Church at tke time, examined the deceased, and stated that death had resulted from apoplexy. For some time back the deceased had complained of pains in her head, neck, and left side, and a short time ago, when at Northwich, she was attended by a medical man. The circumstances were reported to the Coroner, who, however, thought an inquest was unnecessary.
DISTURBING SERVICE AT HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Patty Sessions on Monday, a man named James Tidswell Askew, who styles himself a religious lecturer and doctor," was charged with indecently behaving himself in H4ly Trinity Church on the previous evening. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. Mr. W. H. Rogerson, sidesman, said the prisoner entered Holy Trinity Ci4urch on Wmnday night during the sermon. In taking his seat he caused a great disturbance, and the apparitor seeing that something was wrong, took a seat in the same pew as the prisoner. The prisoner made remarks in a loud tone, and told the appari- tor, who asked him to be quiet, to mind his own business. One of the churchwardens also sat near the prisoner and endeavcured to keep him quiet. When the hymn after the sermon was being sung the collection was made, but the box was not offered to the prisoner, who, thinking he had been slighted, went down the aisle after the collector. A member of the congregation noticing that the prisoner was drunk, stopped him, and be was taken outside and given into custody.—The Magistrates' Clerk (to prisoner): Do you want to ask any question ?—Prisoner: I was muttering and talking to myself. I was not aware that I was disturbing the congregation. When he caine with the box I had no money, and I turned my pockets inside out, and, perhaps, that was an annoyance. (To Mr. Rogerson): Did I not go quietly ?—Mr. Rogerson: You made a great noise and caused the congregation to tern their heads.—The prisoner said he had no intention of doing so. He followed the col- lector because be found he had a sixpence which he wished to contribute. He acted quite instinctively, and was mutter- ing and talking to himself, but he was not aware that he had disturbed the congregation. If they wished it he would apologise to the congregation and to the churchwardens, and he would make a public confession. He had no motive in acting as he did. It was done nnder "an excited stimulatien.' He had three or four glasses of beer in the afternoon, and when he went into the church his idea was to go to the Old Church. He was rambling about from one churc4 to another, and in the future he would try not to commit himself.— Mr. Rogerson remarked that the church officials did not wish to press the case, and hoped the Bench would deal leniently with the prisoner.—The prisoner said he was obliged to gain his living promiscuously in Runcorn. He had been an orphan since he was 16 months old, and of rela- tions he had none. He was brought up to the medical pro- fession, and bad been possessed of £3,000. He was DOT out of the profession, and it was very hard for a man 37 years of age to get in again. Ho got his living by painting and lettering signboards, to which trade he had served a little time before be joined the medical profeseion. He was suffering from liver disease, and his nervous system was ex- ceedingly prostrate. Drink consequently acted very strongly upon him, and he was very sorry for what had occurred.— Mr. Reynolds observed that the prisoner, who seemed to have received a superior education, had acted in a disgrace- ful manner, and he would be fined 20s. and costs, or in default a month's bard labour.—Theeprisaner had no money and he was therefore committed to gaol.
ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES. LECTURE BY MR. DEACON.

After many years of persistent effort on the part of the Vicar of Widnes and his parishioners, the new church at Anderson's corner, which will take the name of St. Paul, is likely to soon be an accomplished fact. Labourers com- menced during the past. week to excavate for the founda- tions, and probably by autumn the nave, the only part it is at present contemplated to erect, will be built. The design of the church includes a chancel and a tower, but owing to the lack of the requisite funds this work cannot at present be undertaken. To erect the building in its entirety would, it is estimated, cost about £7,000, but towards this large amount only £3,500 has been obtained. The completion of the whole church is earnestly desired, and efforts, we understand, are to be made to gain this end. On Thursday evening, with the object of aiding the funds, Mr. H. W. Deacon delivered a lecture in the National School. There was a large audience, and the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the vicar, presided. The lecture, which was entitled "Some objects on the sea shore," was illustrated by magic lantern views, the machine being manipulated by Mr. Dritlield. The artistically painted slides, representing marine plants and animals, were the work of Mr. Deacon himself. He explained that he had gathered the materials for his lecture at Torquay, in South Devon, one of the most celebrated places in Eng- land for collecting marine animals and plants; and went 'on to describe various kinds of seaweed, particularly mentioning coraline. By many naturalists this plant was, for a long time considered to be coral. It stem and branches are of a pink colour, filled with chalk, which it absorbes from the sea water, and is of so brittle a nature, that it might be called a living piece of chalk. Representations of the eggs of several kinds of fish were thrown on the screen, these of the cuttlefish appearing like a bunch of grapes. The construction and habits of the dogfish, popularly known as the "English shark/' the limpit, the piddock, fanfish, shipworm, star, jelly, and cuttle fishes were all described in a manner which riveted the attention of the audience, who evinced great interest. At the conclusion of the lecture, Mr. James White proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Deacon, of whom he spoke in eulogistic terms, remarking that the rise and progress of Widnes would ever be coupled with the names of Deacon, Hutchinson, and Gossage. .Referring to the new church, Mr. White, asked could not the money for the completion of the building be found? Was Widnes to remain the black spot of Lancashire, and were they to make it passible for the Bishop to spread the fact that they possessed one vicar, one curate, and a paltry little building called a church to satisfy the requirements of 16,000 persons? He hoped each and all would use their best endeavours to obtain the £3.000 which was required. Mr. Deacon had set a noble example that night; he had set the ball rolling, and it was his (Mr. White's) earnest wish that it might not be stopped until the church was reared as depicted in the architect's design. (Applause.)—Mr. Ather- ton seconded, and the Vicar supported the motion, which was carried, and Mr. Deacon having replied, the meeting terminated.

CONGUGATIONALI33I IN RUNCORN. Sunday Ine was the anniversary Of the Rev. J. D. Thomas's pastorate at reathesda Chapel, Rumen), and to commemorate the occasion he preached special serm,ens on that day. The subject of his meening's discourse, which was listened to by a large con„eregatite, was These fon? years," and was based upon the text "Beech man's work sl;,all be made mani- fest." He said that day he entered upon the fifth year of his ministry in that sacred building. It was .sometimes said that the fifth year Was the most critical in a C,lngregational pastorate. Why it should be so he could not exi.elain, unless it be that four Years amedy sufficed to wear off I he novelty connected with a man's appearance, voice, ma,nnerisms, and modes of thought, and that during the fifth year he was obliged to stand on what he was in himself, entirely unas- sisted by any,attractions of !levelly. He was then aporeci- ated according to his real worth and the genuine work w biele he was able to do. If that be the true explanation, he co uld only hope now that these four years had worn off all t be novelties, and they were come to see him as he was ruei judge him for what he was worth, they would filed him none ; the less appreciable. But it was not with the future he in- tended to deal that day. So far as the future was concerned, let it suffice to say that as far as in him lay his work should be carried on with the same honesty of purpose and constant attentien as it had been in the pest. ft was his desire to consider the past, to ascertain what had been done, and to examine the aims and objects of his ministry in their midst. If there be one feeling uppermost in his heart as he looked back over these four years, it was akin to that which Samuel of old experienced when he took a stone and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, say- ing " Hitherto 'teeth the Lord helped us." Truly %loci had helped them. In looking for- ward to these years, their fears and doubts were many, but their hope was in God, and they had passed them in safety. 'Twas true that some lamentable losses bed been sustained and grave difficulties experienced. Anything less than that was scarcely to be expected. A derelict vessel was not easily recovered and brought into port. But in surmounting the difficulties which beset their path, they believed they had the guidance of God, and should have it in any that might yet remain. It was im- possible to speak of work done without entering into statistic, which, if not startling, were apt to be very dry. Such as he had to lay before them were far from startling, but he would make their dryness tolerable by making them brief. The sermons he had preached numbered about 330, and although many of them might not know it, he had delivered four of them a se.cond time. That number, how- ever, did not include the many short extempore sermons preached on week nights in the Lecture-room and- at St. Luke's. The number of meetings which he had attended and conducted, taking four as the average per week, was 832. And at these meetings he had administered baptism to more than one hundred infants. He had officiated'at 13 weddings, and at more than 60 funerals. Then during these four years he had received by transfer and profession fit ty- five persons into church fellowship. When he came there 97 names were- on the list, and at the end of last year, after carefully revising the list, the names stood at 108. The congregations also showed a considerable increase up to the close of last year. But this year, owing to removals from the town and other causes, there had been a very serioas diminution in-the number of attendants. This was a state of things which could be speedily remedied by individual effort and increased activity on the part of the church as a whole. In regard to the Sunday schools, he was happy to say that during these four years they had reached a higher average of attendances than in any of the former years of its history. The finances also had been prospereus, enabling the treasurer to meet all liabilities and still keep a little in hand for emereencies. The total amount raised bordered close on £1,550. These were all the statistics with which he would trouble them on that occasion, and he had set them before the congregation not for self adulation, but to pre- vent them from altogether losing heart. For small as had I been the results in some of the departments, they showed that with increased faith in God and renewed zeal, it was possible to achieve far different things. But he would re- mind them that in spiritual work the most carefully pre- I Pared statistics did not always give a correct view of things. He entirely repudiated the claim of any statistician to set before them the results of his or any other man's ministry. Had the membership of the church doubled and trebled, he should not look upon it as a correct guage of his work any more than he looked upon the slight increase of eleven as a correct guage of his work. Our blessed Lord did not regard the small company which habitually consisted with Him as the whole of the results of His ministry. He knew that hearts were captivated who had not yet made confession , to Him of their love, and that others were doing good in ' His name who had not yet received any formal commission from Him to do so. If they would form a correct estimate of the good which they had been enabled to perform they must wait. It might be that they would not be able to see the fruit of their labours; the results would be known only after they were gone. His first and chief aim in his ministry had been to make Christ known. Before he came to them, Christ had been the chief theme of his ministry, and he resolved that it should still be his theme in their midst. He had endeavoured to the I utmost of his ability to exhibit Him in the glory of His ' person and in the completness of His relations to the human family. His second aim had been to make it understood that membership in the Christian Church7meant something more than a profession of faith. He had never ceased to represent to them that earnest and energetic action in be- half of Christ, and for the world's good WAS involved in joining the Church. Like the early disciples, they should cease not, both in the temple and at home, to preach and to teach Jesus as the Christ. A father did not put his children on the mantlepiece. He did not want them to be dumb dogs nor showy dolls. He wished them to do something that they might prove by their activity that they have health in their blood and strength in theic loins. And as a Christian pastor he (Mr. Thomas) wished in a like manner that the members of his flock should show by their diligent service and fervent zeal that they bad spiritual health and strength. If ornamental members only were desired they might order them by the score from the sculptor or the toy maker. When Barnabes had come to Antioch and had seen the grace of God, he exhorted the disciples that with purpose of heart they should* "cleave unto the Lord." Now the Lord was always on the aggressive. He was in the thick of the fight. And how could they cleave unto the Lord if they folded their arms and sat down with ease. Cleaving unto the Lord meant to follow Him whithersoever He led. Ruth cave unto Naomi, and therefore did not return to her own people with Orpah. And in like manner, if they bad joined themselves to the Lord, it became them to share the duties and conflicts of the Lord. Mr. Thomas concluded by a reference to the successful efforts be had made to foster social feeling in the congregation.—ln the evening Mr. Thomas preached on "Mistakes about Christ to a large congregation.

div.head: LIVERPOOL ENGINEER'S ADVEN-
div.p: A LIVERPOOL ENGINEER'S ADVEN-
TURES AT HALE.

At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Messrs. H. S. Hall and George Pilkington, a well-dressed man named John Ludden, described as a labourer, was charged on re- mand with committing a highway robbery, accompanied with violence, upon Mr. A. Bertram Aldridge, engineer, West-street, off Fairclough-lane, Liverpool. Mr. J. 0. Swift, St. Helens, appeared for the prisoner. Prosecutor described at length how, on the night of Sunday, the 29th ult., he was at the Wellington Hotel, Hale, in company with his wife and a friend. On leaving, about ten o'clock, he should have driven home, but his companion would not let him drive, and he (prosecutor) and his wife-started off to walk to Liverpool. When near the school-house, at the environs of Hale, a man snatched his umbrella from him and ran off. He followed and caught the prisoner, who had hidden himself behind a gate. A desperate struggle fol- lowed, and the prisoner said " He would swing for him." He kept hold of the man until Police-constable Roberts came up and took him into custody. During the fight he , said to his wife, "Polly, pass me my revolver." He had no such firearm, but made the observation to frighten the pri- soner. Mr. Swift caused considerable amusement by the admissions he obtained from prosecutor as to the number of times he partook of spirituous liquor during the day. The answers showed that he had had about seven drinks between leaving Liverpool and returning from Hale.—After the hearing of the evidence of prosecutor's wife, Mr. Hall said he was inclined to think no judge would convict in such a case, and the prisoner would be discharged.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the Cemetery. The vice-chairman (Mr. Coleburn) presided, and there were present Messrs. G. Moss, T. Norman, Littler, W. Mellor, P. Briscoe, W. F. Salkeld (secretary). —The SECRETARY reported that there had been 35 inter- ments during the month ending the 25th ult., an increase of 13 on the corresponding period last year. The fees received for the "same period amounted to £36 16s; last year, £25 4s ; increase, £ll us 6d. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amount- ing to £9 is, and on the motion of Mr. MOSS, seconded by Mr. LrrreErt, the accounts were passed.—The CHAIR- MAN read the following letter:—" Runcorn, May 9th, 1883. To the chairman of the Runcorn Burial Board. Sir,—We the undersigned, are aware that permission has been given by your Board to Thomas Simkin to letter gravestones in the Cemetery. We also understood that he was to letter the stones himself or arrange with some other person who resides in Runcorn to letter for him. We find that this is not the case, but he has employed some man to act for him who does not reside in Runcorn ,at all. We think this is very unfair towards us, and trust your Board will fully consider this matter and re- fuse to allow this state of things to continue.—We re- main, your obedient servants, JOHN WARD (parish s:xton), THOMAS ROBINSON (stone mason)."—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that Simkin said he would do the lettering him- self or engage someone in the town, and if he had not done so he had broken faith with the Board. The letter- ing he had done was not according to the sample he had showed the Board.—Mr. MOSS said that perhaps that was done in Manchester or Liverpool..—The secretary was in- structed to see Mr. Simkin, sod the Board rose.
THE SMOKE NUISANCE AT ST. HELENS AND WIDNES.

In many parts of South Lancashire and Cheshire—notably in the neighbourhood of Widnes, St. Helens, and Northwich —the long stretches of blackened and sterile fields, the leafless trees, and the withered hedgerows bear forcible wit- ness to the baleful esegs of smoke up.m vegetation. Cer- tainly in the Lancashlfe districts named the emissions from the forests of chimneys which rise sn all sides are of a more than usually poisonous character, as chemical works abound both at St. Helens and Widnes. But in a district like Northwich, the volume of smoke sent out comes chiefly from saltworks, and, with ordinary care, injury to vegeta- tion ought to be avoided. In his last annual report, just published, Mr. Angus Smith, the inspector of alkali works, makes special reference to this sub- ject. All that is necessary to render it in necuous is that the smoke shall be thoroughly burnt. The process of combustion of the black of the smoke does not make the products of combustion pure, but it goes a long way in that direction. "It may, however," writes the inspector, " be said that it is not suffi- cient to burn the carbon. The sulphur acids are not diminished That may be so, but, as I have repeatedly said, the acid gases are always found most on trees, B:c., which are most blackened by smoke." He suggests that allowing this acid to go into the air is more than a nuisance it is a waste, as manufacturers are finding out. "Already great ironworks and cokeworks are washing their smoke and obtaining from it rich products serving the purpose of im- proving other manufactures and of enrich- ing the soil by supplying it with ammonia." Hitherto, manufacturers have had little personal interest in preventing the smoke nuisance ; but when they are once convinced that a district commercial value attaches to the products of combustion, they are likely to be as careful as they are now negligent in so constructing their furnaces as to make the vapour thrown off comparatively harmless. As a remedy for the smoke nuisance in the salt district of Cheshire, Mr. Smith suggests that the coal used should be first converted into smoke and the gas and coke consumed as fuel, while the ammenia and tar are obtained for sale. Ihe black smoke now 80 commonly to be seen would then disappear, the sulphur would in part be made useful, and the cost of fuel would thus be cheapened. I Here, also, a direct appeal is made to the self-interest of manufacturers: and the advantages of improved combustion Ibeing thus made apparent, we may hope in future to see ' fewer blackened fields and blighted trees in the neightour- • hood of our great manufacturing centres. Liverpool Mercury.

From Calcutta it was telegraphed yesterday engagement has been fou4ht between the Ameer of Afghan- istan's troop and the Shinwaris, iwhich the latter were defeated with a loss of 200 killed. A BRIDGE BLOWN UP WITH DYNAMITE: A New York telegram of yesterday says :—According to intelligence from St. Thomas published here, 600 fugitives had arrived at Port-au-Prince from Miragoane, and reported that the rebels had, blown up a bridge at that place with dynamite, killing 200 persons, and injuring the un-, ' number.

div.head: LOCAL MEMBRRS AND THURSDAY NIGHT'S DIVISION.
div.p: LOCAL MEMBRRS AND THURSDAY NIGHT'S DIVISION.

The majority of 165; which defeated the Government on the question of the Collection of Income-tax, included Sir R. A. Cross, Mr. Ecroyd„, Mr. Egerton (Wigan), Mr. Stagg, Colonel Stanley, and Mr. Tomlinson. In the minority of 161 were Mr. Armitage, Mr. Arnold, Mr. Biggs, Mr. Chest- ham, Mr. Cross (Bolton), Mr. Fort, Mr. Grafton, Lord Hartington, Mr. Ilibbert, Mr. Hopwood, Mr. Leake, Mr. Pennington, Mr. Rylanis, Mr. E. L. Stanley, and Mr. Thomasson. One Conservative, Mr. Broderick, and four Home Rulers were in the minority, and ten Liberals, Mr. Brogden, Sir T. Chambers, Mr. Daniel Grant, Mr. Stewart Macliver, Sir W. M'Arthur, Mr. Marriott, Mr. Pugh, Mr. Slagg, Mr. M. Torrene, and Sir Sydney Waterlow, and 15 Home Rulers were in the majority.

Cardinal MacCabe left Dublin on Thursday for the Isle of Wight. The Attock Bridge over the Indus will be opened on the Queen's birthday. A large warehouse at Dundee, iwned, by Morrison, Anderson, and Buchart, mill spinners, was burned down yesterday. In the London Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, a petition for liquidation was presented by Lewin Barnard Mozley, financier, of Lombard-street, trading as Lewin Mozley. The liabilities, secured aud unsecured, are stated as £523,000.

A daring burglary was committed yesterday morning at the residence of a gentleman named Collidge, at Aston, Birmingham. The burglars picked the locks of all the doors and carried away several articles of jewellery. No one has been arrested.

At a meeting yesterday, at Hanley, of the delegates of the North Staffordshire miners, it was decided to resist the re- duction in wages of which notice expires to-day (Saturday), and to strike against it. About 15,000 men were represented. The Congregational Union passed a resolution yesterday, with only three dissentients, regretting that the Affirmation Bill had been rejected. The Rev. Mr. Arnold, of Northampton, moved an amendment which found no seconder.

In the Divorce Division of the High Court of Justice, yesterday, Sir James Hannon granted a decree nisi for dis- solution of the marriage of the Hon. Wyndham Stanhope, brother of Lord Harrington, by reason of his wife's adultery with Lieutenant Walter Adye, of the Royol Irish Rifles. On Thursday afternoon, a man, whose name is at present unknown, jumped out of an express train between Sheffield and Rotherham, receiving such serious injuries that he died at the Rotherham Hospital yesterday. Deceased was appar- ently a working man. A singular death as occurred at Seaforth. A gentleman named Richard Eskrigge, who was 71. years of age, had been out for a run on a tricycle, and on nearing his own house en the return journey he was seen to fall from the machine. Some bystanders ran to his assistance, but when picked up he was dead. The deceased is said to have suffered from heart disease.

Yesterday morning a heavy thunderstorm broke over the Chester district. Repeated peals of thunder occurred, and the lightening was very vivid. Hailstones of great size fell. The storm was very severe during its continuance. The barometer is now rapidly rising, and fine weather is antici- pated. Vegetationi has received a severe check from the ex- cessively cold winds prevailing during the last 10 days.

THE FENIAN PRISONERS AT LIVERPOOL. At the Liverpool Police Court, On Friday morning, Tinnthy Featherstone and Daniel 011erlihy, the two pri- soners from Cork, were again brought up, charge.' with being in illegal possession of explosives.—Mr. Marks, the prosecuting solicitor, applied for a further remand, stating that there was now in custody another man, not in Liver- pool, but whom he proposed to bring up with the other two prisoners on the same charges.—Mr. Quelch, on behalf of the prisoners, urged the prosecution to bring forward the complete evidence as speedily as possible.—Mr. Marks said he hoped to be able to do so on the next occasion.—The prisoners were then remanded until Saturday.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. -- IMPORTANT SUGGESTIONS BY THE COMMITTEE. The Select Committee of the House of Commons on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill resumed their inquiry yesterday, Sir Joseph Bailey again presiding. Mr. Littler, Q C., continued at great length the argu- ments commenced on Thursday by Mr. Aspinall against the scheme, to the effect that the proposed works in the estuary . of the Mersey for the construction of a low water channel I could not be carried out under the Act of the Mersey Con- servancy Commissioners. The promoters, he said, had no power to act upon any autherieation given to them by the Mersey Commissioners, as toe latter had not the power. They only enjoyed the same jurisdiction as had previously been possessed by the Crown, and it could hardly be main- tained that the Crown could have constructed such works under the Bill as drawn. Th e promoters:could not execute the estuary works, and if they attempted to do so any share- holder mLeht apply in Chancery for an injunction restrain- ing them from going on with them. Mr. Pember, Q.C., replied on behalf of the promoters. He said that provisions had frequently been made for improving the channel of the Mersey under the powers now vested in the Conservators. Admitting that it was impossible to make 1 it demonstrably clear that the promoters could carry out ! the works in question if the Bill were passed, he urged that ' all that was necessary was to show an overwhelming pro- bability in his favour, and this he said it was possible to do. But even if there proved to be some slight imperfection in the machinery supplied by former Acts, or if the argument against the application of the promoters' capital to these works could not be set aside during the present session, these were things Parliament should not allow to stand in the way of the ultimate realisation of a project of this kind, which was feasible, beneficial, and innocuous. The Chairman, after protesting against the length to which arguments on the question had extended, said that the committee did not wish, and would be incompetent to express an opinion on the points of law. It was true they had obtained from the House power to inquire into the feasibility or advisability of the construction of those works, but they were really outside the Bill. The interest of the arguments that had been laid before them was only in so far as they affected the mind of the committee as to the passing or rejection of the bill, and the special question for them at the present time was whether they were such as to induce them to throw out the ' Bill. It was obvious that if they should hereafter pass the measure, and the works were executed about the estuary in the canal proper at a cost of say six millions, very great pressure would be put on the Mersey Commissioners, as that amount of money would be actually thrown away un- less the remainder of the works were carried out. Therefore, without expressing any opinion on the Bill itself, which, of course, they had not heard, he thought he ought to state that the committee had considered, and would probably hereafter suggest, provisos something of this nature : that the Manchester Ship Canal should be divided into two sec- tions, the lower section to include such excavations as should give to the company stone enough to complete the contemplated estuary works. They would then probably think it necessary to restrain the company from proceeding with the other section. Ist. Unless and until plans and sections of the works in the former section bad been submitted and approved by the Mersey Commissioners. 2nd. Until the works had been so far completed as to give a certain depth of water at neap tides in the Mersey estuary. 3rd. Unless the Mer- sey Commissioners had satisfied themselves that no injury would accrue to the lower part of the estuary if the works were allowed to go on; and, fourthly, until a certificate that the above conditions had been complied with had been ob- tained from the Board of Trade. The committee did not give these provisos, as those which they had now insisted on having inserted in the Bill. They were open to argument hereafter, but they thought this a prudent course and one which, if the Bill were passtd, they should consider it their duty to adopt. The Committee adjourned till Thursday, the 24th inst.

TLlOing of the Commission for the trial Of the don- spiracy-prljoners was resumed at the Green-street Court-, house yv.tert-lay morning. Mr. Justice 0 Brien took his oeat on Ws bench shortly after eleven, and at that time there was a.good Attendance of special jurors present, and the Crown vas represented by the Attorney-General, Mr. Murphy, Q.C,and M. O'Brien, Q.C. At 25 minutes past eleven Edward o,Brien was put forward and indicted that, on the 10th November, 1881, and on divers other days in 1882, he did conspire with certain' persons unkewn to mur- der certain persons—to wit, public officials. In reply to the usual question the prisoner said—l a= guilty of conspiracy. The Clerk: That is what you arc charged with. Mr. Murphy: Put him back. The prisoner was then removed. —Thomas Doyle was next put forward, and was charged on the same indictment at.t the other prisoner. Prisoner said: I am guEty of common conspiracy—nothing more. I wish I had a chanc of send- ing for my employer ad other gentlemen to give me a charenter.—Mr. Gerald Byrne said he underctood that the prisoner wished to plead guilty to the indictment, but be, asked for a postponement of the sentence, as the prisoner had borne an excellent character-. He had been drawn into. the matter, and when lie found out the nature Olt be ab- sented himself from its meetings,and he thought-it would' be found that he was present at his lawful employment' when a good many of those transactions which had come to. light took place.—Mr. Justice O'Erion said he cctrldnot leave out or consideration that prim-lees name warintro- duced by Ka7anagh as being present when he himself was introduced int'ar this conspiracy.—Mr. Murphy asked that. the prisoner should be put back for the present, and Doyle was accordingly removed. EcliVard M`Caffery, ono of the four directors of the In- vincibles, was next put forward, and charged on a similar indictment. The Prisoner pleaded not. guilty.—The Clerk: Are von rPady for your trial ?-14isoner: If Mr. Walsh is here, I am quite ready.—Mr. Justice O'Brien said Mr. Walsh had been apprised that the trial would take place to-morrow, but he was not in attendance. They would en- deavour to secure his attendance. The prleoner was put back to await Mr. Walsh's attendance. Eentnally at a quarter to twelve o'clock it was decided to calf over the jury' panel, even in the absence of Mr. Walshraud accord- ingly Edward M`Caffrey was again placed in the dock.—Mr. Justice O'Brien explained to the prisoner that the course that they were now taking was preparatory loawearing a jury, and that the trial would not be proceeded 'with until Mr. Walsh arrived. —Prisoner: Thank you my lord.— Mr. Walsh arrived in court at twelve o'clock, during the calling over of the jury, and had a long consul- tation with the prisoner. He subsequently made 30ine com- munication to Mr. Murphy, who at once left the-court in order tsyhold a conversation with the Attorney-General, who wt.., temporarily absent. On the law oirraers of the Crown coming into court, Mr. Murphy expressed dissent to Mr. WalCh, and said they must proceed with the trial. The Clerk tin read out another indictment against the prisoner, which yeas for the wilful murder of Mr. Thomas Henry Burke, an the 6th of May last. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Asked whether he was prepared for his trial; pri- soner said he would like time to have a consultation, with his solicitor, Mr. Walsh.-171timately the prisonez-was put back, and the Commission adjourned till Tuesday next.
