THE CLBA-N REFUGRES.—On the motion that the House at its rising adjourn to Monday, the 21st inst., Sir R. Cuos,s called attention to the case of the Cuban reftgees. He con- tended that Maceo and his companions had been illegally handed over to the Spanish authorities by theßritish police. They had been allowed to land at Gibraltar, and, being es- caped prisoners it was wrong that they should have been so dealt with. It was true that it had been admitted that they had been surrendered by a gross mistake-of the police, but he insisted unwarrantable delay had; taken place on the part of the British Government. In endeavouring to obtain the re-extradition of the unfor- tunate refugees, who, he insisted, had the right of asylum on British territory, he urged all parts of-the House to ex- press their opinion, because on that Maceo's only hope of release from prison existed. Such an act on the part of the Spanish Government would be looked upon as an act of generosity.—Mr. CARTWRIG= did not believe tbe British Government to blame to the extent set out by Sir R. Cross.— Sir H. D. WOLFF insisted that had the. Government acted with vigour and determination the whole of the unfortunate refugees would have been at liberty; but owing to the jaunty conduct of Earl Granville and the timid manner in which the Spanish Government was approached, the pre- sent unfortunate state of affairs had been brought about. Had Lord Palmerstm been alive the position of the matter certainly would have been different.— Sir C. DIME justided the action of the Government. He denied that the English Government had sacrificed General. Baines in order to clear themselves, and contended that no, unnecessary delay had taken place in approaching tho Spanish Government. He defended the answers he had given in November and December last, and denied that ha, had kept back information. That they had approached,the Spanish Government in an unofficial manner at first he ad- mitted was true; but he denied they bad any legal right to demand the re-extradition of the captives. He thought the course that had taken place had been the best that could have been adopted, and it was proved to be so as two out of three of the persons had been released. Had Lord Palmerston been alive matters would not have been different, as he would not have made claims there no right to do so existed.—Sir H. GIFFARD said the Spanish and English Governments between them had been guilty of trickery, fraud, and conspiracy, and the course taken was a direct violation of international law.—The ATTOANIMGENBRAL denied that such was the case, and said had the British Government acted as Sir H. Giffard desired they would have done' and accused the Spanish Government of trickery and fraud in addition tamaking an unlawful demand they might have been engaged in fight- ing battles.—Mr. O'KBLLY condemned the want of spirit shown by the British Government.— Lord FITZMAIIRICR
felt that the violent speeches that had been made during
the debate would not 'facilitate the efforts of the Govern: ment in the direction of the release of Maceo. He denied

that the Government was open to the charge of indifference, but on the contrary, said they had acted, under the circum- stances, in the best course open to them, and censured the acts of their own officials. The result of the action of the Government had been to release two out of three of the prisoners, and notwithstanding all that had been said they did not despair of inducing the Spanish Government to release Maceo himself.—Sir W. LAMSON urged the Government to interfere in order to procure a fair trial for the Ex-Prefect of Police at Alexandria.—Lord R. CHURCHILL expressed a similar Lope, as he was a an who could give important evidence as to the massacre of the 11th of June.—Mr. GLADSTONH promised to do all that the Government were entitled to secur3 a fair trial, and the as-I sistance of counsel. tie defended Lord Ripon from the aspersion cast upon him by Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, and expressed his belief that the noble lerd would not suffer in the good opinion of any man from the censure just passed on him by the honourable member for Eye. Tne Government believed Lord Ripon to be both wise and just, and when ho returned to Eogland, whenever that might be, ho would be received with honour, and as became a man whose name was written on the hearts of the
people of India.—The motion that the Mouse at its rising adjourn until Monday, the 21st inst., was agreed to; and the Report of Supply having been received, the House adjourned at 6-55.
In the House of Commons, on Friday, Mr. T. Egerton presented a petition in favour of Sunday closing trout Buck ow Hill and hnuteford.

CONTROVERSY Ann= A PIGEON.—A man named Isaac Shufflebottom, living at Thatto Heath, was on Fridayisum- moned before the St. Helens Police Court on a charge of having killed a pigeon, valued at 15e, the property of Win. Hilton.—Mr. Riley prosecuted, and Mr. Swift defended.—lt appeared that the defendant and several others had been in a public licuse at Thatre Heath, on the evening of the 29th, nit, and the pigeon In question, which was in the possession of one of the party n..med Lomax, was there killed by the defendant, and the head put into an envelope and sent to Hilton.—Hilton stated the pigeon was his, but it had been lent to Lomax for the purposes of a " homing" society ; on the other hand, however, Lomax stated that the pigeon !E3- longed to him and had been given to him by the complain- ant in return for several presents, and it was by his (Lomax's) directions that defendant had kilkd the pigeon.—The case was dismissed. GREAT LIBERAL DMION3TRATION 1! AT ST. HELENS. SPEECHES BY MR. THEODORE FRY, M.P., MR. W. SUMMERS, M.P., AND MR. W. S. CAINE, M.P. The commendable activity recently shown by the leaders of the Liberal party in St. Helens culminated on Wednesday evening in what was probably the most euccessful political demonstration ever held in St. Helens. The demonstration was held in the Circus, North-road, which is ROW the most capacious building in the town, but notwithstandingits great capacity the whole of the sitting room was fully occupied for some time before the proceedings commenced. Although every arrangement had been made for the convenience of the audience and those who occupied the platform there was no elaborate display of decorations, and all that was visible in the shape of mottoes, were the words " Peace, Retrench- ment, and Reform," in hold lettere at the end of the building opposite the platform. In the interim between the seating of the audience and the taking of the chair, Mr. G. Barton elicited great applause by a rendering of the much appreciated political song " The pilot of the State," and Mr. Fred. Gordon, who is also a great favourite with a St. Helens audience, was enthusiastically encored after singing in excellent style the " Old brigade." Mr. Edward Grime accompanied these vocalists in a skilful manner on the piano, and the audience heartily joined in the choruses of the songs. Scarcely had the applause which greeted the close of Mr. Gordon's encore song subsided, when it was re- newed in even greater volume by the arrival of Lieutenant- Colonel Gamble, the chairman of the evening, and his ac- companying suit of gentlemen, which was composed of not only the leading Liberals of St. Helens and neighbourhood, but also several prominent leaders of their party from Liver- pool, Widnes, Hnyton, Rainhill, Haydeck, &re. It had been expected that the speaker of the evening would have been the Right lion. J. B. Balfour, M.P., Her Majesty's Lord Advocate of Scotland, but, as announced, that gentleman had unavoidably been detained in London on important business connected with the Government. His place, how- ever, was worthily filled by other members of Parliament present, who were Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P. for Scarborough; Theodore Fry, Esq., M.P. for Darlington; Wm. Summers, Esq., M.P. for Staleybridge. The chairman and the others having taken their seats, Mr. George Barton again sung the "Pilot of the State," which was again enthusiastically received, after which the chairman opened the meeting. During the evening an attention was paid to the remarks of the speakers which spoke volumes for the intelligence of the audience, and it is not too much to say that the great en- thusiasm which prevailed was practically unanimous. It is true that on one or two occasions some instances of isolated dissent occurred, but these had only the effect of bringing out with greater force the complete sympathy which existed between the speakers and the audience. The following gentlemen were on the platform : Alderman Cook, J.P., J. C. Gamble Esq., J.P., R. A. Gas- kell, Esq., J.P., H. S. Hall. Esq., J.P., J. E. Johnson- Ferguson, Esq J.P. (Kenyon), Major Richard Pilkington, ' J.P., Charles Pilkington. Esq., J.P. (Haydock), Arthur Sin- clair, Esq., J.P., E. P. Twvford, Esq., M.D., J.P., Robert 13,1eher, Esq., T.C., H. A. liinney, Esq., W. J. Blinkhorn, Esq., Major Bramwell, Jesse Boydell. Eeq., R. G. Brook, Esq., T.C., Thomas Cook, Esq., T' .C. Ciptain Daffy, Cap- tain Dean (Huyton), James Fisher, Esq , TO., W. H. Fos- ter, TO., W. Gamble, Esq., E. J. Grimshaw' Esq., A. Han- son, Esq, T.C., Joseph Hewitt, Esq., Arthur Jamison, Esq., M.D., T.C., Alderman Johnson, H. R. Lacey, Esq., J. B. Leach, Esq., Henry Martin, Esq., D. McKechnie, Esc!' T.C., Surgeon-Major McNicoll, George Parr H. L. Riley, Esq., Alexander Eccles, Req. (1-lnyton);Enstace Carey, Esq. (Widnes), It. Shaw, Esq. (Widnes), T. S. Timrnis' Esq. (Widnes), A. Meikle (St. Helens Examiner), G. W.Raw- lins, Esq. (Rainhill), R. D. Holt, Esq. (Liverpool), A. Bill. son, Esq, E. R Russell (Liverpool), grc. The Cl/AIRMAN, who was received with loud and con- tinued cheers, said it would be unpardonable in him ta oc- cupy five minute e of their time thet was so valuable to them that evening in saying anything that was likely to ha reported as a speech of his. He was very glad, however, that their time would be very much better occupied than in listening to him. But he had a duty to perform as chair- man, the first part of which was not a very agreeable one. That was to tell them the Lord Advocate of Scotland, whom they expected there that evening, could not be present. He had had a letter from him that morning as follows:—" Lord Advocate's Chambers, Home Office.—The Lord Advocate presents hi s compliments to Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble, and regrets exceedingly that it will be out of lie power to have the pleasure of dining with Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble to- morrow and there- after taking part in the Liberal demonstration at St. Helens, as he will be unavoidably detained in London by urgent official duties, as he explained to Mr. Caine.—London, Whitehall, Bth May, 1883." He (the chairman) believes Mr. Caine would be able to tell them how much the Lord Advocate regretted that he could not be with them and make his own excuses. He had two other letters which he thought he ought to read them. The first was from his friend Mr. Holbrook Gaskell—(cheers)—whose connection with Widnes brought him into very close con- nection with St. Helens, and they knew him as a consistent Liberal for a great number of years. His letter wasas follows "Reform Club, Pall Mall, S.W., May 6, 1883.—Dear Sir,— Your letter enclosing tickets for the great Liberal demon- stration at St. Helens on Wednesday next has been for- warded to me here. I greatly regret that my absence from home will deprive me of the pleasure of !Teeing present at the meetiag, which I do not doubt will be very successful. I hope the meeting will not separate without a very decided ' expression of opinion that the right of con- stituencies to choose their own representatives has been seriously prejudiced by the action on a recent occasion of a small majority of the members of the House of Commons, who seem to have decided an important constitutional question iia the spirit of irresponsible members of a private club.—l am, dear sir, yours very truly, Hoe- s/won Gesnien.—John Cotten, Esq, Hen. Sec., Liberal Club,St. Helens,"—The other letter was from the Rev. R. 3. Ward, Whie was at preeent in the Isle of Man. He wrote —"4, Clarence Terrace, Douglas, May 7, 1833.—My dear Mr. Cotton,—l have to thank you for the tickets which you So kindly sent me for the meeting on Wednesday. I am very sorry that absence from home will prevent me from being presnt. I need hardly tell you how heartily I sympathise with the general principles of Mr. Gladstone'e administration; and eenecially -ieith the recent though for liaa present Inefficient attempt to get the House of Commons to be just, and fear not by passing the Affirmation Bill. The spirit of religious intolerance from which my own ecclesiasti- cal ancestors have suffered so much in d ,ys gone by has once more triumphed for the time being, bat it days are awn- bored. Hoping that you will have a pod meeting.—Yours very truly, R. J. WARD—J. Cotton, Esq.—Although, the Chairman eontinued, they regretted the absence of those friends who were not with them that evening he was quite sore he had to introduce to them three gentlemen who hardly needed any introduction to most of them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Fry, of Darlington, and Mr. Summers, of Staleybridge, gentlemen who represented constituencies very like that of 6t. Helens. and who knew the wants of the struggling classes in this country and who knew and appreciated the efforts which had been made by the present Government to assist those classes. Besides them, and though last not least, was their near friend Mr. Caine—(cheers),—of Liverpool, he was about to say—but Mr. Caine, member for Scarborough. He was 3 Liverpool man, aLancazhire mar and as he had been in St. Helens before they knew more about him than he had time to tell them that evening. (Cheers.) He was very glad that they had such a meeting to welcome those gentlemen to St. Helens, and he believed it was the largest political meeting that had ever aesembled in this town. (Rear, hear, and cheers.) lie would now ask Mr. Richard Pilkington to move the first resolution. (Cheers.) Mr. R. FILICINGTON said he had the honour, as they had heard from Colonel Gamble, to move the first resolution. With their permission he would read the resoluticn to them :—" That this meeting expresses its entire and un- abated confidence in her Majesty'e Government, and its earnest hope that her Majesty's Ministers will prolong the present; session of Parliament until the Government measures are disposed of." (Cheers.) It almost seemed unnecessary before so great and so enthusiastic a Liberal audience as the present to press the resolution. Seldom in the history of the country had the government of the king- dom been in the hands of men so distinguished for ability, and so distinguished for high character as the present one —(hear, hear)—and following as they did a Government which was conspicuous for failure—(" no, no," and hear, hear)—in its policy both at home and abroad, and led as it was by England's greatest and noblest statesman --(loud cheers)—it was not surprising that the present Government bad their full confidence and their full support,. (Hear, hear.) But if they would allow him, as the mover of the resolution, he would allude to one or two matters that the Government had had in hand, and that they had vigor- ously dealt with. The first subject that he would allude to was the manner in which they dealt with the Montenegrin -question. In 1880 the united voice of Europe, initiated and

kept up by England, told the Porte to carry out her obliga- tions to Montenegro under the treaty of Berlin. As usual the Porte as:named a warlike attitude, talked about raising troops, and sullenly refused to do anythinge no doubt recol- lecting that the English Government which preceded the present one had often said threatening thing', but had done nothing. (Hear, hear.) A powerful fleet, consisting of the united ships of every power in Europe went to the Adriatic, and after some time had been wasted in trifling by the Porte she was shown that Europe meant what she said; and she was obliged te carry out her obligations under the treaty of Berlin to the brave little state Montenegro. (Hear, hear.) In a similer manner England, under the guidance of Lord Granville, suggested to Ecrope that the question as to Greece should ease be settled; and the Porte was again requested to carry out her engagements under the same treaty to the little state of Greece. The same operations were again gone through, the fleet had again to show that force was meant if fair -words would not accomplish their purpose, and again the unit-ad voice of Europe, which the former Government had neoesr been able to bring to bear on the Porte, had thedesired effect, and Greece got the territory that was given to her under the treats,- of Berlin. (Cheers.) In all these matters the Government showed a firmness, a patience, and a con- sideration that the late Government had never shown in its dealings with the other Powers of Europe—(hear, hear); and in the course of their efforts to unravel the entangle- ments that had been produced by the late Government, and to carry out the onerous obligations entered into by that Government the present Govern- ment of Mr. Gladstone had found itself face to face with a far more serious and arduous task. Early in 1882 affairs in Egypt were in confusion, and were much aggravated by the Joint Control—a creation held to and, they migkt almost say, brought about by Lord Salis- bury himself. These affairs in Egypt came to a crisis. Arabi, an officer in the army, rebelled against the Khedive. He secured the support of the army, and he defied the Khe- dive and the joint powers England and France. He believed that France immediately remcnstrated, but that remonstrance was treated with the most perfect contempt by Arabi, who was backed up by his master the Sultan, who secretly tried to foment disturbance and encouraged Arabi to resist Eng- land and France an the Khedive. Well, the ambassadors of the powers met at Constantinople, where a conference was held, but the Porte desiring to evade it sent a commissioner, Dervish Pasha. to Cairo. At this moment the massacre in Alexandria took place, and Dervish Pasha had the impu- dence to say that everything was satisfactorily arranged, and at the same time be decorated Arabi. The Tiezes cor- respondent wrote from Constantinople in that comforting and consoling kind of way the Riper so much rejoiced in, to say that England was completely isolated, and Lord Salisbury said that the nave demonstration had demonstrated nothing except the impotence of England and the feebleness of the Ministry. At a time when he ought to have stuck to the country, and stuck to the Government, Lord Selisbery could sly that. However,the ambassadors of the powers,giftecl with more fore- sight than that amiable and sagacious nobleman—(laughter and cheers)—advised the Porte to give way. But the Porte was stupid, and, after strong remonstrances from the Eng- lish admiral, to prevent Arabi raising the defences of Alex- andria and putting the guns in position against the British ' fleets the British admiral was obliged to blow those forts to pieces. No one would go with Enrlend, no one would send troops to help her. However, the Forte seemed desirous of so doing, but Lord Dufferin stipulated that if the Turkish troops put foot in Egypt they would have to be under the command of the British general, and that the Porte should proclaim Arabi a rebel. The Porte would not do this, and the negotiations proceeded with masterly inactivity until September, 1892, when one fine morning the Sultan awoke, and, to his dismay, found that Arabi was a prisoner, that the Egyptian army was dispersed, that Cairo was in the hands of the British, and that his power was gone in Egypt, and let them hope it would never return. (Loud cheers.) He would like to ask those present, and if Lord Salisbury were present he should also like to ask him— where was the impotence of the English people, and where was the feebleness of her Majesty's Ministers ? (Cheers.) Now in all these affairs the conduct of the present Govern- ment was as different from the canduct of the last Govern- ment as light was from darkness. (Cheers.) The late Government in all its negotiations with foreign powers was continually resorting to high-handed threats and circulars which meant nothing, saying that the British Government wanted this, that and the other, and would he offended if they did not get it. They were always talking of the interests of England, and when their representatives went to Berlin they said they went to advocate the rights of Europe, and would see every treaty before it was made, while at the same time they had secret treaties with two of the powers represented at Berlin. ("Shame.") They also came from Berlin, hav- ing thrown over Greece and Montenegro, and when they come to London they said they had brought "peace with honour." (Loud laughter, and a voice "so they did." Another voice: " How about the Kilmeinham treaty P" Laughter, and interruption.) How different was the way in which all the arrangements of the present Government were carried out! They not only admired their actions and the ability with which they were carried oet, but they also ad- mired the fairness and consideration that the Government had shown all through to the nations of Europe with which they had had to deal. (Cheers.) And not only in these foreign matters had, the Government done well. They found the same policy, the same just and true spirit pervading their domestic legislation. They had ruled the country well. They had brought order out of chaos in the financial affairs of the country. (Hear, hear.) They had surpluses where before they had deficits, and to a very large extent the Government had paid off the debts con- tracted by their predecessors. To the sister island the Go— vernment had granted irnpertant measures of reform —(hear, hear)—at the same time saving that country from sedition and famine. (Hear, hear.) Another important thing that the Government had done was that they had passed the new rules of parliamentary procedure, which they trusted would expedite the despatch of public business. But the greatest of all the reasons why they ought to sup- port the present Government, and why they ought to pass the resolution was, because at the head of the Government they had that great chief Mr. Gladstone. (Loud cheers.) For six years, while in Opposition, he carefully and faith- fully watched the policy of the Government, which was generally dangerous and often wicked, and he warned the country what would be the consequences of it if pursued. Besides all that, he had, when returned to power, secured for the country the honour that it ought to have amongst the natien3 of Europe—(hear, hear); and the peace, the retrenchment, and the reform that it ought to have at home—(hear, hear) ; and the wish of every good Liberal was that he might long be spared—(hear, hear,)—to redress their wrongs—(cheers),— to sympathise with every class—(cheers),—and to animate with his splendid spirit the able men who at the present time form with him the Government of the country. (Cheers.) He had great pleasure in moving the first resolu- tion. (Loud cheers.) Mr. H. S. Haar., J.P., who was received with loud ap- plause, said he had the honour and the pleasare of second- ing that resolution of confidence in her Majesty's Govern- ment as proposed by " our " Mr. Pilkington. (Cheers.) He was sure they could not be too thankful that they had such a Government, such a pure, honest Government as they now had. (Cheers ) They had reduced tho taxes, as Mr. Pilkington had said, they had paid their way as they had gone along, and they had paid a lot of old back reckonings —(laughter and cheers)—which the late Tory government left them. (Cheers, and a voice: "What about the income- tai? ") To sound finance they could not attach too much importance in a commercial country like this. (Hear, hear-) It produced confidence all round, and it had already led to a great improvement "...in trade, and he did not see any reason why that improvement should not continue. The government had also given them the blessings of peace. (Hear, hear.) Now.; it 11,a,5 a very strange thing that they never could have peace with a Tory government. (Cheers.) They seemed to have a faculty for getting into wars; and another thing they could say was that they could not have retrenchroeht with a gunpowder and glory policy. 1(1,--=ear, hear, and laughter.) They coulg hot txpect retrenchment from any Ter y Government that ever lived or would live. (Loud cheers and laughter.) One word with regard to Her Majesty's Opposition. Legitimate opposition in a free country like ours was a right thing, but obstruction was altogether another thing. (Hear, hear.) They had only to take up the daily papers to see what was going on in the House of Commons, They would see Home Rulers and the Fourth Party allied with the party which called itself Conservative and constitutional. (Cheers, and a Voice : "What did Gladstone do when in opposition?" and some dis- turbance.) Ho would not take up their time much longer, because they were all most anxious to hear the distinguished members of Parliament they had the honour to see on the platform. There was one thing, however, he would just say in conclusion and that was that he hoped the ministry would stick to the measures that they had now before Parliament, aye, even if the grouse got a respite. (Loud laughter and cheers.)

Mr. TWRODORR FRY, M.P. (Darlington), in supporting the resolution, referred to the glorious battle that had been fought in Liverpool. (Great cheering.) The election in Liverpool had invigorated the whole of the Liberal party, and, he hoped, invigorated to a large extent the Liberal enthusiasm of Lancashire. He came from the county of Durham, where they had 12 Liberal members out of 13. (Cheers.) At that time Punch called them the most notorious county in the kingdom, and they would be glad if the county of Lancaster should be as notorious as theirs, be- cause he could assure the:n they had no wish in their dis- trict to monopolise the good things in reference to this matter. (Applause.) Ho was glad to see so many ladies present, and he would be one of those who, if the oppor- tunity arose, would vote for getting the women ratepayers of Lancashire on the electotal roll. (Cheers.) There was one thing which struck him as a stranger coming to .St. Helens for the first time, and that was why they had not got a member for themselves. (Applause.) He could assure them that when he saw the long list of local narnes appended to the handbill which was sent to him he felt that, surely, there was no need for any of them to go down to St. Helens to plead the Liberal cause, because there was an abundance of local talent who could speak well of the Government. (Applause.) He should be glad if that meeting would have the effec': of raising in any way the i Liberal feeling n that district, and if when the next o'ppor- tunitv came they should strengthen the hands of the Liberal party in endeavournlg to return Liberal members for that division of Lancashire. . But, in the long run, the Libral party had always been successful. It advanced slowly, but surely, until it aCcotnplished the work it was determined to perform.

structionist party. They obstructed only upon Irish measures, and only upon those measures when they believed that the liberties of their fellow-Irishmen were in danger. (Cheers and laughter.) No one could point out a single English eneasnre which had been obstructed by the Irish party during the present session. Reference had been made to that arch-obstructionist, the future leader of the Conservative party, Lord Randolph Churchill. (Laughter.) In a single session of the present Parliament he addressed the House 353 times on 80 different subjects. He, of course, knew nothing about any of them. (Loud laughter.) The less one knew about a thing the longer it took to speak about it. A great many other members had done the same thing, and it seemed to him that it now took a parliament to do the work of a sessien, and if they went on like that, the sooner they had a new reformed Parlia- ment the better it would be for them. (Cheers.) He hoped the policy of the Government would be to insist upon pass- ing the measures to which they stood committed for this session, and that next session they would bring in two great measures upon which they would stake their existence. (Cheers.) The first was a sound county government bill for the United Kingdom, and the second a measure equalising the county franchise through- out the Malted Kingdom, and meaning a fair and equitable distribution of political power. A Parlia- ment elected upon a new franchise would not, in his opinion, stand any nonsense from such men as Lord Randolph Churchill, even though he would go back as minority mem- ber for Manchester. (Laughter and cheers.) The present House of Commons professed to represent the people of this country. Two-fifths of the householders of the community bad no voice in this Parliament at all, and the consequence was minorities were able to overweigh and outvote majori- ties. A division would be possible in the House of Com- mons in which 150 members might be in the " Aye " lobby, and 500 members in the " No " lobby, and the 150 out- voted by the 350 might represent the majority of the people in this country. (Hear, hear.) That was a thing that should no longer be allowed to exist. It was a positive fact that 18,500,000 of people in this country returned 150 members to the Reuse of Commons, while only 17,500,000 returned 500 members. It had been rightly said that during the last ten or a dozen years the Liberal party in Ireland had been steadily increasing. The Parnellites claimed to themselves to be the representatives of Ireland; and certainly if going to the front and asserting themselves on all possible occasions, and insisting upon being heard whenever Irish matters came forward, was any test, they were the Irish party. But they did not represent the majority of the people of Ireland. They did not represent half the constituencies, and not more than a third of the electors. There were 49 Home Rulers in the House of Commons, and they represented 1,860,000 of the Irish people—the population of their con- stituencies. There were 26 Liberals who repre- sented 2,040,000 of the Irish people. (Hear, hear.) There were 26 Tories who represented 1,260,000 Irish people. Therefore, taking the aggregate representation of the various sections of political parties in Ireland, the Liberals represented the majority of the Irish people. Those figures by proportionate representation might easily be reversed, and would give 40 Liberals, 35 Tories, and 27 Home Rulers; and he believed those figures very fairly re- presented the opinion of the Irish people with regard to the present Government, the Parnellites, and the Tories. If the existing franchise in Ireland prevented their reaching the precise political opinion of that country, the sooner it was got rid of the better, and that we know whether or. not Ireland was Parnellite, Home Rule, Revolutionary, or what not. (Cheers.) For instance, Dublin and Belfast— the two largest borough constituencies in that country returned, the former two Liberals, and the latter two Conservatives. The largest county in the south—county Cork—the largest in the north—Donegal —and Galway in the west returned Liberals—Gladstonites ; the county of Mayo in the far west—the poorest, most over- crowded, and the most rack-renting, the one was O'Connor Power, the most uncompromising opponent of the Land League policy in the House of Commons, and the other the Rev. Isaac Nelson, who had the windows of his house in Belfast smashed because he issued a manifesto against the Land League. He mentioned this to show that the majority of the Irish electorate was in favour of Gladstone and the Government, and not in favour of Mr. Parnell and his policy. (Cheers.) Reverting to the fact that two-fifths of the householders of the United Kingdom had no direct voice in returning representatives to the House of Commons, he said there was no trade in the country whose picked workmen were not subject to wholesale disfranchisement in consequence of accidental location. A glassblower who worked in Birmingham, Sunderland, or Newcastle could vote for two members of Parliament. By living in St. Helens the same workman would be disfranchised, being disquali- fied by the £l2 rating. Living in Crewe were the picked workmen of the United Kingdom in the engineering trade, for there they got good wages, steady employment, and capi- tal houses, provided for them by the railway company. At a recent meeting he attended he asked those who had votes to signify, and 170 hands were held up in an assembly of 1,300 people. He asked every householder who had not got a vote to do the same thing, and 300 or 400 hands were held up. But let those men remove to Deroy, and they could help to return two members—one the biggest man ;n the House of Commons, Sir William Harcourt, and the other one of the biggest brewers. Supposing one of these workmen got discharged from Crewe for drunkenness, he could go to Peterborough and have a vote for two mem- bers of Parliament, whilst those remaining in Crewe were disfranchised. The little town of 'Whitby, with a popula- tym of 14,000, returned a member to the House of Commons, whilst Lowestoft, a town four times the size, was disfran- chised. The colliers of Murpeth could return a man to the House of Commons; but the miners of South-West Lanca- shire had to be content with whoever their masters chose for them. (Laughter and cheers.) His friend Mr. Fry had a lot of workingmen in his employ, and they had all got votes. He did not know whether they all voted for Mr. Fry—(laughter)—but supposing that gentleman got slack and had to " sack " some of his men, and they took train across to Barrow-in-Furneas and got work there. Barrow-in-Furness was twice the size of Darlington—and he did not suppose that Mr. Fry would quarrel with him for saying that it was a very much more important centre of industry than Darlington—but the moment they got there they were disfranchised. Take, for instance, the cotton trade. A man spun cotton in Clitheroe, with 14,000 inhabitants, and could send a member to the House of Commons. If he went to Accrington with 40,000 inhabitants, Darwen with 35,000, or half-a-dozen other towns that could be named, he became disfranchised. So with the woollen trade. If a man made linsey-woolsey pet- ticoats in Kendal he could vote for Mr. Cropper, but if he went to Keighley he would not have a vote there. There was another hardship. There were certain districts in this country which were called boroughs, but which were not urban in their character, but purely agricultural, such as Buckingham and Launceston. Launceston was so agricultural that the man who was returned for it was disfranchised because he gave the rabbits to his tenants. (Laughter.) Oh, it was a positive fact. (Renewed laughter.) He was a gin-spinner from Manchester, who bought an estate, and bought the borough along with it, and a gentleman named Drinkwater went down from Manchester to contest the borough with him. The gin-spinner got so frightened that when his tenants came to him and said unless he gave them the rabbits they would not vote for him, he said "Then you shall have the rabbits," and there was such a slaughter of rabbits that day in Launceston as was never known before. (Laughter.) Then when the election was over, and Mr. Deacon was returned at the head of the poll, Mr. prinkwater petitioned. The court sat, the rabbit business was proved, and it was the shortest petition ever heard. It did not last two hours, and Mr. Deacon was unseated. There was a place which was purely agri- cultural in its character. ( Laughter.) Then there was Aylesbury, which supplied London with milk and ducks; that was the trade of the place—ducks and milk. (Laughter.) Now, the people who in Aylesbury fed ducks and the people who in Launceston trapped rabbits had votes, whilst the Scotch shepherds, the best educated working men in the country, the Yorkshire dalesmen, and the Warwickshire agricultural labourers, who would very much like to send Mr. Joseph Arch to the House of Commons, had no votes. What a shame that Morpeth could send Mr. Burt to the House of Commons, anti Stoke-upon-Treet could send Mr. Broadhurst, and the other labouring classes he had named could not be directly represented there, as they ought to be. Tens of thousands of men all over the country who left the slums of the town and went to live in the suburbs where they could lead more respectable lives were disfranehised. All thia injustice could only be set right by giving householders in counties the same right as they had in boroughs. (Hear, hear.) He should like a simple one- clause bill for the United Kingdom—a residential rating bill. He did not see why he should be able to vote for 16 members of Parliament. It was a positive fact that he was represented by 16 members in the House of Commons, and they were nearly all Tories. (Laughter ) He should just like to give them a little idea of the absurdities and incon- gruities which existed in the representation of the country. Some ten years ago, or more, he had the honour of being asked to contest his native borough of Liverpool. He fought it and was beaten, though he polled very nearly 18,000 votes. He had since had the curiosity to find out how many members there were in the House of Commons whose aggregate votes did not reach 18,000, and be found that there were 72 members whose aggregate votes did not reach the number he polled in Liverpool. It was very hard, it seemed to him, that these 72 little trumpery boroughs should have 72 seats in the House, whilst the 18.000 elec- tors who voted, rightly or wronsly, for him in Liverpool could not get their candidates in although be polled more votes than any man in the House of Commons except the man who beat him. Since then 2,000 votes had given him what 13,000 could not do. The boroughs of Bridport, repre- sented by Mr. Warton ; Eye, represented by Mr. Ashmead Bartlett; and Woodstock, which returned Lord Randolph Churchill, who represented the Duke of Marlborough— (laughter)—had between them a populatioa of only 20,000, and yet they had the same influence in the House of Commons as Liverpool with 500,000 inhabitants nay three times the influence, for the minority clause reduced the representation of Liver- pool to one—but the same influence as Glasgow and Birmingham, with their three members each. Whilst these three small places bad representatives, there were other places, such as St. Helens, which had no share in the repre- sentation. (Cheers.) When the last great Reform Bill was Passed, in 1832, there were then all soils of villages which sent members to Parliament. There were now districts with populations of 200,000 without representation. Wands- worth Union, including Battersea, with a population of 210,000, was entirely without representation. That state of , affairs mutt be remedied. Did they expect a Tory Govern-

ment to do it ? (Cries of "No.") All be had to say wai that if they returned Sir Richard Cross for South-West Lancashire without getting an :opinion from him now on that question they were not the sort of people he took them for. What was to be done ? He was no great advocate of what was called fancy franchises. He was quite content to proceed on the old lines, and he shoul:I be quite ready to disfranchise a sufficient number of small constituencies to meet the wants of the great constituencies, and so that they might be adequately repre- sented. (Cheers.) If they disfranchise all the boroughs under 10,000, and teck away one member from all the boroughs of 20,000 who returned two, that would give 96 seats available for re-distribution; and if they went a step further, and took away the representation from boroughs of 15,000, and one member from boroughs of 30,000 with two members, they would have 134 seats for re-distribution. If they went so far, it would be impossible for the claims of St. Helens to be ignored. He hoped that before the next election came they would meet in that circus, not merely to hear speeches in favour of the equalisation of the borough and county franchise and the re-distribution of seats, but that they would meet to listen to an address from a candi- date of their own choice, and that they would send him to represent them in the House of Commons with the com- manding majority which that meeting would lead him to expect. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was then put and carried with great enthusiasm.

Dr. McNicola, who was received with applause, said he was sure that meeting would be of one accord in going along with him when he read the following resolution :—" That the hearty thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. Fry, Mr. Summers and Mr. Caine for their kindness in coming from their Parliamentary duties to be present at that meeting to help the Liberal cause, and for the excellent addresses that they have delivered." (Cheers.) He was sure they would agree that by their presence on that occasion, by their ring- ing and eloquent voices—for they all had good voices—by their vigour and by their argument, and more especially by the Liberal and noble sentiments which they expressed, and by the statesmanlike views which they enunciated,they had done a great deal towards kindline the enthusiasm of that meeting, and had stirred up, by add ing fuel to the Liberal fires which sometimes smouldered a little bit. Their speeches, as it were, had saved those present the trouble of going to St. Stephen's—they had had there a St. Stephen's that night. The chairman had been the Speaker, and they all had been in the strangers' gallery. (Loud cheers.) Alderman Joirersoer, who was cordially received, said he had pleasure in seconding the resolution which had been proposed by Dr. McNicoll, and he thought it was of great importance to the people of St. Helens that they should have the opportunity from time to time of listening to suc': gentle- men as they had had the pleasure of listening to that night, and he hoped the Liberal party would take the opportunity a little oftener of bringing persons down to St. Helens such as had been before them that night, and lay before them the cause of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) And he had no objection whatever to the Tories being brought down also, as it allowed the people of St. Helens to listen to both sides, and those who were willing to do most for them let them , win. A resolution had been moved With respect to the lowering of the county franchise and the re-distribution of seats, and mention had been made of that audience there that night, and he asked from those gentlemen that when the day arrived that they would bring back their memory to that evening, and that they would bring back before their minds' eye that audience and he asked that when that fine old man they had in London—(loud applause)—introduced that measure—he (Alderman Johnson) hoped he might have the pleasure of introducing it—they would rise on their part and advocate the cause of the people of St. Helens, and would tell Parliament that with a population of 60,000 or more this town had not any direct representation. The time had now come when they thought that ought to be rectified; and that with its peculiar interests—its menu- ! , factures of glass, its alkali, and its copper—St. Helens should take part in the councils and deliberations in debat- ing Acts of Parliament of this great and glorious country. (Loud cheers.) Mention bad been made of the time which might arrive when Mr. Gladstone might no longer be able to take the control he now took in the government of this country, but he (Alderman Johnson) would say on the part of the people of St. Helens that when that day did arrive he might have the consolation and the happiness in his own family circle of being able to think that he had done much for the advantage and benefit of his fellow-men. (Loud cheers.) Mr. FRY responded on behalf of Mr. Summers, Mr. Caine, and himself, and thanked the meeting heartily for their very sincere vote of thanks, and for the very cordial reception they had given them. Mr. Summers and himself were there for the first time, but Mr. Caine was an old friend of theirs. They could not, however, take all that kindness to themselves, but they took it because they came there to represent Liberal principles, which they believed were as dear to the audience as they were to the speakers. (Cheers.) They hoped those principles would grow and prosper in St. Helens. and that the next time they came there they should come and find that they had a member of their own —(cheers)—and, he hoped, who represented them on the Liberal side. (Loud cheers.) All that he had to say in reference to the Liberal Association in this town would be best said in the words of a tradesman whom he once saw looking through a list of persons who owed him debts. Against one or two names he saw the letters S. T., and he asked what it was those letters meant. The tradesman re- plied "These are very bad cases, and the letters S. T. means 'stick to them "—(laughter and hear, hear)—and he (Mr. Fry) hoped they would stick to the Liberal Association of this district. (Cheers.) He then moved a very hearty vote of thanes to Colonel Gamble for the very kind way in which he had presided over that meet- ing that evening. (Loud cheers) Mr. It. D. HOLY, chairman of the Liverpool Liberal Association who was received with loud applause, seconded the motion, and expressed a hope that although that meeting was the first of its kind it would not be the last ouri . He was sure after the experience they had had in a neigh- ' b •ng town that the more meetings they had and the more they talked about Liberal principles the stronger they ; grew, and the more united they became. (Cheers.) I Mr. CAINE also responded, and said that in view of St. i Helens becoming a constituency in the future, the better it would be for them to hold as many meetings as they could so as to educate the constituency, because educated con- stituencies were always Liberal constituencies. (Hear, hear. and laughter.) The vote of thanks was then accorded by acclamation. The CHAIRMAN, in responding, was somewhat indistinctly I heard owing to people leaving the building. He said he ; thanked them very much for the way in which they had expressed their thanks to him for the little time he had t given to presiding over that meeting. He could not sit down without telling them that very much of the success of that meeting was due to Mr. Leach and Mr. Martin, who were the means of obtaining the presence of their friend Mr. !Cain and the other gentlemen who had spoken so eloquently ' and given them so much information that evening. (Hear, hear, and Cheers.) He hoped that that meeting would be the commencement of more frequent meetings of the Litoral party in the town. He quite agreed with the remarks asio the community becomigg more educated, and therefore more Liberal. (Hear, hear.) He trusted, therefore, that they would have more frequent opportunities of hearing such gentlemen as they had heard that night, and that more earnestness would be shown in bringing up the rising genera- tion of their country. (Loud cheers.) The meeting then terminated.
LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE BAND OF HOPE UNION.

The half-yearly conference and meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union, under the auspices of the Liverpool Band of Hope Union, was held on Saturday, in the lecture room of the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion, Mount-pleasant. At the afternoon conference Mr. J. Earnshaw, of Manchester, presided, and among those present were the following; The Revs„ J. Johnson, J. K. Kirby, A. Holland, Messrs. C. H. Srott, William Hoyle, W. B. Suttle (Openshaw), T. Hallsworth, Robert Brown (Manchester), Theodore Gregory, and T. E. Hallsworth, the honorary secretary. Encouraging reports were received from the following towns respecting the operations of the society; —Ashton, Burnley, Chorley, Denton, Glossop, Liverpool, Manchester, Openshaw, Rochdale, Huyton, and St. Helens. Over sixty delegates from these and other towns were present. The Rev. E. Franks, of Wigan, delivered an interesting address en "The bearing of temperance principles on the more successful teaching of the youth in our day and Sunday schools." He argued that systematic temperance teaching was an urgent necessity in both Sunday and day schools, and said it was also necessary to make the Sunday schools as attractive as possible.—Mr. WILLIAM HOYLE, of Man- chester, moved a resolution to the effect that the confer- ence rejoiced in the SUCCeS3 of the Gospel Temperance and Blue Ribbon Mission, but hoped and trusted that neither that nor any other kindred movement would b.t permitted to interfere with the regular work of hands of hope. The conference also called upon band of hope conductors to remain faithful in the discharge of their duties, and to recognise their responsibility in the all-important work of training the youth of our cauntry in habits of temper:ia?ce. Mr. Isaac MILLEra, of Liverpool, seconded the proposition, which was carried after some discussion.—ln the evening a largely-attended public meeting was held in the lecture- hall of the Young Men's Christian Association. Mr. Aloer- man lihallcross presided, and he was supported by the Revs A. Haworth, S. K. Hocking, J. Johnson, Enoch Franks, Messrs. M. Bebbington, John Brown, J. Hargrove, W. J. Sutcliffe, William Hoyle, and T. E. Hallsworth (county secretaries), and C. T. Fielding and Lot Whitworth (local secretaries). The chairman spoke of the advantages of sobriety and of the energy with which temperance was being promoted by the adherents of the various bands of hope. In Liverpool these associations had been by no means idle during the past year. In 1882 seven new branches were formed, and there were now 95 branches in all, having 14,970 members, an increase of 1,059 on the preceding year. There had been 2,062 meetings held, at which 193,497 par- sons attended and 3,642 pledges were taken, whilst no fewer than 40,000 temperance publications were circulated by the different branches during the year. The entire union com- prised 830 branches, with a membership of 136,873. (ap- plause.)—The meeting was also addressed by the Rev. A. Haworth and the Rev. Silas K. Hocking, of Manchester, and the proceedings were varied with musical selections by the choir of the Liverpool Young Men's Temperance Asso- ciation. The conductor was Mr. Joseph Hartley, and the accompanist Miss Hartley, Mr. Joseph Dixon leading.

div.head: T:- ES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: T:- ES LOCAL BOARD.

1M onthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. F. H. an Gossage prebided, d there were present- Dr. O'Reefie, Messrs. E. Carey, P. H. Pankhurst, T. Handley, D. Wright, S. Sadler, S. W-ebster, J. E Johnson, J. Houghton, B. Dutton, Hoyle (depetty clerk), Carr (gas engineer), and. Dickson (nuisance inspector).

SULICUARG B. A letter WAS read from the Local Government Board asking for the Board's observations upon the surcharge of £383 18s 2d made upon Mr. Dun, the treasurer, by Mr. Hazle- hurst, the auditor. The letter was referred to the Finance Committee. _ .

BOWERS BROOK A GLARING EVIL. The following letter was read Whitehall S.W., 26th 1883.—Sir,-1 am directed by the Local Government Board to forward you herewith for the consideration of the I Widnes Local Board, a copy of a letter which has been addressed to the Board on behalf of the London and North- Western Railway Cempany complaining of the nuisance and injury alleged to be caused by the discharge of liquids from certain chemical works at Widnes into the Bowers Brook, together with an extract from a report which has been ma,le to the Board on the subject by their inspector, Dr. Angus Smith. The Board request that they may be furnished with the observation of the Locil Board with regard to the complaint of the Itiilway Company. —I am. sir, your obedient servant, WALTER SENDALL."— The letter from the railway company called the att mtion of the Local Government Board to the nuisance and injury done to the company's proparty at Widnes owing to certain chemical manuf cturers continuing to discharge noxious liquids into the Bowers Brook, the c3nsequence being that a great nuisance was created and considerable injury in- flicted upon the company. Although the attention of the manufacturers had been called by the company's officials to the inconvenience created by their action, they had hitherto taken no steps to abate such nuisance, and he was therefore directed by his clients to call the attention of the Board to the pollution which was causing the company so much in- jury. An extract from Dr. Angus Smith's report was enclosed. It stated that the brook received Some impurities before it entered Widnes. From the Tharsia Copper Works it received solutions of sulphate of soda and sulphate of iron. From the Widnes Alkali Works it received acid, and chloride of calcium ; and from Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, where an increase of the same salt was obtained. When the salts above named, sulphates and chlorides met, ' they ferried a deposit of sulphate of lime or plaster of Paris. The precipitate was very abundant, and very soon filled up that part of the brook immediately outside ef Messrs. Muspratt's works. The Loudon and North-Western Railway Co. had hitherto cleared the brook from the deposit, but were unwilling to continue to du so. A large quantity of deposit was carried beyond the point alluded to in the complaint, but as the brook became covered it was not easy to now the condition below. After a time, however, the flow was sufficient to drive forward a large amount of the solid matter into the channel of the Mersey. There could be no doubt of the amount of the deposit. It was a great and glaring evil.—Mr. MARTLEY asked if the water in the brook was used for domestic pur- poses. (Loud laughter.)—The CHAIRILLN observed that the fact of the matter was that the railway company were tired of clearing the brook. He thought the Board 'would have some influence with the manufacturers in making an arrangement. —The subject was referred to the Sewerage Committee, on the motion of Mr. CAREY. A.NNE-STIVILET CROSSING.

The Darter: CLERIC read the following letter:—" The Widnes Alkali Company, Limited, 30th April, 1883.—James T. Allen, EK.—The Widnes Local Board, Widnes.—Dear Sir.—Referring to yours of the 27th inst., it appears that the action of the Local Board was not as efficient in obtain- ing protection for Anne-street crossing as for that in Waterloo-road. Wa beg to call the attention of the Board to the evidence of Mr. Wor- thington given on behalf of the Railway Company before the Committee of the House of Commons that the road was closed for 5i hours out of the 12. This appears unreasonable, and we find that two fifths of the occasions in which such closings occur are for shunting or other operations thou the legitimate one of allowing trains to pees and we hops this subject will receive the attention it deserves at the hands of the Local Board.—Yours respect- fully, C. L. Barlow Secretary.—Mr. SADLER said he did not think that Mr:Worthington ever made such a state- ment. How was it that the Board did not find that out when they had a man stationed there ?—Dr. OTBEFFE re- marked that perhaps Mr. Worthington made the statement to show that the crossing was not so important as the Local Board wished to make out.—Mr. WRIGHT pointed out that the railway company were under an agreement not to keep Waterloo-road crossing closed mere than four minutes, while there was no such agreement with regard to Anne-street crossing.—Mr. MARTLEY said the four minutes were ex- ceeded many times at Waterloo-road crossing.—The High- way Committee were instructed to deal with the matter.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The EXOINIAER in his report stated that as they were now entirely without coke he would re- commend that the price be increased from 7s to 8s per ton. The water in stock on April 18th, ISS3, was 6,188,702 gallons. The rainfall for the month has been, per gas yard gauge, 1.030 inches; per Pex Hill gauge, 1.115 inches; mean, 1 072 inches. Water pumped four weeks endingl 18th April, 1383 :—Stock's Well, 23,246,567 gallons; cor- responding period, 19th April, 1882, 27,522,072 gallons; decrease per cent., 15.53. Netherley, 9,088,162; 15,068,364; 39 69. Total, 32.334,729; 42,591,436; 2408. Water delivered, 35,190,049 ; 41.290,492; 1477. Gas made, 4,800,000 cubic feet; 4,871,000 cubic feet; 1.45. Gas delivered, 4,735,000; 4,791,000; HO. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 1595 candles. Thomas Johnson, Wigan, asked the lowest price for the double 181 n. Cameron pump, and it was recom- aneaded that £2OO be accepted for the pump as it stood. It was also recommended that the price for wagon loads of 1 coke be Bs. per ton in yard, until further notice. A cor- respondence with Messrs. J. Nicholson and Sons had taken place with reference to the carriage of spent oxide, which had hitherto been paid by the Board, and the committee recommended that the Board pay one-half of the carriage of the oxide ready to be returned. The engineer was instructed to attend the annual meeting of the Gas , Institute at Sheffield at the cost of the Board. It was ' recommended that Mr. A. Redfern's salary be increased from 465 $O £BO per annum. ...., L Aluctrutitst moved, and Ar. EII3TE2 secluded the confirmation of the minutes. Ia reply to questions, Mr. PANIECHIIRST said the recommendation with regard to spent oxide, if adopted, would save the Board £75. The engineer was attending the meeting of the GAS Institute because he

would there receive most valuable information with regard to the latest improvements in gas manufacture and every- thing connected therewith. Redfern had been a servant of the Board for five years and had not had an increase during that period. Hs had now a great deal more work than he had before, and the c)mneittee thought his services deserved an increase. 3he minutes were passed.
THE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.-A DEMUR.- THE CHAIRMAN'S POSITION.

On the minutes of this committee coming up for confir- mation, Mr. Sam,En said he bad stated at the cotaraittee meeting that it was Hot necessary for Mr. Hindley to go to London with regard to the Ship Canal Bill, and subsequent events had proved he was right, because on Monday a tele- gram came to the Board's offices saying the thin was 4- 'ready settled and that Mr. flindley's presence was not te- quired in London. He also objected to the appointinent on another ground. When the matter WaS undcr discussion a letter was read front Mr. H. W. Deacon, in which he stated he was going to Loudon on behalf of the Traders' Associa- tion, and as their ciente was no different from the Board's he objected to Mr. Handley going. He believed that if it 'had not been for some remarks that fell from the chairman Mr. Handley would not have been appointed to the deputa- tion. When the letter was read he remembered the chair- man saying, "Mr. Handley, you had better go," and the committee had no choice in the matter. He granted that a motion was afterwards put to the committee, but he held that it was pushed down their throats.—Mr. HANDLEY: Mr. Gossage said "Will you go, Mr. Handley ?"—Mr. SADLER: I believe that if Mr. Gosaage had not used those remarks the effect would have been quite different, because members voted for the recommendation that would not have done.— The CHAIRMAN said when he sat as chairman of the Board or as chairman of a committee, he was only as one member. He really did not think he made use of the terms men- tioned by Mr. Sadler. He might have said, and he thought he did say, that it would be more courteous on the part of the Board to send someone to assist Mr. Deacon who was going to London. He hod sent for the letter which had been referred to, but he was of opinion that it stated that Mr. Deacon hoped someone from the Local Board woud joitt him to make his hands stronger, or something to that effect. During the discussion it was stated that Mr. Midweod would be in London, and his (the chairman's) impression was that he would be sufficient, but it afterwards transpired that Mr. Midwood could not attend to the matter as he would be engaged in the Court of Chancery. He then certainly named Mr. Handley, but he should be sorry to occupy the position of chairman of that Board, or of any committee, if any member of the Board considered he had any desire or ever made any attempt to cram any matter down their throats. If the "lumbers of the Ratepayers' ASSOciation having seats on the Local Board were not men enough to state their opinions and vote on them, there was nothing to be said. When a man spoke from the chair, or anywhere around the table, he speaks only for himself.' It was for the Board to affirm what he states, or vete against it. Whenever a vote was taken at the committee or the Board, he accepted it as representing the feeling of those present at the meeting.—Mr. SADLER said what he meant was that the person who occupied the choir weitded a great influence over the members—The CHAIRMAN now obtained Mr. Deacon's letter, a portion of which he read. It etated that Mr. Deacon hoped that 80M' members of the Local Board would be able to go with him and see the promoters and get the clause filially settled. lie (the chairman) was still of opinion that it was necessary that someone from the Board should go to London. If he had been able to go he should have asked the Board to allow him to do co, as chairman of the Board. Mr. Handley did attend, and be- fore the passing of the minutes he thought it would be as well if Mr. Handley would explain what was done in Lon- don. Another member of the Traders' Association, besides Mr. Deacon, thought the nutter was important enough as to give a full day of his private business to attend before the House of Commons on behalf of the traders —Mr. HANDLEY said he went to London and saw Mr. Dtvies, who informed him that he had settled terms, but said it was necessary for someone to go up on behalf of the Local Vnird. It turned out that they did not want anyone but

_ accidents sometimes happened, and it was a proper thing for a person to represent the Board. He went to London by the request of the committee, and he stated most distinctly that Mr. Gossage did not say "You must go, Mr. Handley.", His words were "Will you go, Mr. Handley ?" and he re- plied "If it is the request of the c,,intnittee I will cf,o."—Tile CHAIRMAN said he might say that it was Mr. Timmis who was in London, and they knew that Mr. Timmis was not a man who usually threw his time away.—Tiae minutes were passed.

HEILTET COMMI r TEE. The minutes of this committee contained the Medical Officer's report for April. It stated that there had been 96 births and 31 deaths, the latter including 10 children under one year, and nine between one and tire years. Zymotic diseases caused two deaths. The birth-rate was 40 per 1,000, and the death-rate 14.9 per 1,000. 'The Market Super- intendent reported that the receipts tor lest month were £32 103 101, being an increase of LL lie 5d as compared with April, 1883, There were now four shops let; and the re- ceipts from the fair ground amounted to £l9 63 61—In moving the adoption of the minutes, Dr. O'KEEFFE said the death-rate of the United Kingdom for 1652 was 1962. per 1,000, England and Wales 22 6, and Widnes 20 5. For the first quarter cf 1833 the death-rate for the United Kingdom was 22.6 per 1,000, for England and Wales 22.3, and for Widnes 19.4.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: _ TILE SEWAGE COMMITTEE AND TEE coNntAcron.
div.p: _ TILE SEWAGE COMMITTEE AND TEE coNntAcron.

At an adjourned meeting of the Sewerage Committee, held on the 4th May, Mr. Pierpoint attended and explained what had been done during the past month, and the re- commendations in his report. Instructions were given to Mr. Copland to prepare quantities, specifications, and draw- ings for the main sewer from Little Briton to Simm's Cross. The Clerk reported having, w,th Mr. Handley, called upon Mr. Rowcliffe, solicitor to the Leigh estate, re extension of time for completion of sewer, and the result was considered eatisfactory.—Mr. CAREY moved the adoption of the minutes, and the motion having been seconded, Mr. SADLER said it had been stated that £5O or £OO worth of bricks had been taken away from the sewerage works and used in a certain works in Widnes. He should like to know whether it was true or not ; the report was general.—Mr. JOHNSON remarked that the committee had four men engaged in the oversight af the work. They would soon have all managers or overseers instead of workmen. Referring to the instruc- tions to Mr. Copeland, he thought it would he wise to get one sewer finished before they launched into a second one —Mr. Cb.RRY said the matter with regard to the bricks he naderstood to be simply this. The bricks had been ordered by the Local Board for the purposes of the sewer from a brickrnaking firm at Buckley. The bricks had been delivered by that firm. As they were delivered they were counted and charged for, and Mr. Jeffrey's men accepted the count. The bricks were in Mr. Jeffrey's own hands; in one sense the bricks were his pro- perty. That was to say he paid for the whole of the bricks, and only got paid by the Board by the measurement of the brick work which be had done, so that unless he was using a great portion of these bricks on some other job, and so ap- portioned the account that the Bard had against him, the Board were perfectly right. He (Mr. Carey) believed Mr. Jeffrey asked the resident engineer, Mr. Copeland, if he nsight have some of the bricks for some work somewhere or other. Mr. Copeland said "No ; I cannot without the con- sent of the Board." Mr. Jeffrey then helped himself to the bricks, and used abut £5O or £OO worth. Mr. Jeffrey was respeinsible for the bricks, and he (Mr. Carey) did not see that the Board would suffer in the slightest. The com- mittee, however, wrote him a peremptory letter, siying that on no account whatever had he to take any bricks, so that he (Mr. Carey) presumed that he would not take any more. 1 Replying to Mr. Johnson, Mr. Carey said the committee had not yet determined when Mr. Pierpoint should leave, and Mr. Capeland resume duties as resident engineer of work number 1. The work Mr. Copeland had now in hand would occupy him bra fortnight or three weeks.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £1,992 is. 31, and on the motion of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. SA.DLRR, the minutes were adopted.—This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was bald on Wednesday under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Present—Rev. Father Fannelly, Messrs. James Simpson, T. Nortnny J. Pritchard, P. Briscoe, and R. Lea.

div.head: CLERK.
div.p: THE CLERK.

The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. F. Rigby, the clerk, stating that owing to the sudden death of his sister he had had to leave home for Paris. He also wrote that owing to the want of co-operation the Shrewsbury Confer- ence respecting the establishment of Truant schools for the district had fallen through.

div.head: TILE BOARD AND WATERLOO uorsm.
div.p: TILE BOARD AND WATERLOO uorsm.

A letter was read from the Commissioners stating that they had decided to remove from their present offices to Waterloo House, where there was ample accommodation for all the public offices in the town. A committee had made a suitable appropriation of the rooms, and they wished to say that they would be glad if the School Bard could eel their way to take the offices at a rent to be agreed upon hereafter. The Waterloo House Committee would be glad to meet a deputation of the Board at an early day.—Mr. NORMAN spoke of the great advantages which were likely to accrue it the School Board and other public offices in the town were brought together under one roof. Waterloo House would make a good town hall and be a great saving to the ratepayers.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the School Board held their present offices on a lease of ten years, which commenced on the 31st December, 1877. There were thigeOrc several years unexpired.—Mr. SIMPSON' observed thai perhaps the CommissionerS would allow the School Board to have offices in Waterloo House free of rent during the period that the lease for the present offices had yet to run. Supposing, however, that these offices could be let, the Commissioners might claim the rent.—Other members of the Board spoke in favour of the removal to Waterloo House. It was generally thought it would be an advantage to the Board and a saving to the ratepayers.—dr. PRIT- CHARD said some alteration would have to be made in the rooms appropriated for school board purposes. He did not think the rooms the Commissioners proposed were worth £25 per annum.—Mr. BOWYER said the Board require a room to accommodate 30 persons at the meetings of the School Attendance Committee.—lt was decided that Mr. Simpson, Father Fennelly, and the Clerk meet the Waterloo House Committee, and discuss the propriety of taking rooms for school board purp3ses at Waterloo House.

div.head: AN APPLICATION.
div.p: AN APPLICATION.

The Superintendent of the Rigged School wrote asking for the use of the Board School on Whit-Monday, and also asking the Board to be kind enough to allow a class room to be used for the purposes of a penny bank on Saturday nights.—The first request was granted, but the second was deferred for a month. VISITORS' REPORT.

Mr. BOWYEU read the following report :—Returns from the public elementary schools for April, 1883. Certificated Government accommodation, 2,716; total number on the rolls, 2,928; number on the rolls corresponding period of last year, 2,803; increase in the number on the rolls, 125 ; total average attendance, 2,139 2; average attendance cor- responding period of last year, 2,006 8; increase in average attendance, 132 4; per eentage of attendance, 73; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252 ; increase in average at- tendance as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 8872; accommodation in excess of average attendance 576 8 ; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 212; number in attendance at private ad- venture schools, under 9.1. per week. 60. In the returns for the past month ending April 27th, you will notice that there is an improvement in the attendance of boys and girls; the attendance of infants is still below the usual percentage. Sickness has somewhat abated, and parents are beginning to send their children more regularly. During the past month I have taken a census of that portion of Halton- within-Runcorn, which has recently been added to the school district. The increased district contains 38 families, and the number of children from 3 to 13 years of age is 31; the number from sto 13, 20. All children of school age, with the exception of five, were in attendance at the various schools in the town. Those not attending I have served notices on the parents. In that portion of Halton-within- Runcorn, in the Mill Brow district, which has always been very complicated, there has been no alteration. I have also a list of incorrigibles to report, which it will again be necessary to deal with before the magistrates. This list I lay before you, showing their attendance for the past four months. Thera was no other business.
