A STORY OF LOVE, 'LAZINESS, AND
LIQUOR.

determined-looking man, was Robert Mulholland, a tp:l, charged on warrant at. Warrington Borough Court, yester- day, with having, on 9th inst., assaulted and beaten his wife, Mary.—Frorn the etatetnent of Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for the prosecutrix, it seemed the parties had been married six years; but those years had been years of great misery and abuse for the prosecutrix. The prisoner had travelled considerably, apd about six years ago arrived in Warrington from America. He met the prosecutrix, then a buxom widow, and was enamoured by her charms. She was, however, encumbered with six children, but as these were counterbalanced by a furniture broking shop and a well- patronised lodging-house kept by the prosecutrix, he married her. The family had since been increased by two more children which had been borne to the prisoner; bet during the last three years he had done no work, and had subjected his wife to continual abuse. Recently he had suffered ten weeks' imprison- ment for his illusage of the prosecutrix, to whom the magistrates granted a reparation order, but on leaving poi he came beck, wept before the house, and begged to be taken in. The pro- secutrix was obdurate for a time, but Tie cried the whole of Sunday, and at length the tears melted the heart of the prosecutrix, who, unfortunately for herself, Mr. Davies said, forgave him and took him in. Since then the prisoner had not only been master of the house, but of the whale sitaation. He took the money from the lodgers, stole and sold a box the property of the wife on Wednesday, and with the proceeds he got drunk. He then went to the house, ran at his wife, knocked her down on the sofa, caught her by the throat and almost throttled her, knelt upon her, and otherwise roughly abused her. The wife screamed, and her elder daughter went to her assistance, but although she was suffering from St. Vitus's dance, the prisoner "threw" her through the door, and she fell to the ground. The prosecu- trix did not wish the prisoner to be committed to gaol, as she believed him to be ill, and thought he would die.—Pro- secutrix stated that if she got over this she would never let him in the house again.—Captain Reynolds: You won't let him in if he cries week, then? (Laughter.)—Prisoner was committed to gaol for fourteen days, and the magistrates said it would be for the woman herself to carry the separa- tion order out.
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT WARRINGTON: OPPOSITION BY MR. DIGGLE.

A meeting of ratepayers to consider the resolution passed by the Town Council in reference to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and to sanction the cost of opposing the Bill in Committee, was behl at Warrington Public Hall, on Tues- day evening. The Mayor (Councillor Crosfield) presided, and there were also present the ex-Mayor (Alderman Pick- mere), Aldermen Davies, Burgess, Kean, Harrison, and Web- ster, Councillors Greening, Brown, Litton, Caldwell; Dakin, Whittle, W. Pierpoint, Barker, and Francomb, Messrs. C. J. Morris, T. Morris, John Fairclough, E. Bolton, F. A. Roberts, J. Ellison, Rev. S. Wilkinson, S. Davies, J. C. Ridgway, James Fairclough, H. Fairclough, J. T. Picton, W. Diggle, J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), drc. The MAYOR, after explaining that the meeting was called to authorise the Corporation to appear before the Commit- tee of the House of Commons that was considering the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill, read the following letter which Councillor Broadbent bad written to the Town Clerk :—"I am extremely sorry not to be well enough to attend the meeting to-night to support the Mayor. I quite approve of the course he has taken in the interests of Warrington dur- ing the ship canal negotiations. I feel sure that the meet- ing to-night may safely and heartily support the course that the Mayor recommends far adoption." He then read the following resolution :—" The Council of this borough, hav- ing been advised that the provisions of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill are prejudicial to the interests represented by them, and the Council having on the 17th day of April last unanimously resolved to take all necessary proceedings, as may be deemed expedient, for the due protection of the rights and interests of the borough of Warrington as represented by them—it is resolved that the resolution passed by the Council at the meeting held on the 17th day of April, 1883, be approved and confirmed; and that the Council do take all necessary steps before Par. ' liament in opposition to the Bill for the due protection of , the rights and interests of this borough; and that the costs, charges, and expenses incurred, and to be incurred thereby, be charged upon the borough fund and borough rate." For the benefit of the public in Warrington he might say that the meeting was called to autho-ise the expenditure of money by the Town Council in defending the interests of Warring- ton as affected by the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The Council did not wish the inhabitants of Warrington to imagine that they were opposed in any way to an improved water communication between Manchester and the sea, and between Warrington and the sea; but there were certain interests affected—seriously affected—by the Manchester I canal scheme, which it was their bounden duty to protect.' There were four principal points that they had had under consideration. The first one was the making of swing bridges, one over Wilderspool-road, and the other over Knutsford-road. In reference to this the Council objected to the inconvenience—the serious inconvenience—that the public would be put to seeing that the whole of the traffic from Cheshire into Warrington might be very seriously interrupted by these two swing bridges The next point that they considered was the navigation of the river. The promoters gave the Council pretty good satisfaction as far as that was con- cerned; but the next point as to the quality of the water was a matter upon which it was very difficult indeed for the promoters to meet the Council. [Mr. Diggle: Hear, hear. j The promoters hardly dared to say that the quality of the water, after the canal was made, would be equal t) the quality of the water now; and he did not think that any- thing less than that would satisfy the Corporation or the manufacturers of Warringq.on. (Hear, hear.) He need not tell those present that the river water was inestimable in value to the Warrington manufacturers—(hear, hear); and if that water was saturated with brine and rendered unfit for steam boiler purposes it might have the effect of shutting up most of the large manufactories in town. (Hear, hear.) He took it that the Town Council were bound to protect the manufacturers as far as possible.' (Hear, hear.) The fourth point was as to the sewerage which he need not tell them was a most important point, because if the river was silted up, as it was quite possible it might be, and there was a largo accumulation of sewage matter in the river at Bank Quay, it might in hot weather produce fever, and do very serious damage to the inhabitants of the town. He just mentioned these points that the public might know that the Council had not need- lessly opposed the Manchester canal scheme. All they had done had been done to maintain their present rights and privileges, and it was impossible to do that without some expenditure. The Council were bound to engage an en- gineer and counsel to represent them before the Committee of the House of Commons. He therefore hoped that everyone present and the ratepayers generally would consider that the Council bad only done their duty in the course they had taken. He moved the resolution which he , had read. I

Mr. Tllos. Mounts seconded the motion, and pointed oat the importance of maintaining the present quality of the river water, remarking that if they did not do so it would nymn the total closing of the manufactories in the town. Alderman DAvius supported the motion, and repeated the arguments he used at the Council meeting as to the incon- venience of the swing bridges. The MAYOR then asked if anyone wished to speak to the resolution, and - -

Mr. W. DIM:ME, who occupied a prominent position on the platform, rose amid loud applause. The veteran oppon- ent of local public improvements had got as far as "Mr. Mayor," when he was greeted with "Be as short as you can, Mr. Diggle, please," from the Mayor. "Oh," drawled Mr. Diggle, "that's a nice sort of thing to say before I start. If I had been slow you might have said something !" He went on te remark that "he knew what public meetings were," when he was met with an ironical cry of " Speak up." The inflammatory speeches of Councillor Mackie, Alderman Davies, and others, he declared, had got them into "this mess," for they offered subscriptions and seemed to go on without any consideration at all. But, he said, with a knowing looking which created much amusement, "he saw things from the beginning," and that meeting might have been avoided if the Council "had taken a proper course." "Pay your share," cried some one in the meeting. "I shall have to do," mournfully responded Mr. Diggle. "I am a ratepayer of about £5O a year, and therefore my share will be something." Amid laughter, he asserted that the canal would neither benefit Manchester nor Warrington, and if there was time he would show them why. This caused the Mayor to remark " We don't want that to-night," to which Mr. Diggle sharply replied "I am a ratepayer." The Mayor said he was aware of that fact, but they were not going to discuss the merits of the canal scheme. Mr. Diggle stated that he was only giving hisopinion, and asked, what was to become of Howley Quay during the construction of the canal ?—The MAYOR : This meeting is not to discuss that.—Mr. DIGGLE : Oh, you have only given a few ' opinions and nothing else.—The MAYOR: I have only given the public a few of the points we consider most im- portant. We are here asking you to sanction the Council appearing before the House of Ccmmons. What you are saying has nothing to do with it.—Mr. DIGGLE: I will show you it has something Co do with it.—Ths MAYon : Are you going to support this resolution or not ?—Mr. DIGGLE : I am going to enlaree upon it and then I will sup- port it. (Loud laughter.) He then said one great point for consideration was the Manchester sewage, and another that the canal would be a long way from Warrington.—The MAYOR : These points have nothing to do with the words ,f the resolution which I have just moved. You must al— low me to put the resolution first, and than if you want to make a speech afterwards yen can do so.—Mr. DIGGLE : Thank you. (He then resumed his seat.) The resolution was then put to the vote and carried un- animously. On the motion of Councillor LITTON, seconded by Alder- man DAVIES, a vote of thanks was passed to the Mayor for presiding, and the proceedings terminated, to the amusement of the audience, one of whom exclaimed " Diggle's done

again." Mr. Diggle, however, was not to be " done " out of his speech. He remained in sole possession of the platform, and proudly asserting that he "was master now," proceeded to harangue about fifty of the audience who staved to enjoy the fun. He referred satirically to the speeches made at the meeting of workingmen when "Alderman Davies act, i as showman," and emphatically stated that the workingmen would not benefit from the scheme in the least. He ridiculed the remark that young ladies should not have young men

for sweethearts if they had no shares in the canal, and strongly advised workingmen to keep their money in their pockets. Mr. Diggle was asked if he had any money in his, when he said he could show £l,OOO, but he doubted whether the person who asked the question could do so. Mr. Diggle was plied with numerous questions, which he at once answered instead of giving the reasons her his opposition to the scheme; and when he thought he had given his ques- tioners a clencher be placed his bands beneath his coat tails and proudly strode about the platform. This practice caused one.gentleman to ask whether that was " a meeting or a monkey show," a remark that provoked much merri- ment. Mr. Diggle, however, always proved himself equal to the occasion, and his stinging retorts kept the audience in roars of laughter. The speaker boldly asked if there was no one who dare ascend the platform and discuss the matter with him ; but as no person offered to do so be said they were all cowards. At length there were cries of "turn the gas out," but Mr. Diggle said they dare not as the Mayor , had given him the privilege of speaking. Of this privilege he availed himself until everyone was satisfied, when a vote , of thanks was proposed to him for his speech, but he I haughtily said he would not accept a vote of thanks from the person who proposed it, and who it may be remarked had subjected Mr. Diggle to considerable "chaff." As no one else proposed a vote of thanks, Mr. Diggle descended the platform, and as he made his way out be was asked if he was going to be called as a witness for the opposition, but he replied that he did not know.

MR. L. FILDES' PICTURE, THE "VILLAGE WEDDING." The Stnalard, referring to this picture, says—Mr. Fildes comes before the world very prominently through his one contribution to the present Academy. " The Village Wed- ding "(No. 515) will say little to the honest nailids who, as the Idler tells us, by the excitement of an artificial fas- tidiousness are debarred from pleasure ; it will appeal not at all to those whom a little dangerous learning has mOt "too wise to concur with their own sensations." But the pub- lic, which makes little claim to special culture in these matters, and many of those whose culture is extended beyond the boundaries of a remote art, will agree in enjoy- ing Mr. Fildes' presentation of some of the healthiest girls and best hearted banipkins and funniest humours of an Eng- , lish village. This is one of the pictures which help to sus- tain a reputation, probably even to add to it. In a subject in which it would have been so easy to have gone wrong at every turn the painter has held his own. He has neither yielded to the facile seductions of sentimentality nor fallen into the grosser vices of caricature. In the abundant realism of his picture he has not ceased to be artistic, and his artistic effects are obtained with no too obvious sacrifice of natural truths. The Daily News says :—ln the Fifth Gallery, we come to the" Piazza" (477). The painter crowds the Piazza of St. , Mark's, in Venice, with colour, character, a host of national types, portraits, blonde Venetian girls, a rainbow of coloured costumes, an embroglio of faces, all subtly discriminated. The work is not of the sort which we prefer; but its clever- ness, claboratenees, and brilliance are undeniable. Very much the same qualities, done out of Italian into English, and made British and blowsy, mark Mr. Fades' " Village Wedding" (515), a noisy, jolly procession of bride and bridegroom, and buxom girls, and brown, well-fed boys, dressed in all the crude contrasts of rural splendour. It is admirable, it is" immense," and we hope Mr. Fildes will take Ihruer's advice" Never may he who fashioned with his craft this marvel, never may he fashion another like unto it."

The following is from the pen of the Liverpool Courier's London Correspondent :—Mr. Fildes has only one picture in the Academy," The Village Wedding." We have heard much of this picture for a long time past, and if I mistake not we shall hoar more of it in the future. Every face on the canvas possesses distinct individuality and life. I am in- clined to think that the picture will attract popular attention and be the talk of the Academy. It is the result obviously of immense labour, of great skill, and of a keen appreciation of English rural life. The Manchester Guardian thus comments on the picture: —This is a very noteworthy example of realistic invention, executed in a style that is strongly individual, and bearing testimony in every part of the composition to the most earnest and careful study. Mr. Fildes always has his heart in his work, and whatever may be the measure of success which he attains it is the result of sincere and honest labour. Per- haps the first observation that suggests itself in regard to the pictere is that it deserves and ought to have received more generous treatment at the hands of the Hanging Com- mittee. We shall not be suspected of exaggerated enthu- siasm for the particular idea in art by which it is inspired, but we must recognise at the same time that we have here a performance of uncommon power and ability, and that in the class of painting to which it belongs the .picture holds a position of undisputed pre-eminence. ft is in the true sense of the word a representative achievement, and there would seem to be no good reason why in an exhibition that is cer- tainly not overburdened with remarkable pictures it should not have been hung in a prominent place in the large gallery. The gay and busy scene Mr. Fildes has chosen to depict passes in the quiet street of a Berkshire village, along which the happy pair aad their friends press through an eager throng of interested spectators. In the front rank come the bride and bridegroom, obviously em- barrassed, not merely by tire novelty of the occasion, but also, and perhaps even more acutely, by the unaccustomed splendour of their new clothes. Behind them a stalwart guardsman, divided between the claims of gallantry and duty, supports on either arm the aged mother of the bride hnd a laughing girl, who is officiating as principal brides- maid, while still further off in the proeession follows the second bridesmaid, attired in freshly-starched muslin frock, and accompanied by the elders of the party, who walk with the air of men who have seen the world, and whose gaiety is tempered by dignity and experience. This group of the principal actors in the scene is supported and balanced by a crowd of supernumerary figures scattered on either side of the roadway. Young men and maidens, aged crones and tiny children, have all rushed taut to feast their eyes upon the splendid pageant, and on every face there is an , expression of eager curiosity which seems to betoken the conviction that such things do not occur every day, and that perhaps years may pass before the buff waistcoat and 1 shining hat of the blushing bridegroom shell again cast ' their meteoric brilliance upon the quiet village street. From a dramatic point of view Mr. Fildes has, we think, been en- tirely successful in his work, and if there is anything lacking in the result, the defect will only be felt by a class I of critics whom the picture was perhaps not designed to please. In a purely artistic sense the problem which the painter set himself was scarcely capable of complete solu- tion, for the taste of honest villagers when they desert their , garments of working-day life and seek for magnificence is I not the taste which recommends itself to a cultivated sense. 'Jibe faithful chronicler of such festive scenes is no doubt justified in reproducing the unhappy itints of scarlet and pink and mauve that are the accepted symbols of rustic gaiety; but when all due praise has been awarded to the spirit of unflinching accuracy with which the scene is pre- sented, the doubt will still remain as to whether art is well advised in undertaking a task which leaves no hope of beauty.

IA WARRINGTON SINGER ROBBED OF HER BANK BOOK. A young girl named Rosalie Vanderstock-, bookbinder, 5, All Saints'-street, was in custody at the Bolton Town Hall on Thursday forenoon for stealing a bank book and £ll, on March 21st, the property of Mrs. Lizzie Lawes, a singer, professionally known as Lizzie Tabra. Prisoner seems to have gone about the robbery in a very systematic manner. According to the statement of Mr. John Hall, borough pro- secutor, the prosecutrix formerly lodged with prisoner's mother, and it was during that time that she obtained pos- session of the bank book. Under this authority the girl went to the Post Office, Bradshawgate. Bolton, and gave notice that she intended to withdraw £l4 of the £4O men- tioned in the account. She filled up the necessary declara- tion, and four days afterwards again called at the office and drew the money, presenting the order received from London and signing the receipt as "Lizzie Lawes." The prosecutrix, a persm of very attractive appear- ance, then stated she was the wife of Harry Augustus Lawes, and that she and her hus- band were professional singers now living at 51, Buttermar- ket-streat, Warrington. They formerly tilled an engage- ment at the Victoria Theatre of Varieties, Bolton. She saw the bank book safe a few days prior to the theft being com- mitted, and certainly never gave prisoner authority to draw money from her account at the bank.—E. W. Gough, sort- ing clerk at the Post Office, proved giving prisoner a notice of withdrawal, and stated that anyone possessed of an ac- count in the Post Office Savings' Bank could make a with- drawal at any Post Office in the kingdom.—W. Tyldesley, another clerk, sai Ihe paid prisoner the .£l4, for which she produced the order, and gave the necessary receipt.—Mr. Fielding who was for the defence, said it was exceedingly difficult to urge anything on behalf of a girl who seemed to have been possessed of so much cunning in obtaining the money. He would, however, call medical testimony to prove that the girl had always been subject to some kind of mania, and that for years she had been treated as a paralytic patient. Her parents were highly respectable, and sire herself had received a good education at the Congregational school. It was almost absurd, however, to suppose she had received no help from persons out- side, for as he understood the bank book produced was the first one she had ever seen. On obtaining the money the girl went to Manchester, and thence with a girl she met with to London from the London-road Station. At the end of six weeks her mother received a letter saying that the girl was being maintained in some institute for the destitute in Lon- don, and Mrs. Vanderstock immediately forwarded sufficient money to pay for her return. Thd girl reached Manchester in care of the guard of the train, and ptisoner was then brought to Bolton.—Dr. Treadgold said he had attended pri- soner for several years. She was a confirmed epileptic, and after each fit was not quite accountable for her actions. By his instructions at such times great care was taken of her by her parents.—Mrs. Vanderstock said the girl had had 14 tits a day. For three weeks prior to the robbery the girl fol- lowed her occupation as a bookbinder, but had a fit on the Sunday night before the robbery was committed.—The Bench, after some consideration, said they must mark their sense of the gravity of the offence, and prisoner would be committed for three months' hard labour.

div.head: CLAIM BY A FRODSHAM LEGATEE.
div.p: CLAIM BY A FRODSHAM LEGATEE.

Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge of Warrington County Court, was occupied for a considerable time on Thursday afternoon in hearing a case in which Margaret Ellis, com- mercial Hotel, Frodeham, spinster, was plaintiff, and Wm. Worrell, Whitley Superior, smith, and Charles Chetwood Rose, of Lower Whitley, gentleman, defendants, "being a contract commenced in the High District Registry of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice, and sent by order of a Judge of Chambers, under section 7 of the County Court Acts 1867, to be tried at this court. To amount of legacy payable by defendants to plaintiff under the will of the late Margaret Percival, de- ceased, and interest thereon £BB 15a., received on account £5O, balance £3B 15s."—Mr. Taylor, solicitor, Chester, re- presented the plaintiff; and Mr. Fleming, barrister, Man- cheater (instructed by Messrs. Cobbett and Co.), appeared 1 for the defendant Worrell. His Honour said he did not know what position he held. This was a remitted case by order of Mr. Justice Stephens, and remitted to that court under the seventh section of Act 1867, as an action of con- tract. The particulars did not disclose any contract what- ever. It placed him under some difficulty. He did not know that he ought to sit in any way in judgment upon an order of Mr. Justice Stephens. Mr. Fleming said he had noticed the order, and was about to submit that it was sent down here as an action of contract from the common law side jurisdiction of the court; and he was about to submit that it came before his Honour as a common law, and not as an equity judge. They all knew an executor in a common law court could not be sued by a beneficiary under a will for a legacy. It might be said but this action having originally commenced in the High Court of Justice, which had power to decree all matters both in common law and equity, that objection would have no validity; but seeing the order which his Honour had already drawn attention to sending this action down upon contract, he submitted that was an insuper- able objection. His Honour thought he could not do otherwise than hear the case, but he thought it right to draw the attention of the parties to the order.—Mr. Tay- lor drew his Honour's attention to the fact that it was an order made at the instance of the defendants. His Honour: Still that does not affect the question of my juris- diction.—Ultimately his Honour decided to hear the case.—Mr. Taylor then said this was an action originally commenced in the Chester District Registry of the High Court of Jus- tice for the recovery of £3B 155., being the balance ef a legacy and interest due to plaintiff under the will of Mar- garet Percival, deceased. Defendants were the executors under that will, which was proved by them- on the 29th July, 1866, at Chester. The devise was as follows :—"Also I give and bequeath unto my two great nieces Margaret Ellis the sum of £5O of lawful money of Oreat Britain." Margaret Ellis, the plaintiff in this action, at the time of the death of the testatrix was five years of age, and her father saw Mr. Worrall, who was the acting executor, on the day of the funeral. Mr. Worrall suggested that this money should be paid into the Chester Savings Bank, but Mr. Ellis suggested the Warrington Savings Bank. To that Mr. Worrell seemed to assent, and it was always understhod that that money was invested the savings bank at Warlington. However, when Miss Ellis came of age, as ehe did in Sep- tember last, she applied for payment of her legacy. Then it transpired that the money had not been invested at all; but that Mr. Worrell held it in his own hands. Ultimately Mr. Worrell paid her £5O in the presence of Mr. Moore's clerk, Mr. Moore having been acting as solicitor of the executors from the first. She then asked for the interest which was due, at the rate of 4 per cent. Mr. Worrell made no statement in regard to there not tieing sufficient assets of the estate or anything of that kind ; but simply put her off 3aying they would consider the question of interest. It was arranged that they should meet in War- rington in reference to the interest, but they did not so meet, and Mr. Worrell made an offer to the father to pay the sum of £2O 45., being at the rate of 3 per cent. interest. This Mr. Ellis declined, saying he was entitled to 4 per cent., and it ought to be paid. Not a word was said about the estate being insolvent. On the contrary, a sister of the plaintiff whose legacy followed immediately that of plain- tiff, was actually paid her legacy of £25 and 3 per cent when she came of age. He contended this was a specific legacy which was really payable upon the will being proved, that was to say, if there was sufficieht in the estate to pay the legatees; and it was a first charge, that it ought to have been inwated, the legatee being a minor, until she came of age; and that it had been clearly laid down that four per cent. was the usual rate if interest.—Mr. Fleming said the broad outline of the facts did not require proving, because he admitted them. It was undoubtedly a fact that the plaintiff had this legacy left to her under this will of which the defendant Worrell, for whom he appeared, was one of the executors; and what he would say in regard to the offer that Mr. Taylor had mentioned of three per cent was this. Worrell was a black- smith, and unlettered, having no experience in business of this kind; and he did not know at the time the exact state of the account of the estate. He had been, to use his own words, pestered a great deal by the plaintiff's father about this legacy before the legatee came of age; and when she came of age he paid her the £5O. They, however, wanted not merely the legacy of £5O, but interest on it, which they demanded at the time; but the sum the plaintiff now sued for was at the rate of 5 per cent.—His Honour said that was so; but Mr. Taylor said it was a mistake, as they only asked for 4 per cent. Mr. Fleming said Worrall's offer of 3 per cent., which was refused, was made to buy peace, and was one which he submitted ought not to prejuuice him in his defence. Mr. Taylor had said this was a specific legacy, but it was obvious that it was a general legacy. The defence of Mr. Worrell was that he was quite anxious conscientiously to administer this estate, though at the time that he paid the plaintiff and her father the £5O he had not anything like that amount from the estate or property of the testatrix. He had even after th it payment overpaid the estate, and was out of pocket something like £l9 odd. His defence was that the sum of £5O which he had paid to the plaintiff when she came of age more than covered the legacy that she should then have had from the testatrix, with isiterest from the time the estate came into the hands of the executors; and that she, instead of taking action, was very fortunate indeed in receiving the full £5O which she had received from Mr. Worrall.—The defendant Worrall was then called, and examined as to a statement of account which had been prepared for him as executor. He stated that the assets which came into his hand: amounted to £292 12e. 61., and the disbursements had been £312 03. 5d., leaving a balance of £l9 is. 11. d, which he had overpaid. Defendant was cross-examined as to certain amounts which he had charge such as journeys to Chester, consultationi with solicitors' fetching the doctor, charges for sitting up with deceased, &c.—ln summing up his Honour reduced and disallowed several of these items, and as to the question of liability to pay intesest on the legacy, he said if defendant had money enough to pay this interest then no doubt he ought. Four per cent. seemed to him to be a reasonable sum to charge, and as it appeared to him defendant had sufficient money te meet the legacy after making the deductions he had already made from the account, he therefore gave a verdict for the plaintiff for £32 with costs.

TUE LANCASIIIIIE HUSSARS.—This regiment of yeomanry arrived in Southport on Monday afternoon for their annual eight days' training. The regiment consists of the A troop from Ashton-in-Makerfield, the B troop from St. llelens and Wigan neighbourhood, the C troop from Newton-le-Willows and Liverpool, and the D troop from Ormskirk, Latham, ttc. The regiment marched into the town under command of Major Earle. The inspcction will take place to-day (Saturday.)

div.head: WARRINGTO-N ROGUE AND VAGABOND.
div.p: A WARRINGTO-N ROGUE AND VAGABOND.

An rxernplary sentence was passed on a Warrington family deserter at the Borough Court, yesterday. Michael Fogarty, puddler, was charged before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White, with having in May, last year, run away from the borough and left his three children charge- able to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer, who prosecuted, said three of the prisoner's chil- dren were admittei to the Workhouse for the first time on 25th October, 1870, and the prisoner was sent to gaol on the 9th January, 1880. The children were again admitted in August, and two of them had remained in the Workhouse ever since, one haying been taken out by some friends in February, this year. A warrant had been issued for the ap- prehension of the prisoner, and it had been all over the country. The prisoner's family had cost the ratepayers £ll2 9s. 6d., and in addition to that there was a reward of £3 offered for tne prisoner's apprehension.—The Assistant- Clerk (Mr. A. Brown) : Have you (prisoner) anything to say why you should not be convicted as a rogue and vagabond ?—Prisoner: Nothing.—The Chief- Constable said if there was one man more than another for the apprehension of whom the police had been to great trouble, besides expense, it was the prisoner. It was wonder- ful how the prisoner had escaped. The police had hounded him down, and then at last he surrendered himself to the Macclesfield police. Even last week Inspector Berry was close upon the prisoner's heels in Manchester, but he got away.—Captain Reynolds: Is be very cunning in eluding you P—lnspe:tor Berry said there was some one on the watch for him.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner could not get bread, and had therefore surrendered himself. He WAS four times convicted in 1880 for various offences, and once for neglecting his wife and family.—Captain Reynolds said the prisoner would be committed for three months' imprisonment, with hard labour.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write May 10th) :

Except for some compulsory cleating out, and the stir It has occasioned, there is no amelioration of the condition of the share markets to be noticed. Business is dull, and prices in th great majority of oases are further depreciated, the instances where any improvement in figures is marked being very excep- tional. The weather lends no help, being miserably unsea-on able, and should it continue so during next week must seriously affect railway traffics during the holidays. The effect produced by the continued cold has also a wider area, azrcul- tural prospects being darkened, and fears entertained for the safety of the harvest, on the success of which trade so much depends Fears of disasters at the settlement, which concludes to-morrow, have, with the usual curtailment of business dur- ing the arrangement of the aco iunts, all helpe I to make the market sluggish; forced sales, though producing transactions, being by no means an exhilarating agency. Movements in the several clssses of miscellaneous shares tell the same tale, lower prices being in great majority, the only exceptions being in banks and canals, which show steadiness and, in the latter. improvement. Foreign Funds are irregular, and only frac- tionally altered. Mexican rails have shared the common fate, being If down on the week.

COAL, JEON, &C., AND- MINING shares continue to recede In value generally, there being only one instance in which any advance is made, viz , Nant-y-glo and Blaina efe,red, whilst I there are several concerns whose quotations exh.bit decline. 'LEWIS'S TN LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVIDING Ott THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, , HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGH- OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM, Who are Lewis's? Well, lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known in London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago, and lewia's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of prc curing a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints, and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at 'last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such a change for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make the sale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20,000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future t.s make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other prioe Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite price with Lewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public fis and 2s 8d for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every householder to the great advantage there is in buying Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength es very great, that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tt a; they are sure to be satisfied and astonished with the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; It is only to send 2s in stamps to i ewls's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, peeked neatly in a boa. mriar paid, to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewis's in Liverpool.
